en: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna*, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command. Chapter One:
The Nidāna. A Summary Verse for the General Overview of the Main Section states:
First, the explanation of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*); next, the distribution of the belongings of the deceased;
the circular altar and the door-bolt; and the five gates of the Bodhisattva image.
Regarding the first section, the general summary verse states:
Knowing the number of days since full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), not entering the earth when boundaries are distinct,
the five groups of monks dwelling at the edge of a boundary, and not cutting raw hide or eating raw meat.
The summary verse for the first section says:
The appearance of one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), whether male or female; one who has not received full ordination acting as a preceptor;
the ten difficulties and so forth where there is no preceptor; "Do not confer [ordination] upon me, for I am seven years old.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Upāli approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. Joining his palms in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“If a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon another, and that person’s gender changes, is it considered a valid ordination?
The Buddha said, “This is indeed a valid ordination; one should transfer them to the community of bhikṣuṇīs.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

if a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon another man, yet this man utters a woman’s voice, possesses a woman’s intention, and assumes a woman’s appearance and manner, can this person be said to have received full ordination?"
The Buddha said, "Upāli! This is a full ordination;
the bhikṣus who performed it have committed an offense against the Dharma."

"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon another woman, yet this woman utters a male voice, possesses a male intention, and assumes a male form and appearance, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes the conferral of full ordination; all the bhikṣuṇīs [involved] incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
[He asked: "If one who has not received full ordination is appointed as the preceptor (upādhyāyī), does that person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes the conferral of full ordination; the bhikṣus have committed an offense against the Dharma.
[The questioner asked: "If a person has a difficulty and declares, 'I have it,' and the bhikṣus confer full ordination upon him, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not called 'having received full ordination' (upasampadā), and the bhikṣus incur an offense against the Dharma.
[The questioner asked: "If a person has no physical impediments but falsely claims they do, and the bhikṣus grant him full ordination, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes the conferral of full ordination; the bhikṣus have committed an offense against the Dharma.

[The questioner asked: "If a person who actually has obstacles declares, 'I have no obstacles,' and the bhikṣus confer full ordination upon him, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination; the bhikṣus have committed no offense.

[The questioner asked: "If a person truly has no obstacles and further declares that they have none, and the bhikṣus confer full ordination upon them, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said,
"This is called 'properly received.
If a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon one who has gone forth but has not yet received the ten precepts, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes an acceptance; all bhikṣus shall incur an offense against the Dharma.

[He asked: "If, at the time a person receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is not present, and the bhikṣus confer full ordination upon them, does this person count as having received full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"This is a valid reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*), yet those bhikṣus incur an offense against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
"If, at the time of receiving full ordination, a person speaks as follows:"
"If one says, 'Do not grant me full ordination,' yet the bhikṣus nevertheless confer it upon him, does this person count as having received full ordination?
The Buddha said:
"If one has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*), all bhikṣus incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
"As the Blessed One has said:
'If a person is seven years of age and is able to drive away crows, they should be granted the going forth (*pravrajyā*')."
"O Virtuous One! If there is a youth only six years of age who is able to drive away crows and birds from the monastic kitchen, should this person be granted ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"Even if they have reached seven years of age, this [ordination] should not be granted.
[The question was asked: "If one has reached seven years of age but cannot drive away crows, may they be granted the going forth?"
The Buddha said: "It should not;
it is permitted because it can drive away crows.
The second son’s summary verse says:
The number of days should always be known; on the day of the formal announcement (*ārocana*), the night must be subtracted.
On the sixth and eighteenth days, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) should not be performed too frequently.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. There were Brahmins and householders who went to the place of the Bhikṣus and asked them:
“Ārya! What day is it today? He replied:
“I do not know. The people said to him,
“O Noble One!”
The various classes of non-Buddhists are thoroughly proficient in the calculation of days and the science of astrology; you, too, ought to know the number of days and the constellations.
Why have you gone forth as renunciants without understanding these?
He remained silent and did not answer.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to know the number of days and the movements of the stars and constellations."
At that time, all the bhikṣus studied astrology and mathematics; consequently, they became distracted and neglected the cultivation of wholesome deeds. The Buddha said:
"Only one person should be permitted to study these."
Although they heard the Buddha’s teaching, they did not know who should perform the counting.
The Buddha said:
"The foremost elder of the assembly should be ordered to count them."
At that time, the Elder had forgotten the count, and even the administrative officer could not remember it. The Buddha said:
"You may make clay beads or bamboo tally-sticks; prepare fifteen of them and move one each day."
When he did so, it was scattered by the wind. The Buddha said:

"One should take fifteen bamboo slips, each about four or five finger-widths long, pierce a hole at one end, thread them with a cord, and hang them in a prominent place on the wall, moving one each day."
Then the entire assembly together moved the counting sticks (*śalākā*).
The Buddha said, "The senior monk (*sthavira*) and the administrative officer (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) should move them.
At that time, a Brahmin householder came to where the bhikṣus were and asked:
"Noble One! What day is it today? He replied:
"You may now question the Elder and the administrators. The people replied,
"Do you also have those who take turns on duty to oversee the day?"
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and gave no answer.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should make a formal announcement (jñapti) to inform all the people."
At that time, the bhikṣus made their formal announcements (jñapti) in various places. The Buddha said:
"One should not make formal announcements in various places; rather, when the assembly has gathered, one should perform the announcement before the elder (sthavira), saying:
'The Great Assembly should know:'"
"Today is the first day of this month.
When the laypeople heard this, they said again,
"How can you not mention the division of the fortnights into the dark and bright halves?"
He replied, “I did not.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should refer to the waxing and waning phases of the moon.
It should be stated as follows:
When the great assembly has gathered in the afternoon, let one bhikṣu stand with palms joined before the elder, and with single-minded reverence, make this formal announcement (jñapti):"
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today is the first day of the dark fortnight; you should each recite pure and sublime verses from the Sūtras for the sake of the donors who have built this monastery, the devas who protect the monastery, and the devas who have long resided here.”
At that time, although the bhikṣus made their daily proclamations, they did not mention the names of the donors who had built the monasteries. The Buddha said:

"You must mention the names of the donors who built the monasteries, and you should also mention the names of the donors who provide the meal for the following day; this will cause the merit and virtue of those donors to increase boundlessly according to their wishes."

If there are other donors, they should all be addressed in the same manner; likewise, the various classes of celestial beings, the eight divisions of spirits, teachers, monks, and parents should all have their names invoked, extending the merit universally to all sentient beings so that the benefits and blessings of all may increase.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they each recited this verse of purity:
"Whoever practices giving shall surely obtain its benefit;
If one gives for the sake of happiness, one will certainly attain peace and joy in the future."
"The meritorious retribution of a bodhisattva is as inexhaustible as space;
having bestowed such gifts, one attains such fruits, increasing them without ceasing.
At that time, there was a donor who invited the bhikṣus to provide an offering. When the bhikṣus learned of this, they did not announce the donor's name or residence. The Buddha said:
"One should announce the donor's name in advance, saying:
'A certain donor will provide a meal for the great assembly tomorrow; he resides at such-and-such a place!'"
Furthermore, there were brahmins and householders who went to where the bhikṣus were and asked:
"Venerable ones! What day is it today?"
He replied, "It was the fifteenth day. He asked again:
"The people of the time all say it is the fourteenth day; how can you, venerable sirs, say it is the fifteenth?
Is it possible that the bhikṣus do not perform the reduction of the night? They replied:
"I shall not do so. Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should shorten the night."
At that time, as the bhikṣus repeatedly shortened the night during the fortnightly observances,
a layperson asked, "Noble ones!
What day is it today?"
He replied, "There are fourteen. The other said:
"Noble ones! Everyone at this time says it is the fifteenth day; why do you venerable ones repeatedly shorten the night every half-month?
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“You should not shorten the nights more frequently than once every half-month.

Rather, you must calculate the time such that the shortening occurs after the half-month has passed; that is, from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the second month constitutes one month.”

From the sixteenth day of the second month until the end of the month—that is, the half-month—one night is subtracted to constitute a "small month"; all other months follow this pattern. Because the systems of the East and West differ, there are thus six days in a year that are the fourteenth day, and six days that are the fifteenth day for the purpose of the *poṣadha* (fortnightly confession).
At that time, some brahmins and householders came and asked the bhikṣus,
"Venerable ones! What month is it now?"
He replied, "It is now the month of Śrāvaṇa, from the sixteenth day of the fifth month until the fifteenth day of the sixth month. He asked again:
“Venerable ones!

All people say that the month of Āṣāḍha runs from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, yet you say it is the month of Śrāvaṇa; could it be that you do not observe the intercalary month?”
He replied, "I do not.
Everyone laughed at him together.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"An intercalary month should be observed.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus consistently observed an intercalary month every year, and laypeople came and asked:
“Noble One! What month is it now? He replied:
"It is the month of Āṣāḍha. He asked again, "Noble one!"
Everyone said, "It is now the month of Śrāvaṇa," yet you all say:
"This is the month of Āṣāḍha.
"Can it be that you, Venerable Ones, have made this an intercalary month within the year?
They replied:
"So it is," they replied, mocking him as before.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not insert an intercalary month within each year; rather, an intercalary month should be added only after six years, which means that five such six-year periods amount to thirty months.
This refers to the ancient method, which differs from the present one."
At that time, there was a king who added an intercalary month every two and a half years, yet the bhikṣus did not follow this practice, leading people to feel resentment and shame toward them.
The Buddha said:

"Bhikṣus should follow the royal law in determining the intercalary month; if the movements of the celestial paths are irregular, they should likewise follow those celestial paths in their calculations."

Therefore, you should recognize that the divisions of the sun, moon, and stars move in accordance with worldly convention, so that those non-Buddhists who come seeking to find fault shall find no opportunity.
“Venerable Sir! Is there a case where a bhikṣu residing in a monastery may allow a person under training (śikṣamāṇa) to recite the Prātimokṣa?
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
The third son’s summary verse says:
"If the boundaries are distinct, one does not announce purity; nor does one perform the *karmavācanā*."
"Riding through the air without holding onto desire, one unties what is in front before binding what is behind.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One:
"May those dwelling within the boundary go outside the boundary to announce their purity?"
The Buddha said, “No. [The monk asked:
“If one who dwells outside the boundary goes into the interior of the boundary, may he announce his purity?”
The Buddha said, "No. [The questioner asked:
"May those who reside within the boundary perform a *karmavācanā* for one who is outside the boundary?"
The Buddha said, "It is not permitted. [He asked again:
"If one resides outside the boundary, may they perform a *karmavācanā* for those within the boundary?"
The Buddha said, “It is not permitted. [The interlocutor asked:
“If one were to travel through the air while carrying the *kṣānti* (consent), would it then constitute carrying the *kṣānti*?”
The Buddha said, "It is not accomplished; you should take the *chanda* (consent) again. [He asked:
"If one does not understand the previous boundary, may one establish a subsequent boundary?"
The Buddha said: "It is not permitted;
one should first resolve the previous [boundary] by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations), and only then establish [the new boundary].
The fourth section is summarized in a verse:
Not entering a boundary, relinquishing a boundary; a tree-boundary where the World-Honored One resides;
not crossing over and crossing over; the death of the one performing the *karmavācanā*.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
“Is it possible to enter another realm by means of a particular realm?
The Buddha said,
“It is not possible.”
“How many kinds of boundaries do not overlap?
The Buddha said:
“They are the small ritual altars, the places where water currently remains, as well as the boundaries of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; none of these overlap.”
“If a boundary has already been established, how many methods for its relinquishment are there?
The Buddha said,
“There are five:”

First, it refers to the entire assembly all returning to lay life; second, it refers to the entire assembly simultaneously changing their gender; third, it refers to the entire assembly resolutely deciding to depart; fourth, it refers to the entire assembly passing away at the same time; fifth, it refers to the formal act of resolving through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the white fourfold motion).
“Can a single tree be used as the boundary marker for two territories?

The Buddha said, “One may take one side of it to serve as the marker for three territories, or as the marker for four territories; provided that the measurements and limits are clearly known, all such arrangements will be valid.”
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm among the people of Kāśī. Upon reaching a certain place, he smiled.

It is the constant custom of the World-Honored One that when he smiles, five kinds of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson—issue forth from his mouth; at times they shine downward, and at other times they ascend upward.

The light that shone downward reached the Sañjīva hell, the Kālasūtra hell, the Saṃghāta hell, the Raurava hell, the Mahāraurava hell, the Tapana hell, the Pratāpana hell, the Avīci hell, the Arbuda hell, the Nirarbuda hell, the Aṭaṭa hell, the Hahava hell, the Huhuva hell, the Utpala hell, the Padma hell, and the Mahāpadma hell.
In such places as these, those who were suffering from scorching heat all attained coolness, while those dwelling in icy cold obtained warmth.
Those sentient beings each found peace and happiness, and all spoke these words:
"Have you and I died here and been reborn in another place?"
At that time, in order to inspire faith in those sentient beings, the World-Honored One manifested further signs.
Having seen these signs, they all spoke thus:
"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; rather, it must be due to the majestic spiritual power of this rare Great Being that our bodies and minds now experience such peace and happiness."

Having thus conceived respectful faith, they will be able to extinguish all the sufferings of the hells and receive superior, wondrous bodies among humans and devas; they shall become vessels for the Dharma and attain the vision of the True Reality.

The light that ascended upward proceeded from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings through the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Within this light, he expounded the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and spoke these two verses:
"You should seek renunciation, And diligently practice the Buddha’s teaching."
Subdue the army of birth and death, As an elephant destroys a thatched hut.
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by always practicing heedfulness,
one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Then that radiance, having illuminated the trichiliocosm, returned to the presence of the Buddha.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of past events, the light enters through his back.
If he speaks of future events, the light enters through his chest.
If he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet.
If he speaks of matters concerning animals, the light enters through the heels;
if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, the light enters through the toes;
if he speaks of matters concerning humans, the light enters through the knees.
If he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin King of Power, the light enters through the palm of his left hand.
If he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin Universal Monarch, the light enters through the palm of his right hand.
If he speaks of celestial matters, the light enters through his navel.
If he speaks of the matters concerning śrāvakas, the light enters through his mouth;
if he speaks of the matters concerning pratyekabuddhas, the light enters between his eyebrows;
if he speaks of the matters concerning anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and entered through the crown of his head.
Then the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not smile without cause or condition.
He then spoke these verses to request the Buddha’s teaching:
“From his mouth issue various wondrous rays of light, Flowing and filling the great trichiliocosm in manifold forms;”
Pervading all lands throughout the ten directions, like the sun’s light illuminating the entirety of space;
the Buddha is the most supreme cause for sentient beings, able to eliminate pride as well as grief and sorrow.
Without a specific cause, he does not open his golden mouth; when he smiles, he will surely proclaim something rare and marvelous.
The serene and discerning Honored One of the Munis, who delights in speaking for those who wish to hear, roars like the lion king; we pray that you will resolve our doubts.
Like the King of Wondrous Mountains within the great ocean, Which does not tremble without a cause or condition;
So you, with sovereign compassion, manifest a smile, To explain the causes and conditions for those who look up with longing.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda: "So it is, so it is, Ānanda!"
It is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, suddenly manifests a smile. Ānanda!
This very spot is where, in the past, the Buddha Kāśyapa taught the Dharma to the assembly of his śrāvakas.
When Ānanda heard these words, he quickly took his seven-strip robe and folded it into four layers. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have already prepared the seat; I pray that the Buddha will know the time is right and sit here, so that this place may become the site where two Perfectly Enlightened Ones have enjoyed its use—namely, the Buddha Kāśyapa and the present World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Excellent, excellent! Although I have not spoken, you yourself know the proper time."
At that time, the World-Honored One took his seat and further addressed Ānanda, saying:

"You should know that this location was the monastery where Kāśyapa Buddha resided; this is the place for walking meditation (caṅkrama); this is the corridor, the gatehouse, and the place for washing the feet; this is the ground for the pure kitchen; and this is the location of the bathhouse."
At that time, Upāli said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the Buddha has taught concerning pure and impure ground, I do not know up to what point they are designated as pure or impure.”
The Buddha said:
"As long as the True Dharma remains in the world, there is both purity and impurity.
If the True Dharma should perish, all shall become impure."
“World-Honored One!
To what extent is it said that the True Dharma abides in the world?
In what way is it said to perish?”
The Buddha told Upāli:
"As long as there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and those who act according to what has been taught, this is called the True Dharma abiding in the world."
"If the *karmavācanā* is not performed, there will be no practice according to what has been taught; this is called the destruction of the True Dharma.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the Unsurpassed Great Teacher is outside the boundary, may the bhikṣus perform the *karmavācanā*?"
The Buddha said, “It is not permitted. [The questioner asked:
“If the Great Master is within the boundary, may others perform the *karmavācanā*?”
The Buddha said,
“It is permitted.
[The questioner asked,] “Furthermore, may the number of monks be completed by including the World-Honored One’s feet?”
The Buddha said: "It cannot be;
for the Dharma-jewel and the Sangha-jewel differ in their essential nature.
[He asked again: "Can one transcend that which is not to be transcended?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
[He asked,] "Venerable Sir!"
"I do not know how many instances there are where one must not cross the boundary.
The Buddha said,
"There are five such kinds:"
"They are: the boundary of the bhikṣus, the boundary of the bhikṣuṇīs, a small ritual site, a place where water currently stands, and the space between two boundaries.
"Venerable Sir! If there is a deep ditch or a river stream that makes it impossible to cross the boundary, is it permissible to cross over them?"
The Buddha said:
"If there is always a bridge, crossing over it is not a fault.
[The monk asked: "If the bridge is destroyed, for how long may one remain without losing the boundary?"
The Buddha said:
"It may be maintained for up to seven nights.
This applies to those who maintain it with a conscious intention; if one maintains it without such intention, it is lost as soon as it is broken."

“If there is a bhikṣu who, while the formal boundary is being established, suddenly passes away while the *karmavācanā* is being performed, can the establishment of the boundary be accomplished? The Buddha said,
“If the boundary markers are known and the majority of the *karmavācanā* has already been performed, then even though he has passed away, the establishment of the boundary is accomplished.”

"If one has not yet recognized the boundary markers and the *karmavācanā* being performed has not yet reached its majority, should one die at this time, the establishment of the boundary is not accomplished.
"If a bhikṣuṇī establishes a boundary, is it accomplished?"
"Based on this, it should be understood.
The summary verse for the fifth section says:
"The ritual procedures for grounds, walls, and so forth; establishing boundaries and the absence of granting consent."
"However, one may perform four types of *karmas* while sitting in a single location.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One:
“If those dwelling on the ground perform the *karmavācanā* at a distance for those also dwelling on the ground, is the performance of the *karmavācanā* valid?
The Buddha said, “It is not valid;
it becomes valid if one has given their consent (*chanda*).”
"Venerable Sir! If those standing on the ground and those atop a wall perform the *karmavācanā* together, is the performance of the *karma* valid?
The Buddha said:
"It is not valid.
"Venerable Sir! If those on the ground perform the *karmavācanā* together with those in the tree, is the performance of the *karmavācanā* valid?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not accomplished.
[The monk asked,] "Venerable Sir!"
"If those on the ground and those dwelling in the air perform the *karmavācanā* together,
will it be validly performed? The Buddha said, "It is not valid."
"It should be understood that taking trees, walls, and open space as the first [categories], each likewise has four permutations.
As the Blessed One said:
'There are one hundred and one formal acts (kamma). How many of these permit the giving of consent?"
"In how many cases is it improper to grant consent (*chanda*)? The Buddha said,
"Except for the case of establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*), in all other instances it is proper to grant consent."
“Venerable Sir! If one were to create a sign by means of supernatural transformations or illusory arts, would that constitute a valid sign?
The Buddha said:
"No, for supernatural powers and illusory arts are not substantially real.
"If one uses the sun, moon, or stars as a sign, can that sign be established?"
The Buddha said, “No, because the sun, moon, and stars do not remain fixed. [The interlocutor asked:
“If one were to use the waves of water, could they serve as a marker?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted, because the waves shift and move rapidly. [The questioner asked:
"If a bhikṣu carries the *kṣānti* (consent) for another and travels through the air, does this count as carrying the *kṣānti*?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not accomplished; one should take the *chanda* (consent) again.
[The questioner asked: "If a bhikṣu performs a single *karmavācanā*, is it accomplished in all four residential quarters?"
The Buddha said:
“It is permitted.
Just as there are four persons for each of the four elements present before him, one should separately station three persons at each respective location.”
At that time, those who uphold the Dharma—whether on a mat, a bed, a board, or a straw mat—shall maintain the *karmavācanā* by pressing down upon the four boundaries.
By adding their number to those four, the formal ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*) is fully accomplished.

Likewise, if distinct matters arise concerning the four boundaries, seven types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) are performed, namely: the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the act of causing fear (*tarjanīya-karman*), the act of subjugation (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*), the act of requesting an apology (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*), the act for one who does not acknowledge an offense (*adarśana-utkṣepaṇīya-karman*), the act for one who does not repent according to the Dharma (*apratiniḥsarga-utkṣepaṇīya-karman*), and the act for one who does not relinquish a wrong view (*pāpikā-dṛṣṭi-anutsarga-utkṣepaṇīya-karman*).

When performing such formal acts (karmas), the presiding person should sit near the corners of the four boundaries; if they sit with mats, boards, beds, or cushions all pressed together beneath them, the performance of the formal act is fully accomplished.

The eighth section, the summary verse (uddāna), states:
"Even if one does not cut the robe, if there is a valid reason, one may wear it."
"Robes may be made according to the dimensions of one's own body; if they are short, one may make them into *caṇḍāla*-robes (basket-robes).
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the Blessed One:
"May an uncut robe be formally accepted as one's own?"
The Buddha said, "It is not permitted;
however, it is permitted if there are circumstances of difficulty.
[He asked again: "If one wears an uncut robe, is it permissible to enter a village?"
"May one go to the houses of laypeople?
May one enter the dwellings of non-Buddhists?
The Buddha said:
"In all such cases, it is not permitted; however, if there are unavoidable circumstances, even if one wears [the robe], there is no offense.
"If one wears an uncut robe, is it permissible to sit in the dwelling of a non-Buddhist?"
The Buddha said:
“It is not permitted; however, if a non-Buddhist is not present in the house, there is no offense even if one sits.
As the World-Honored One has said:
Regarding the statement, "A robe measured by the cubit is appropriate to wear," if a person has a large body but short arms, should they also make the robe according to the measurement of the cubit?
The Buddha said:
"This person should take his own body measurements as the size for the robe.
"Even if one takes the body measurements, will it still not be sufficient?
The Buddha said:

"If it is not sufficient for all [the robes], one should sew them into a *kūṭāgāra* robe (here translated as *chuán*) and maintain it; it is four cubits long and two cubits wide, sewn together so that they join, entered into which one pulls oneself up, and tied with a cord, as described elsewhere."
Regarding what was previously called the *kīra-sūra*, no one recognized its significance.
Its shape is like a small basket; it belongs to the category of the five robes of a *bhikṣuṇī* and should serve as a lower garment (*śāṭaka*).
The ninth section, summarized in verse, says:
One shall not keep five kinds of skins because they involve faults;
however, their use is permitted in certain circumstances, provided one sits or lies down upon them only as much as is necessary to accommodate the body.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
as the World-Honored One has said:"
"If the hide of an elephant king is not used to make shoes,
may the hides of other elephants be used for shoes?
The Buddha said:
"This also will not do. Why? Because this elephant likewise possesses a trunk, tusks, and strength."
“As the Blessed One has said:
‘The hide of a wise horse should not be used to make shoes.
May the hides of other horses be used for shoes?”
The Buddha said:
"It cannot. This too is because it can run and possesses great strength."
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘The skins of lions, tigers, and leopards should not be used to make shoes.
Even if it is not the skin of these specific animals but belongs to their class, may it be used?”
The Buddha said: "They may not;
for these beings also possess the strength of claws and fangs."
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘If the skins of these various beasts are all unfit for sitting upon, then others are fit.
To what extent, in terms of size, may they be kept and used?”
The Buddha said:
"One should keep [a seat-cover] sufficient for one's own seating area.
As the World-Honored One has said:
Regarding the phrase "one may lie on a hide," does this mean one should lie on hides of equal size?
The Buddha said:
"If it is just large enough to accommodate the body, keeping it is not an offense."
The tenth section, summarized in verse, says:
Raw meat and various types of vinegar—there are five kinds that should not be used;
regarding hemorrhoids, one should not injure them with the nails; and regarding the redirection of gifts, one should recognize the underlying intention.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"As the Venerable One has said:..."
Regarding the statement, "The monk Kṣaudraka was permitted to eat raw meat due to the cause of illness," [the monks] did not know where they should obtain it.
The Buddha said:
"Take it from five types of slaughterers. What are the five?
They are those who kill sheep, chickens, pigs, those who catch birds, and those who hunt wild animals."
“Venerable One! Who should take it?
The Buddha said:
"Let those who have faith and reverence take it.
"Who shall be made to bestow it?
The Buddha said:
"Send back a messenger.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in this city who, suffering from illness, went to a physician and asked:
"I have a disease of emaciation and thirst."
"O Worthy One!
Please provide a prescription.
The physician replied:
"You ought to consume ghee; you will surely recover.
The bhikṣu replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to consume ghee for the sake of illness."
The physician replied, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; for the sake of what is required by illness, it should also be permitted to be taken.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu who is ill and has been instructed by a physician to consume ghee should indeed consume it.
At that time, although the sick bhikṣu had already consumed the ghee, he was still oppressed by thirst.
The physician asked him, "Venerable sir, how is your physical strength after consuming the ghee?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I am still oppressed by thirst.
The physician said:
"If clarified butter is not permitted, why not drink sour gruel or various vinegars?
The bhikṣu replied, "The World-Honored One does not allow us to drink at improper times; how could we possibly consume them?"
The physician replied, "The World-Honored One is compassionate; for what is required by illness, he should also permit its consumption.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit you to drink fermented rice-gruel vinegar.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know what kind of fermented rice-gruel vinegar it was,
nor how they should drink it.
They went again to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are six kinds of fermented grain drinks (sukta), all of which may be consumed:
first, great vinegar; second, barley vinegar; third, medicinal vinegar; fourth, small vinegar; fifth, curd-fermented drink; and sixth, churned curd-fermented drink."

When one wishes to drink these sour gruels, they should be purified by adding a few drops of water; they should then be filtered through layers of fine silk cloth until they become clear and transparent, the color of bamboo or reeds.
Whether at the proper time or the improper time, whether one is ill or not, drinking it constitutes no offense; do not harbor any doubt regarding this.

As for what is called "great vinegar" (mahāśukta), it refers to granulated sugar mixed with water and various fruits—such as grapes, wood-apple, or *āmalaka*—and fermented over a long period to produce vinegar.
Barley vinegar refers to that which is produced by grinding various substances such as parched barley until they are crushed and then fermenting them to form vinegar.
Medicinal vinegar refers to that which is produced by fermenting medicinal roots and stalks, etc., along with fruits such as jujubes, to form vinegar.
"Light vinegar" refers to hot rice-boiling water or rice-washings poured into cooked rice, which may be taken and replenished continuously for long-term use without spoiling.
"Curd-juice" refers to the liquid water found within curd.
"Churning the whey" means churning curdled milk to extract butter; the remaining liquid is water.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in this city who suffered from hemorrhoids. The protruding growths at the base of his anus were cut off with his fingernails, causing him such extreme and agonizing pain that it overwhelmed both body and mind beyond endurance.
He then thought: "I am beset by this suffering which is most difficult to bear; how could the World-Honored One, in His great compassion, not take pity on me?"
At that time, impelled by the power of great compassion, the World-Honored One went to where the bhikṣu was and asked: "Bhikṣu,
what is it that pains you?"

Then the sick bhikṣu joined his palms, gazed up at the World-Honored One, and with deep inner sorrow, his tears flowing and his voice choked, he related his suffering in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Did I not previously forbid you who suffer from hemorrhoids from cutting them off?
They replied: [Yes, we did.]
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha has already forbidden it.
“If that is so, why do you now perform such an act?”
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I am oppressed by suffering.
The Buddha said:
"Because you were oppressed by suffering, you have committed no offense.
Now I tell you all: even when afflicted by the pain of illness, one must not cut away hemorrhoids with fingernails or similar means."
Now, there are two methods for treating hemorrhoids:
either through the application of medicine or by means of incantations.
If a bhikṣu should suffer from such pain, he must not cut his hemorrhoids himself, nor should he cause another to cut them.
"Whoever violates this instruction shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Sūtra on Hemorrhoids has already been proclaimed by me in other places; now I shall proclaim it once more for you. Those who recite and uphold it will surely be cured."

If there are those who recite it, until the end of their lives they shall never be afflicted by the painful symptoms of hemorrhoids; they shall also attain the knowledge of past lives, being able to remember the events of seven births in previous existences.
He then spoke the mantra:
“Tadyathā | Arune | Marune | Bhrūṇe | Kurubhe | Vāśi | Śavāśi | Sambhavi | Svāhā. “O bhikṣus! [he said.]
When reciting the mantra, one should further say:
"In this northern direction there is the Great Snowy Mountain King; within it is a great tree named Bhṛṅgīta."
There are three kinds of flowers on trees:
first, the continuous; second, the supple; and third, the withered.

Just as those withered flowers fall away when they reach full dryness, may my hemorrhoids—whether caused by wind, heat, phlegm, blood, or feces, or any other types of hemorrhoids—all likewise fall away and become dry. May no more blood flow or pus discharge to cause further pain; let them be dried up, svāhā!
Furthermore, he spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | camme | cammani | svāhā. When the bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Naḍika, a merchant village within the domain of the Śākyas.
At that time, there was an elder in that village who had long possessed faith and a disposition toward joyful giving; he constructed a dwelling place and offered it as a gift to the Venerable Rāhula.
At that time, the Venerable One did not remain for long, but took up his bowl and robe and traveled through the human world.
When the householder heard that he had departed, he thought to himself:
"I do not yet know whether the Venerable One will return during his travels."
He then offered this monastery to the Saṃgha.

After Rāhula had wandered about as he pleased, he took up his robes and bowl and returned to the place where the merchant of Nādika was. Having learned that [the monastery] had been given to the Saṃgha, he went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and said to the Buddha:
"There was a householder who, having long possessed faith and a heart of deep reverence, built a dwelling and offered it to me alone; I resided there for some time."
"Not long after I have gone out on some business, I shall give it to the rest of the Saṃgha.
What should I do? I pray that the Buddha will resolve this for me."
The World-Honored One said:
"You may go to that householder’s place and speak these words:
'O virtuous one, have you ever conceived even the slightest thought of aversion toward me, whether in body, speech, or mind?'"
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Rāhula went to the householder and said,
"O noble one, have you ever conceived even the slightest feeling of aversion toward me, whether in body, speech, or mind?"
The householder replied,
"I have never had such an intention toward your venerable self.
Rāhula returned to the Buddha's presence and reported in detail that the householder had no intention of renouncing him.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Go to that village of Nāḍika and have all the bhikṣus currently residing there assemble at the place of the service hall."
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s command, went to that village; upon arriving at their residence, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should all assemble together in the hall for serving."
When Ānanda had finished speaking, he returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have already gone to that village of Nādika and respectfully proclaimed the holy command; all the bhikṣus currently residing there have now assembled."
At that time, the World-Honored One, taking the bhikṣus and Rāhula with him, arrived at that monastery and sat down upon the seat. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this!"

If there is a donor who gives a certain object to one person, and subsequently transfers that same object to another person, this is an unrighteous act for the donor and an unrighteous act for the recipient; it is called impure utilization.

If, in this manner, one further diverts it to two persons, or to three persons, or to the Saṃgha, all such cases are termed giving that is contrary to the Dharma, receiving that is contrary to the Dharma, and impure utilization.

"O Bhikṣus! If there is a donor who gives a certain object to two individuals, and later returns that same object to give it to one individual, then both the giver and the receiver are said to act contrary to the Dharma; all such enjoyment is impure."
Likewise, if it is further redirected to two persons, three persons, or the Saṃgha, both the donor and the recipient are said to act contrary to the Dharma, and all such enjoyment is impure.

"O Bhikṣus! If there is a donor who gives a gift to three individuals, and later returns that object to give it to one, two, or three others, or to the Saṃgha, both the giver and the receiver are said to act contrary to the Dharma; all such enjoyment is impure."

"O Bhikṣus! If there is a donor who gives a gift to the Saṃgha, and later diverts that object to give it to one, two, or three individuals rather than to the rest of the Saṃgha, both the giver and the receiver are said to act contrary to the Dharma; all such enjoyment is impure."
If one first offers to the community of bhikṣus and later diverts it to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, or conversely, these are all termed impure. You, O bhikṣus!
If the Saṃgha has split into two factions, and one first gives these items to one faction and then subsequently diverts them to the other faction, all such instances constitute impure enjoyment.

"O Bhikṣus! If one gives to a single person without diverting it to another, both the giver and the receiver are said to be acting in accordance with the Dharma, and all that is enjoyed is said to be pure."

In this way, if one gives to two persons, three persons, the Saṃgha, this nun, or this group, and does not subsequently divert it to others, even the subsequent enjoyment of it is called pure, as explained in detail above.
"O bhikṣus! The former is giving; the latter is not giving. O bhikṣus!"

The land belongs to the king; the goods belong to their owners; for houses and bedding, the donor is the master; for robes, bowls, and requisites, the bhikṣu is the master. If any of the donated temple property or other items falls into ruin, the donor should repair it themselves; one must not take these and redirect them as gifts to others. What was previously given remains a gift; what is later taken away is no longer a gift.
"O Bhikṣus! You should give Rāhula his former dwelling place.
If a bhikṣu gives that [dwelling] to someone else instead of this [person], except in the case of an emergency, he incurs an offense against the Dharma."
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus immediately granted Rāhula his former residence.
As the Blessed One had said:
"A Great Assembly for the Tonsure Ceremony should be held every five years and every six years."
At that time, there were devout brahmins and householders who all offered various kinds of cakes, fruits, and food to the Saṃgha.
However, the bhikṣus could not finish eating it all, so they took what remained and gave it to the śrāmaṇeras.
When the śrāmaṇeras arrived at dawn the following day, they again brought cakes and fruits to give to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus asked,
"From where did you obtain these cakes?"
He replied, "This is a gift from you, O virtuous one.
The bhikṣu then had a doubt:
"These cakes and fruits were leftovers from my own meal; to eat them again now would be a transgression according to the Dharma.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one eats with the intention of hoping for more, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense at the moment of giving, and a *pāyattika* offense upon eating."
If one gives with a mind free from expectation, but the recipient eats with a mind of expectation, there is no offense at the time of giving, but at the time of eating, one falls into an offense.

If one gives with a mind of expectation, but the recipient eats with a mind free from expectation, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the time of giving, but no offense at the time of eating.
"If one gives with no expectation and receives the food back without expectation, neither incurs an offense.
The summary verse for the second section of the Nidāna states:
"The distribution of the deceased's property and the proclamation [of the assembly], the spreading of the robe-cloth, and the instruction of the student."
Re-enacting the gathering and expulsion; the novice likewise [behaves] upon the wall.
The summary verse for the first section says:
Regarding the distribution of the deceased’s belongings, if there is no mutual [claim], one should take from the other.
"When witnessing a quarrel, one ought to offer counsel; assign [the parties] according to the direction of their heads.
At that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī.

There was a householder who had an only son; when the son had grown up, he took delight in leaving the household life and received full ordination within the True Dharma. Suddenly, he encountered the suffering of illness and consequently passed away.
At that time, the monks discarded the robes, bowls, and the corpse all together. When the laypeople saw this, they came and said to the monks:

"Among us common folk, we currently have children and grandchildren, so whatever we seek is easily obtained; even for the belongings of the deceased, we do not discard them lightly. Since you, Venerable Ones, have left the household life and have no sons or daughters, and since all your requisites were obtained only through great hardship, why do you not take back the belongings of the deceased?"
The bhikṣus replied, “The Blessed One has not yet permitted the collection of the clothing of the deceased.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When a bhikṣu has passed away, his robes and bowl must not be discarded.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who died of illness; they collected his robes but sent him off with his body exposed. Seeing this, the laypeople felt disdain. The Buddha said:
"One must not discard the body with it exposed; one should cover the body with a lower robe and an upper robe before sending it off."
At that time, the bhikṣus covered [the body] with fine robes. The Buddha said, "Do not use fine robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus covered it with tattered robes. The Buddha said:
"It should be covered with a robe that is neither fine nor coarse,
but of the middle quality. Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"How should the remaining robes and bowls be disposed of?"
The Buddha said,
"There is a poor bhikṣu who should be given [this].
At that time, the group of six monks was habitually very destitute, so the Buddha said:
"Do not give it to the group of six; you should distribute it by serving it in order starting from the senior monk.
Since the young bhikṣus did not receive any at all, the Buddha said:
"The assembly should gather together and first announce the matter. Once the assembly has reached a consensus and granted permission, it may be sold and divided among them."
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣu suddenly passed away; all his robes and bowl had been entrusted to a bhikṣuṇī, and the funeral rites were completed.
At that time, the bhikṣus, knowing that he had died, requested [the robe] from the bhikṣuṇīs. When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of the request, they asked:
"Where did he die? They replied:
"A nunnery. The nun said, "If I die in a monastery for monks, my property may belong to you; [but if I die here, it shall not]."
"If one dies in a nunnery, that person is my fellow brother in the Dharma; I am entitled to all their robes and bowls.
When the nun did not return them, the bhikṣu informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It is not appropriate to give them to the nun; the bhikṣus should divide them among themselves."
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣuṇī fell ill and died; her robes and bowl remained with the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
“Venerable sir!
A nun named so-and-so has now passed away; we pray that you will grant us the robe she entrusted to you.
Upon hearing of her death, the bhikṣu spoke as follows:
"That nun who has died was my sister in the Dharma; it is right that I should receive her robes and bowl.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should return them to the nuns."
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣu, while traveling through the human world, arrived at a village and stayed in the house of a layperson; he suddenly fell ill and passed away.
At that time, after the elder had finished the funeral rites, he took charge of [the nun's] robes and bowl.
Then, some bhikṣuṇīs traveling through the region arrived there; seeing them, the elder said:
"Noble ladies!..."
"Previously, a bhikṣu died in our home; his robes and bowl are all here with us, so you should take them away.
At that time, the community of nuns replied to the elder, saying, "It is not permissible for nuns to receive the robes of a deceased bhikṣu."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus of this matter, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"In a place where there are no bhikṣus, the bhikṣuṇīs should receive [the precepts] themselves."
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣuṇī, carrying her robes and bowl, was traveling through the countryside when she arrived at a village and stayed in the home of a layperson, where she fell ill and died.
At that time, the head of the household went to the charnel ground to collect the robes and bowl.
As some bhikṣus were traveling there, the elder saw them and said,
"Noble ones!..."
"Previously, a nun died in my house; her robes and bowl are all here with me. You, sir, should take them.
The bhikṣu replied, "It is not appropriate for me to receive the belongings of a deceased nun."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are no nuns in that place, the bhikṣus should take [the robes]; in this case, there is no offense."
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta,
if a bhikṣu should pass away while in the home of a layperson, who is entitled to receive his robes and alms bowl?"
The Buddha said, "The one who arrives first should receive it. [They asked:
"If two people arrive together, who should rightfully receive it?"
The Buddha said, "The one who requested it first shall receive it. [The other asked:
"If both request it simultaneously, who should rightfully receive it?"
The Buddha said, "Both cases are permissible; or, according to the customs and inclinations of worldly people, the giver should take [the bowl].
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
There were two bhikṣus who were quarreling with one another; other bhikṣus stood by watching the fight, and when a layperson saw this, he spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!..."
“I am a layman; when I see others fighting, I still intervene to resolve it.
How is it that you, Venerable Sir, stand by and watch the fight?
The bhikṣu replied:
"These are all weak-willed people who delight in quarreling; who could possibly resolve this?
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should offer counsel to stop them, but you should not remain watching."
At that time, although the bhikṣus offered verbal admonitions, he still did not cease [his conduct]. The Buddha said:
"If one does not cease despite being admonished, you should perform the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) against him."
There were two bhikṣus who engaged in debate with one another, scrutinizing right and wrong; consequently, they became angry and remained in a state of contention.
At that time, the other bhikṣus performed the *jñapti-karman* of *pratisaṃharaṇīya* (suspension) against them. Then those two men said:
"We were debating and investigating the principles of the Dharma; for what reason have you gentlemen suddenly performed this formal ritual (*karman*)?"
The bhikṣu replied, "The Buddha has commanded that those who engage in quarreling be set aside; for this reason, we have performed the *karmavācanā* against you.
He reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) in this manner.
If there are currently two teachers present, they should offer counsel and admonition.
If [the candidate] has completed ten years of seniority and is independent of a teacher's reliance (*niśraya*), the bhikṣus should offer counsel."
"If they do not cease [the dispute], the assembly should perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against them.
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the Blessed One:
"If a bhikṣu should pass away within the boundaries of two monastic districts (*sīmā*), who is entitled to receive his robes and bowl?"
The Buddha said:
“It may be obtained according to the direction the head is facing.
[The questioner asked: “If the head is situated between two boundaries, how should this be handled?”
The Buddha said,
“One may obtain [the result] in both places.
The second section is summarized in a verse:
When leading the chant while riding in a carriage, one should raise the hand when receiving robes;
whatever robe-offerings the Saṃgha obtains should be shared equally by both the ordinary and the noble.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, many non-Buddhists had previously resided within this city; however, because the Buddha arrived there, those non-Buddhists lost their majestic splendor, and their offerings and gains became meager.
At that time, those among the laypeople who followed non-Buddhist paths all begged for alms in order to provide offerings for their teachers.

Every morning, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was traveling to the Buddha’s dwelling, he encountered these non-Buddhists on the road, who begged from him, desiring to provide offerings for their own teachers.
Having seen this, the householder thought to himself:
"Even these followers of heterodox paths, who practice evil dharmas, are still able to beg for offerings to support their own teachers.
Yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has stated in various sūtras as follows:"
"If there are those who do not believe, I shall exhort them to give rise to faith, so that they may be tamed and abide within the True Dharma.
If my Great Teacher grants his permission, I will tell the multitude:
"Offer worship to this field of merit."

Having formed this thought, he entered the Jeta Grove, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and stood to one side. He then reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that you will grant me leave to offer whatever I desire by way of alms-giving to the Buddha and the Saṅgha."
The World-Honored One replied,
“You may do as you wish.
The householder then went about begging for alms, whereupon the lay devotees and brahmins all said to him:
"If the assembly of noble ones should come together to beg for alms, our merit and benefit will increase even further.
At that time, the elder reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should assist the elder in this matter."
When the bhikṣus had received these instructions, they went along with the elder to beg for alms.
People said to them, "If, when giving a gift, you announce our names so that we may all be known, it would be excellent!"
The World-Honored One said:
"When a donor presents an offering, you should chant the donor's name and offer a prayer of blessing; only then should you accept it."
He then dispatched a layperson to announce his name, and the people replied,
"If the Noble Assembly would announce our names, our merit would increase."
The Buddha said, "One should have a bhikṣu call out their names.
At that time, there was a donor who brought his wealth to the monastery to offer it as a gift; the Buddha said:
"If anyone comes to the monastery, you must first recite their name and offer prayers for their welfare before accepting them.
At that time, the bhikṣu made a general announcement; as he led the service, the crowd gathered like clouds, pressing so closely together that they had no leisure to approach him. The Buddha said:
"The one who leads the service should ride in a carriage or ascend a high palanquin."
When it was hot or when they encountered wind and rain, the Buddha said:
"One should provide a canopy to cover the body entirely.
When many people crowded at one side where the door was open, the Buddha said:
"One should open four gates and have four people lead the chant.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went about making his proclamation, he obtained many hundreds of thousands of pairs of fine cotton cloths and other wealth amounting to billions. He then thought:

"Now that I have sought alms and obtained such vast treasures, I ought to establish a great assembly for giving. I shall make offerings to the Buddha and the noble Saṅgha in their entirety; I will place these goods before the assembly and offer them all at once."

Having formed this thought, he adorned the Jetavana Grove on all sides with various silks and fabrics; the stands for his three robes and requisites were filled to capacity, and he assigned various people to guard them. He then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I wish to hold a grand assembly tomorrow to honor the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.

That very night, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink; at dawn, he arranged seats and mats within the monastery and went to inform the Buddha that the time had come.

The Buddha and the great assembly all took their seats; when the meal was finished and the bowls had been withdrawn, and after the chewing of tooth-sticks and rinsing were completed, the elder placed various garments before the head of the assembly and then stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How many such persons in this human world are fields of merit?
The Buddha said,
"There are two."
This refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There are eighteen types of persons in training and nine types of persons beyond training; these are called fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra), capable of digesting material offerings and benefits.

What are the eighteen types of persons in training (*śaikṣa*)? They are: the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*), the fruit of stream-entry; the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*), the fruit of once-returning; the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*), the fruit of non-returning; the candidate for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*); those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); those attained through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); those from family to family (*kulaṃkula*); those with one interval (*ekavīcika*); those reborn in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*); those reborn upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); those with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); those without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*). These are called the eighteen.
What are the nine types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)? They are:

the one of falling away (parihāṇadharman), the one of reflection (cetanādharman), the one of protection (anurakṣaṇādharman), the one of abiding (sthitākampya), the one capable of penetration (prativedhanādharman), the unshakable one (akopyadharman), the one not subject to falling away (aparihāṇadharman), liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti), and twofold liberation (ubhayatobhāgavimukti). These are the nine.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he further recited these verses:
“In this world, those who are in training and those beyond training are worthy of respect and should be venerated;
With body, speech, and mind upright and pure, Giving to such a field of merit brings forth great fruit.”
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada stood before the elder and requested the proclaimer,
saying: "I pray only that the Noble One will make the formal announcement as follows:"

"If you are a disciple of the World-Honored One, one worthy of veneration, one to whom prostrations should be made, a supreme field of merit, and one capable of receiving all worldly offerings and benefits, then you may accept these robes and articles as you please."
The one who proclaims this shall stand before the Elder and make the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If these are disciples of the Blessed One, worthy of respect, worthy of veneration, the unsurpassed field of merit, and capable of receiving all material offerings from the world, then these robes and requisites may be accepted as you please."
At that time, having heard this announcement, those among the great assembly who were free from greed, hatred, and delusion thought to themselves:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍika has made this proclamation:

'If there be any disciples of the Blessed One who are worthy of respect, who should be venerated, who are unsurpassed fields of merit, and who are capable of receiving all the material offerings of the world—may they accept these garments and robes as they please.'"
The Arhats thought to themselves:
"I am one who has attained the unsurpassed fruit within this Saṃgha; therefore, I ought to enjoy this share of material goods."
As the Blessed One has said:
"O bhikṣus, you possess superior goodness within; you ought to keep it secret and manifest only a coarse and unattractive appearance.
How can I now, for the sake of the profit from this robe, proclaim my own virtues and claim that I am a supreme one who has transcended desire?
Having formed this thought, they all remained silent.
Those who still possessed residual afflictions (*kleśa*) that had not yet been exhausted also thought:
"This object is intended as a gift for the unsurpassed field of merit; since my afflictions are not yet exhausted, I do not deserve it."
He too remained silent.
All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) also thought:
"This is the unsurpassed field of merit; I, being currently bound by all fetters, clearly have no share in it."
At that time, not a single person among the assembly took any of the shared goods.
Then the householder thought to himself:
"Am I now to place my bowl upside down before these holy ones and ordinary folk alike?"

After a short while, his appearance became haggard and his complexion turned jaundiced; he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported all that had occurred in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the answer, intentionally asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has offered many garments as a gift to the great assembly; for what reason is there no one in the assembly to accept them?"
Ānanda said, “The householder Anāthapiṇḍada made this announcement:

‘In this assembly, whoever is a disciple of the Blessed One’s voice-hearers— those who are worthy of respect, those to whom one should prostrate, the unsurpassed field of merit, and those capable of receiving all material offerings from the world— may they accept these garments and requisites as they please.’”
When the great assembly heard this request, both the noble and the ordinary remained silent; for this reason, no one came forward to accept [the precepts].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus:"
"Let all those currently residing in Śrāvastī and in other places assemble together in the Hall of Service.
When the Venerable Ānanda had received the Buddha’s instruction, he went to inform the assembly to gather in the hall, and then returned to the Buddha’s presence to prostrate at his feet.
He addressed them, saying:
"The great assembly has gathered; may the Buddha know that the time is right.
Thereupon, the Sugata proceeded to the hall, took his seat, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Anāthapiṇḍada the Elder bestows many robes; for what reason do you not accept them?
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and offered no reply.
Then the Great Master, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"Why is it, bhikṣus, that when I questioned you, you remained silent and gave no answer?
At that time, Ānanda related the preceding events in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Is it not the case that you previously approached me with faith, having left the household life and renounced worldly affairs to seek *nirvāṇa*?
The bhikṣus replied, “It is so.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“If you, out of faith, have come to me to leave the household life, seeking nirvana and practicing pure conduct, then these bhikṣus’ robes, worth one hundred million gold coins; the dwellings they inhabit, worth five hundred gold coins; and the food and drink they consume, complete with a hundred flavors—all such things as these I permit them to accept, and you are all capable of digesting them.”

If there is a bhikṣu who has violated a grave precept, he shall not consume even a single mouthful of food within the monastery grounds, nor shall he set even one foot upon the land of the saṃghārāma.

Why is this? You should know that there are ten kinds of faults for one who violates the precepts: they know themselves to be an evil person who has broken the precepts; others also know them to be such a violator; all the celestial deities do not come to associate with them; fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life and virtuous people who understand the Dharma all treat them with contempt; the sound of their sinful reputation is known far and wide; those who have not yet attained realization will no longer be able to attain it; those who have already realized the Dharma will all fall away from it; what they have previously heard and studied they will entirely forget; at the time of death, their minds will be filled with anguish; and after they pass away, they will be reborn in the hells.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!
You should know that there are five kinds of enjoyment:
first, enjoyment as a master; second, enjoyment of paternal wealth; third, enjoyment by permission; fourth, enjoyment of borrowed goods; and fifth, enjoyment like a thief.
What is meant by "enjoyment as a master"?
It refers to an Arhat who has forever eliminated the three poisons.
What is meant by "enjoyment of paternal wealth"?
This refers to those trainees who still possess residual afflictions;
how, then, can their enjoyment [of requisites] be permitted?
It refers to ordinary persons of pure virtue who diligently cultivate meditation and recitation with a mind free from indolence, maintaining purity of ethical discipline.
What is enjoyment like that of one who owes a debt?
It refers to one who, though guarding the prohibitions of the precepts, does not diligently cultivate the wholesome dharmas of the factors of enlightenment.
What is enjoyment like that of a thief?
That is to say, should one among the four grave prohibitions be transgressed by any of you,
you must recognize this matter and train yourselves accordingly.
Furthermore, whatever robes and other benefits this householder has bestowed shall be shared equally by the entire assembly.
