The third section, a summary verse, says:
There is opening and there is not opening; there is taking out and there is not taking out.
If one is outside the boundary, hearing [the announcement], he gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One:
"Is it possible for the Saṃgha of bhikṣus to collectively spread the kaṭhina robe, yet there be one within the assembly who has not spread the robe?"
The Buddha said: "There is.

If a bhikṣu, while the robes are being spread together, falls asleep or enters meditative absorption without having given his consent (kāya-vinaya), although this person is physically present within the assembly, he cannot be said to be participating in the spreading of the robes."
"However, the Great Assembly is called 'those who well spread the robe.
Is it possible that there are bhikṣus in the Saṃgha who, while collectively spreading the *kaṭhina*, do not receive it such that the spreading of the robe is accomplished?"
The Buddha said: "There is!

If, when the bhikṣu-saṃgha is collectively spreading the robe-cloth, a monk has given his consent to another and then enters meditative absorption or falls asleep, even though he does not perceive it, the spreading of the robe-cloth is nonetheless accomplished."
“Is there a case where the Bhikṣu Saṃgha collectively performs the *kaṭhina* ceremony, yet although one is present within the assembly, it is not said that they have ‘put forth’ the robe?
The Buddha said: “There is.”

If, at the time the Bhikṣu Saṃgha distributes the robes, a monk does not give his consent (*chanda*) but instead enters meditative absorption or falls asleep, this person is not said to have participated in the distribution of robes; nevertheless, the Saṃgha is still said to have distributed the robes.

"Is there a case where a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha of bhikṣus together distributes the robes, is physically present within the assembly but does not mentally accept it—would this be called 'distributing the robes'?
The Buddha said: "There is."

If a bhikṣu has given his consent for the robe to be distributed (*cīvara-niḥsarga*) to another, or has entered meditative absorption or fallen asleep, yet the Saṃgha completes the distribution of the robe, it is considered that he has participated in the distribution.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu goes outside the boundary and hears that the assembly has already performed the ritual for the *kaṭhina* robe, and he gives rise to a mind of rejoicing (*anumodanā*), this is also called participating in the distribution of the robe.
The fourth section, the summary verse, says:
"Teaching those under training and so forth, not holding [the rite]; the formal act is not accomplished, nor is there censure;
twelve persons constitute censure; impurity constitutes a root offense."
The setting is as before.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"May one who is undergoing training (śikṣādattaka) perform all formal acts of the Saṃgha (karmavācanā)?"
The Buddha said, “No.
[The questioner asked: “May those who have difficulties, such as the *ardhaka* and others, obtain it?”
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
[The questioner asked,] "Is it appropriate for one who is under training (śikṣamāṇā) to cast a voting tally (śalākā)?"
The Buddha said, "No.
[He asked again,] "Can one who has committed the four pārājika offenses participate in the voting by counting sticks?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
[He asked,] "As the World-Honored One has said:..."
"If, for that person, a formal act (kamma) is performed in accordance with the Dharma,
yet that person's censure does not constitute valid censure," [then] if an unlawful formal act is performed for that person, does that person's censure constitute valid censure?
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes a formal reprimand.
[He continued: "If a group of twelve kinds of people, when being dispatched, speaks as follows:"
"There is no need to appoint me.
Would these people have been rebuked for saying this?
The Buddha said: "Yes."
"This constitutes a valid censure.
However, regarding these individuals based on two factors, I have spoken with intentional ambiguity, saying that a censure is not a valid censure; namely, in the case of those who are impure."
"Venerable Sir! As the Blessed One has said:
'If an impure person censures, it does not constitute a valid censure.'"
As for the phrase "what is called impure," the Buddha said:
"If one commits even a single offense among the four *parājika* (defeats), that person is then called an impure person."
Regarding the statement "based on two matters":
first, performing a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) in accordance with the Dharma; second, that this person is impure and is included as the fifth son. The summary verse says:
One should again perform the ritual correctly, And not allow a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) to act [in such a manner].
Guarding the mind with wholesome attention, one should dwell where there is seeing but no hearing.
The setting is as before.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
“If one who is under training (śikṣamāṇa) performs a ritual for another, having held the *karmavācanā*, is the ritual successfully accomplished?
The Buddha said:
“It is not accomplished; it must be performed again.”
"Those who have committed the four grave offenses are all likewise.

At that time, there was a śrāmaṇera who wished to receive full ordination; his preceptor prepared the robes and bowl for him, and both the teachers and the witnesses summoned him to come, but he was sent out of the boundary due to other business.

When his relatives heard that he wished to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they came seeking the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) and, upon finding him, took him away; this hindered his superior practice and obstructed his ordination.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"Just as when the eldest son of a Cakravartin King has received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and is about to ascend the throne, people are stationed day and night to guard and protect him."
This śrāmaṇera is also like this: as he approaches the time for full ordination, he must be strictly guarded.
Whenever a śrāmaṇera wishes to receive full ordination, you should not allow him to go outside;
place him where he can see [the assembly] but away from where he can hear [private conversation], and have him stand before the community with palms joined in reverent devotion.
The sixth section, a summary verse, says:
Restraining within the boundary, Subduing the minds of the assembly,
Cutting pillars and doorframes, Nuns and others likewise expelled.
The setting was as before.
Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
“As the Blessed One has said:”

"If one has already performed the *bhaya-karman* (act of causing fear) against a person, and later seeks to request the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* (act of reconciliation) within the assembly for their release—
how many dharmas must be fulfilled for them to be eligible for such reconciliation?"
The Buddha said: "One must possess five qualities to be properly reconciled:

first, the mind is filled with joy; second, one submits harmoniously to the assembly; third, one requests the removal of the offense; fourth, one expresses formal respect; and fifth, one completely abandons all causes for contention."
“Venerable Sir! In what place is the method for granting absolution performed?
The Buddha said:
"It may be performed within the boundary.
"As the Blessed One has said:
'A bhikṣu who engages in quarreling should be subjected to the formal act of causing fear (bhayānīya-karman).'"
"If there are those who do not submit while the Dharma is being correctly administered, how should this be handled?
The Buddha said:
"One should take their robes and bowls and drive them out beyond the boundaries."
"If they refuse to leave and cling to the doorpost, the doorpost they are clinging to should be cut away; if they cling to the doorframe, that too must be chopped off.
"Who is responsible for repairing the damaged pillars and doors?"
The Buddha said:
"The great assembly may perhaps be converted to work together with the laity on construction projects.
[The questioner asked: "If it is a bhikṣuṇī who is involved in a dispute, how should this be handled?"
The Buddha said:
"The ritual procedure for expulsion shall be conducted in the same manner as that for bhikṣus.

If the two assemblies—the śrāmaṇeras and the śikṣamāṇās—perform the formal act (karmavācanā) of expulsion against someone who refuses to depart, they may all proceed in the same way as previously described."
“Venerable Sir! If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī acts as a defiler of families, should the formal act of banishment also be performed against them?
The Buddha said:
"It should be done. For both groups of śrāmaṇeras and śikṣamāṇās, it is exactly the same.
The seventh section concludes with this summary verse:
Those who break the precepts should be expelled; those who remain in hiding should also be removed.
Those who cause distress to the laity should be made to offer an apology; the rest of the assembly should all follow this same rule.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has said:
'A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts should be expelled.'"
As for the question, "Who should perform the act of banishment?
the Buddha said:
"If the Saṃgha does not submit, one should take their robes and belongings and drive them out; whether they cling to a pillar or a doorframe, the procedure is in all respects the same as before."
“Venerable Sir! As the World-Honored One has said:
‘If there are bhikṣus who mutually disparage and revile lay devotees (gṛhapati), one should perform for them the formal act of seeking forgiveness (kṣānti-karman).’”
"If one mutually insults or disparages another bhikṣu, should one also perform the ritual of seeking forgiveness for him?
The Buddha said,
"One should do so."
“Venerable Sir! If one should treat a bhikṣuṇī or any of the three lower assemblies with contempt or disparagement, should one also perform the ritual for seeking forgiveness toward them?
The Buddha said:
"It is also performed.
If nuns or those of lower status likewise disturb one another, the same procedure for performing the *karmavācanā* and the rite of expulsion shall be carried out.
The eighth sub-section is summarized in a verse:
When one causes a śrāmaṇera to feel fear, and then, for the sake of receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā),
the five factors are accomplished, at that time, after five summer retreats, one may depart from dependence.
The Venerable Upāli requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"If the Saṃgha performs the rite of instilling fear for a śrāmaṇera, and later the Saṃgha confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon him, does the reception of ordination become valid?
The Buddha said:
"The reception of full ordination is indeed valid; however, those who conferred it commit an offense."
"One should first perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal act of resolution) for that person. As the Blessed One said:

"One who has accomplished five dharmas and completed five years of residence may leave their *niśraya* (dependence) and travel wherever they wish; however, even one with ten years of residence must still rely upon a *niśraya* at every place they arrive."
Regarding the phrase, "If one has completed four summer retreats and accomplished the five dharmas, may they leave their formal dependence and travel wherever they please?
the Buddha said: "They may not;
this is so that they may fulfill five summer retreats."
“If one has completed five years of summer retreat but still lacks five qualities, may they be released from the requirement of dependence?
The Buddha said, “They may not,
because the five qualities are lacking.”

“If one has reached the third summer retreat, is thoroughly proficient in the Tripiṭaka, has fully realized the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā), and has completely eliminated the three impurities (trimala)—must such a person still rely upon a teacher?
The Buddha said:
“They must also rely [upon one], for the established teaching is definitive.”

"If one has completed five years of seniority and has accomplished the five dharmas, one is permitted to go among people and travel as one pleases. When reaching such places, for how many days may one remain without a preceptor?"
The Buddha said:
"One may remain for up to five nights; this is based on having the intention [to stay].
If one lacks the intention to seek [such things], one may not remain for even a single night, and it is improper to receive any food, drink, or similar items used by the Saṃgha."
The ninth section, summarized in verse, says:
Homogeneous and non-homogeneous, With limits and without,
Distinguished as obscured and unobscured, And named as one kind yet different.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"As the Bhadanta has said:
'There are offenses that are of the same category and offenses that are not of the same category.'"
"What are these? The Buddha said, "Regarding 'similar offenses' (sabhāga-āpatti):
for instance, a *pārājika* offense in relation to another *pārājika* offense is called 'similar';"
"If compared to other categories, they are called 'non-homogeneous' (asabhāga).
The same applies to the four subsequent categories.
As the Blessed One said:"
"There are offenses with limits and offenses without limits.
Which ones are these?
The Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who cannot recall his offenses or the number of nights [they have occurred], this is called 'without limit.
If there is one who can remember and know his offenses and the number of nights, this is called 'with limit.'"
“As the Buddha has said:
‘There are concealed offenses and unconcealed offenses. What are these?”
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of concealment:
first, concealment by night; second, concealment of the mind."
"If there is a bhikṣu who conceals [an offense], even if he conceals it for only a single night, it is not called 'concealment'; however, if he conceals his own mind, it is then called 'concealment.
World-Honored One, you have spoken of various categories of names regarding the grounds of offenses; what is meant by 'name'?"
“What constitutes the ‘seed’?
The Buddha said:
“The *pārājika* is called the name; the act committed therein is called the seed. The same applies to the names and seeds of the four categories that follow.”
The summary verse for the tenth section says:
One should not practice the Dharma while walking upon a wall; it is not [permissible] with one, two, or three people;
one should not face a person who has broken the precepts; and one should not accept the formal consent (*śikṣādattaka*) of another.
The setting is as before.
As the Blessed One has said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to undergo the *parivāsa* and *mānatva* penances, he should be granted the formal procedure (*dharma*)."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus abandoned their designated boundary and performed their ritual practices atop a wall.
The other bhikṣus asked the group of six:
"Virtuous ones, what are you doing?"
The group of six replied,
"We are practicing the *pārivāsika* penance. The bhikṣus said:
"This is a concealment; how can it constitute the performance of the ritual?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not perform the ritual atop a wall, nor should you perform it in the presence of only one, two, or three bhikṣus."
"It is appropriate that among the four *bhikṣus*, at times this disciplinary rite of restoration should be performed.

At that time, the group of six *bhikṣus* performed the rite of restoring their original status (*pārivāsika*) by receiving the dharma from the four persons under training (*śikṣādattaka*). The Buddha said:

"One should not perform the rite of restoring the original status before those persons under training; nor should one perform the rite of restoration before the four *pārivāsikas*; nor should one cause those who have committed a *pārājika* offense to preside over the dharma or receive the rite of restoration."
It is not the case that one who has committed three grave offenses may add a single pure person, nor may they add two or three.

Just as when performing the *parivāsa* (probation) rite for one individual, the entire assembly must be entirely pure and possess the same view; likewise, even until the six-night *āvarhaṇa* (expiation of the offense), all must be pure.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May one who is under training (śikṣādattaka) give his consent (chanda)?
The Buddha said:
"No. "May one receive the formal consent (*chanda*) of this person?
The Buddha said:
"It is obtained, because of this bhikṣu.
The summary verse for the third section of the Nidāna says:
"The full ordination platform, the śrāmaṇera, falling [from the precepts], / A single robe, smoke, medicine, and vessels."
An iron mallet, hair, and a door—these should not be made of iron.
The summary verse of the first section says:
A circular alms-bowl, a temple of the gods, and a residence within two and a half *yojanas*.
"One who lacks a bowl shall not ordain others; bowls must not be inscribed with characters.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that moment, the bhikṣus were washing their bowls and rinsing their feet in various places, which resulted in the ground becoming infested with many flies and ants.
Then the brahmins and householders asked the bhikṣus,
"Is this the place where the Noble Ones relieved themselves?
The bhikṣus replied:
"This is not a place for relieving oneself; it is where I wash my bowl and bathe my feet.
Upon hearing this, the householder gave rise to contempt and spoke these words:
"All these bhikṣus are utterly impure; they wash their bowls and bathe their feet without choosing a proper location."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wash one's bowl or rinse one's feet in just any place.
You should know this!"
"If it is a place for washing bowls, one should smear it and create a small water altar.
At that time, the bhikṣus made circular maṇḍalas; when the householders saw them, they all said, "The Śākyas worship the sun!"
The World-Honored One replied,
"It should not be made circular.
At that time, the bhikṣus made maṇḍalas in the shape of a half-moon, and the lay devotees spoke again:
“The bhikṣus shall attend to the moon.
The Buddha said,
“There are two kinds of altars:”
One is like the blade of a spear, and the other is like the shape of a jar.
Alternatively, they may be made according to the direction of the water's flow.
If one makes a maṇḍala in the shape of the sun or moon, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"If it is for the sake of the Triple Gem, there is no offense whatsoever regardless of the circumstances.
At that time, the World-Honored One briefly proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma for the brahmin minister of the kingdom of Magadha named Varṣākāra, speaking in verse:
"If a man of right faith Makes offerings to the hosts of devas..."
"One who can follow the Great Teacher’s instructions is praised by all Buddhas.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus immediately made offerings to the deities Kaṭapūtana and Maṇḍūka-Gorī.
At that time, the brahmins and householders all said: "Venerable One!
Since you have gone forth as a renunciant within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, how could you possibly turn back again to revere and serve celestial deities?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I spoke with intentional ambiguity for the sake of laypeople; it was not intended for you, the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, you all should not show reverence or service to the various devas.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who began to treat the devas with contempt. Those devas said:
"What fault have we committed against you that you should thus deceive and insult us?"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you should not make offerings to celestial deities, nor should you treat them with contempt."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who later saw images of Kaṭapūtana and Maṇḍūka-Gaurī in another place, and he immediately broke them apart.
At that time, the lay devotees spoke thus:
"This image of a celestial deity has no consciousness; why, O Noble One, have you willfully destroyed it?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus! You should not destroy images of devas.
At one time, some bhikṣus were traveling through various places; on their way, they happened to circumambulate a temple of a deva to the right. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not circumambulate a temple of the gods to the right.
He then avoided the path and was injured by thorns; the Buddha said, "One should take the old path."
"If one circumambulates to the right for the sake of convenience while on the path, one should recite a noble verse (gāthā) and clear one's throat or snap one's fingers to alert them.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

As it is said, within a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) extending at most two and a half yojanas, the Buddha personally ordained that all disciples should request instruction and report their affairs three times each day to their preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya).
"Those disciples are two and a half *yojanas* away from their preceptors and instructors; since the distance is great and time is short, I do not know how they should proceed.
The Buddha said, "They should go to pay their respects every half-month."
If one is five *krośas* away from the teacher, one should go to pay respects once every seven or eight days.
If one is one *krośa* away, one should go once every day.
If one is even closer, or even in the same location, one should pay homage three times each day.
"If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

At that time, Upānanda was ordaining people without possessing a bowl. When the bhikṣus had each washed their bowls and placed them in the niches, they invited the two teachers to circumambulate the caitya.
A disciple ordained by Upānanda had need of a bowl due to certain circumstances, so he went to the side of the Venerable Kauṇḍinya’s bowl, intending to take it.
The Venerable said to him, "This is my bowl; you must not touch it."
Then he went again to another bhikṣu’s bowl and, as before, attempted to take some, only to be stopped once more.
The bhikṣus then asked him, "Who is your teacher?"
He replied, "Upānanda.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not ordain another person by granting them the going forth or the full admission (upasampadā) without a bowl;
one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta). You bhikṣus!
Whenever you wish to ordain someone as a śrāmaṇera, you should provide them with a bowl, a small bowl, and a copper cup, so that there is no deficiency."

At that time, Aniruddha had a disciple who served as his bowl-attendant. Because the teacher’s bowl and the disciple’s bowl were identical in shape, the disciple could not distinguish between them and thus became doubtful, saying:
"Is this my teacher’s bowl, or is it mine?"
Thereupon, they each wrote their names on the bottom of their bowls.
A certain householder invited the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus to his home to receive a meal.
The householder had previously been in an illicit liaison with a courtesan; he therefore dispatched a messenger to inform her, saying:
"Today I have invited the Buddha and the Sangha; tomorrow I shall respectfully prepare offerings at my home. You should come there and receive the food with your own hands."
At that time, the courtesan encountered some other business and was unable to go in person.
When the Buddha and the Saṅgha arrived for the invitation, they finished the meal of cakes; having recited the verses on giving, they rose from their seats and departed.

At that time, the householder was a friend and acquaintance of Āniruddha’s disciples; after the Buddha and the Saṅgha had departed, only those disciples had not yet left his house. Then the householder addressed them, saying:
“Venerable sirs!...”
"I wish to borrow this bowl for a short while so that I may entrust the remaining food to someone else.
The bhikṣu immediately gave his teacher’s bowl to him.
The householder filled the bowl with fragrant food and sent it to the courtesan, adding these words:
“O virtuous one! I have invited the Triple Gem to partake of this food; the Buddha and the Saṃgha have already finished eating. You may rejoice in this.

At that time, the courtesan, having received the bowl of food, placed it in another vessel and saw the name of the Venerable upon the bottom of the bowl. Knowing it was the bowl used by the noble Āniruddha, she thought to herself:

"The Ācārya is one who receives the offerings of devas and humans; I am now fortunate to have seen his bowl. If I were to send it back empty-handed, I would lose a great benefit; such a course of action would not be right."

He immediately took the bowl and wiped it clean on all sides; he then washed it repeatedly with fragrant water, smeared it with scented clay, and placed it upon an exquisite seat. With his right knee touching the ground and holding a magnificent garland of flowers, he made offerings with profound sincerity, burning incense that perfumed everywhere as he remained there making aspirations.
At that time, there was a brahmin who also had a prior acquaintance with the courtesan; he came to her place and, seeing the woman making offerings, asked:
"O fair-faced one!..."
"What are you doing? He replied, "This bowl is the vessel used by the Venerable Aniruddha; it is one that is revered by both humans and devas."
"I wish to offer a brief act of veneration to this bowl.
The brahmin said, "You have used lustful corruption to gather all these people together, yet you do not even let go of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas."
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Whenever bhikṣus write their own names upon their belongings, such faults as these arise; therefore, one should not write one's own name."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know which things were not to be written down.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of things that must not be written down:"

This refers to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Extensive Explanation of the Prātimokṣa), and various procedural matters (*vastu*)—all meanings consistent with the Vinaya teachings—as well as one's own private property. One should not write characters upon one's own property; rather, it may be used for personal mnemonic retention.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the Vinaya teachings and so forth are all not to be committed to writing, then in future generations there will be many bhikṣus whose minds lack the power of retention and who are largely forgetful; they will be unable even to remember the various nidānas. In such circumstances, what should be done?”
The Buddha said:
"If it is so, you should write it down on paper or leaves and uphold it.
The second sub-section contains a summary verse:
When a *śrāmaṇera* dropped his bowl and it broke,
[the Buddha] permitted others who remained mindful to make two kinds of nested covers, along with whatever other items were required.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who kept a śrāmaṇera and constantly had him carry his alms-bowl.
Later, at another time, the bowl slipped from the śrāmaṇera’s hand and was damaged, causing the preceptor to be deprived of it.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not have that śrāmaṇera wash the bowl.
At that time, Śāriputra had a śrāmaṇera named Cunda whom he regularly instructed to carry his bowl; the śrāmaṇera came and requested of his teacher, "Upādhyāya!..."
"I wish for you to give me the bowl; I shall wash it.
Śāriputra said, "The Buddha has already established a training rule (śikṣāpada) prohibiting the damaging of bowls."
He then replied, "How could I possibly commit such a transgression?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you know that a śrāmaṇera is capable of maintaining and protecting it, allow him to wash the bowl.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who possessed an iron bowl that had become stained, damaged, and full of cracks. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whenever one keeps an iron bowl, it should be thoroughly fired."
At that time, the bhikṣus piled up a great deal of firewood to burn their bowls, which caused them to break. The Buddha said:
"One should not burn the bowls with fire in this manner; they may be placed inside a basket and burned."
He did not know how to make the basket.
The Buddha said,
"There are two kinds of baskets:"
First is that made by a craftsman; second is that made by oneself.
Regarding "made by a craftsman," this refers to a potter.
Regarding "made by oneself," it means using either a jar or a large pitcher, cutting them apart for use.
He placed it on the ground and struck it, whereupon it shattered. The Buddha said:
"Fill it with ashes until it is full and have someone carry it; then, using a chisel, gradually bore holes through it at intervals until it is split into two pieces."
At that time, they did not apply mud to the exterior. The Buddha said:
"One should make mud from grass and bran and apply it everywhere.
They did not apply any substance to wipe or plaster the interior. The Buddha said:
"One should use hemp dregs to make a paste for smearing and allow it to dry.
However, the fired bowl still did not take on its proper color. The Buddha said:
"Place rice bran inside, cover it with a lid, and apply a coating of clay around the rim."
He then placed the bowl on the ground to fumigate it. The Buddha said:
"One should use a support made of some material; placing another object on top of it for this purpose is also done in the same manner.
Because that support was thin and small, the bowl would stick to it. The Buddha said:
"One should place them on high supports so that they do not touch one another.
Still, the color did not take hold; the Buddha said:
"One should wash them repeatedly and then burn them again."
Smoke issued from within the basket, and the Buddha said:
"One should block the opening with ashes.
When he piled up cow dung into a large heap and burned it, the bowl was damaged; the Buddha said:
"One should pile up cow dung and set fire to it from the top.
Not knowing whom he should send to watch the fire,
the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should guard [the bowl] himself; if there is another reason, he may entrust it to another bhikṣu to watch over before departing.
Because many insects were harmed by the bowls being heated on the ground, the Buddha said:
"One should sprinkle and sweep [the area] thoroughly to purify it."
Therefore, I now permit the bhikṣus to possess a bowl-smoking rack and all items necessary for it; their use shall involve no offense.
The summary verse of the third section says:
“One should not interchange robes; when bathing, one may screen oneself from others.”
"One does not shave one's head on a mat; a sick person may take food according to their needs.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a donor who constructed a bathhouse and offered it to the Saṃgha; at that time, the six bhikṣus each wore a single lower garment and rubbed their bodies against one another.
When laypeople entered and saw them, they spoke thus:
"What kind of non-Buddhists are these people?
At that time, those who were respectful and faithful replied:
“They are the sons of Śākya.
Upon hearing this, the householder immediately gave rise to derision and reproach:
“Their Great Teacher is always possessed of a sense of shame and modesty; how can these people be so devoid of shame?”
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not rub or wash against one another using only a single lower garment.
Should anyone violate this, they shall incur a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, the bhikṣus allowed laypeople to enter the bathhouse. Seeing the bhikṣus scrubbing their feet with their hands and then rubbing their heads, the laypeople criticized them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, practice such vulgar methods; they are not clean or pure, for having scrubbed their feet, they then use those same hands to rub their heads."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When entering the bathhouse, one should not allow those who lack faith and respect to enter, nor should one have them perform work there."
"If one instructs another to do so, they incur the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

At that time, while the bhikṣus were inside the bathhouse with no one to guard them, some lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) entered the room. Seeing the bhikṣus rubbing their feet with their hands and then using those same hands to wash their faces, they spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are truly base and wicked; they rub their feet with their hands and then use those very hands to wash their faces."
The Buddha said, "When bathing, do not allow laypeople to enter the bathhouse; you should appoint a bhikṣu to act as a guardian.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the Jetavana with a certain Brahmin who lacked faith. When the bhikṣus saw them, they addressed the householder, saying:
"Do not allow this man to enter the bathhouse.
The brahmin asked, "What fault have I committed that I am being barred?"
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you know that the person has pure faith, you should permit them to enter the room.
At that time, there was a brahmin who, having been barred upon entering, saw others who were not obstructed and said:
"All those laypeople are permitted to enter the room; why am I alone being barred?
The bhikṣu replied, "This person has already taken refuge and received the various precepts."
He replied, "I too take refuge and accept the precepts; I pray that you will allow me to enter. He was told:
"Very well," he replied, and immediately granted him the precepts and permitted his entry.
Once he had entered, he saw the bhikṣus rubbing their lower bodies and then using those same hands to rub their heads; he then gave rise to derision, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are indeed base and impure.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you know that a person has long harbored faith, allow them to enter; if they are newly faithful, do not permit it."
The setting was as before.

At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to enter his chamber for a bath. Thereupon, the World-Honored One led the bhikṣus to the bathing place of that householder, where he saw one bhikṣu massaging the body of another bhikṣu.
The Blessed One asked,
"Do you see this bhikṣu rubbing and massaging the body of that bhikṣu?
They replied, "We do."
“I have seen it,” [the monk replied]. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“He who has performed the rubbing is an arhat whose outflows are exhausted.”
Those who accept such massages are practitioners of broken precepts who perform evil deeds.
You should know this!
A lion should not serve as an attendant to a jackal.
The setting is the same as before.
There was a certain householder who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son.

When the boy had grown up, he went forth into homelessness within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya. Constantly seeking what was superior to himself and investigating the meaning [of the teachings], he traveled to other regions to study extensively and gain great learning, and has now returned here to this city of Śrāvastī.
When the father heard that his son had arrived, he went to where he was and exchanged greetings with him.
At that time, the bhikṣu briefly proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma for his father, exhorting him to take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts.
Later, at another time, he again explained to his father the merit and virtues of the seven types of meritorious actions involving material things.
Upon hearing his son’s explanation, the father conceived deep reverence and faith, saying:
"Venerable sir, you should know!"
"I now also wish to perform the meritorious deeds of the seven types of material offerings. He replied, "Do as you please."
The father then asked,
"What did you do previously? He replied:
"You should manage the construction of a bathhouse for the Saṃgha.
Having heard this, he returned home, completed the management of the construction, and came to report to his son, saying:
"Venerable One!"
"You should invoke my name and invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to come to my house to bathe.
Having heard this, the son immediately went to where the Buddha was and, invoking his father's name, made the invitation on his behalf.
At that time, the householder conceived a deep sense of faith; he personally applied oil to the bhikṣu’s body and rubbed it off with rice bran.
When the bathing was finished, he said to his son, "I am extremely fatigued; please massage my back for me."
The son replied, "The World-Honored One has already established a training rule regarding this.
The father then asked:
"What was the matter for which the training rule was established?
He replied, "Do not serve a jackal as you would a teacher; therefore, I should not perform such service."
The father asked his son,
"Who is the lion? Who is the jackal?"
The son replied to his father, "I am a lion; you are a jackal.
The father said:
"This is a marvelous thing, for I, a jackal, am able to give birth to a lion.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"In all cases, parents perform difficult deeds for their children and bear manifold sufferings on their behalf; even if the parents are utterly corrupt in their precepts, the child should still provide them with service and support."
Therefore, I permit that one should provide for five persons even if they have utterly violated the precepts: namely, one’s father, mother, preceptor, instructor, and all those who are sick.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who built a dwelling in a forest hermitage (āraṇya) and invited the bhikṣus to rely upon it while they went about begging for food according to their needs.
At that time, the mendicant’s beard and hair had grown long, so he went to the house of the elder. Upon seeing him, the elder asked, "Noble one!
Why is your beard and hair so very long?"
He replied, "O noble sir! There is no one to shave my hair."
The householder said, "I have sent someone here; please have him shave [your hair].
That barber went to the bhikṣu's location and had him shave his hair upon the bedding.
At that time, the householder thought to himself, "I should observe whether the Venerable One has shaved his hair or not.
He then went to the forest hermitage where the bhikṣus resided; having arrived, he sat down upon a bedding mat, and his hair became caught in his garment.
When the elder returned home, his wife saw hair upon his garment and said,
"Why did you pass by that barber's house, causing this garment to be defiled by hair?"
The householder reflected:
"Could it be that the Noble One shaved his hair upon that mat?
He went back to look closely and, seeing the place where the hair had been shaved upon the mat, he said:
“Venerable Sir!
You may shave your hair elsewhere; do not let it soil the mat.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not shave the beard and hair upon a bedding mat.
He then shaved off his beard and hair on a clean patch of ground. The Buddha said:
"In general, one should not shave one's hair on a clean patch of ground that has been swept by the Saṃgha; whoever violates this incurs the offense of duṣkṛta."
At that time, there was an elderly and infirm bhikṣu who was unable to go outside to have his hair shaved; furthermore, he encountered wind and rain. The Buddha said:
"If one lacks the strength, one may shave oneself wherever one is; however, one must sweep and wipe the area clean. If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
Furthermore, when the bhikṣus trimmed their fingernails and toenails and discarded them wherever they pleased, the Buddha said:
"If one discards fingernails or toenails upon the Saṃgha’s pure ground (śuddhasthāna), one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted by a grave illness and oppressed by suffering; he went to a physician and said, "O worthy one!
"Please prescribe for me the medicine that is appropriate.
The physician replied, "Mix flour with water; it may be eaten at an improper time."
He replied, "O virtuous one!
The World-Honored One has already established a precept, not permitting us to eat at improper times."
The physician replied, "Noble one!
Our Great Teacher is compassionate; he will surely grant permission for all sick people on this account."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are toothless oxen that eat broken grains of rice and barley; later, when they excrete them, the kernels remain whole. One may use these as flour and consume them at improper times."
At that time, although the sick bhikṣu took the medicine, he was not cured. The physician asked him, "Venerable One!
Has the ailment you previously suffered from improved?"
He replied, "O worthy one! Even now it has not yet been removed."
The physician said,
"Is it not because the Venerable One has not yet consumed water and parched grain that his illness has not been cured?
The Bhikṣu replied:
"I have finished taking it.
The physician asked,
"How did you take it?"
At that time, the sick bhikṣu related the matter in detail, and the physician said:
"Noble one! This is not the medicine; you should instead use raw barley flour."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Take a large amount of water, stir it, filter it through a cloth, and then you should drink it.
When the illness still did not improve, he again informed the physician of this matter, and the physician replied:
"Do not drink it without filtering.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"If a physician prescribes that one should drink gruel, whether it be thick or in the form of a bolus, it should be taken as desired."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted with a serious illness; he went to a physician and asked, "O worthy one!"
"Prescribe for me a medicinal decoction using whatever herbs are appropriate.
The physician replied,
"Prepare a large mass of flesh, boil it at an improper time, and drink it."
He replied: "O worthy one! The World-Honored One has already established a prohibition."
The physician replied, "Noble One!
Our Great Teacher is compassionate; he will surely grant permission for all the sick on account of this matter."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"There is a beast called a jackal whose intestines are straight; it excretes its meat immediately after eating, and the body [of the meat] has not yet changed. One should take that meat, boil it, and drink it."
Although his treatment did not improve his condition, the physician asked,
"Venerable One, has your ailment been relieved?"
He replied, "It has not been damaged.
The physician said:
"How could it be that this illness has not been alleviated because the Noble One has not yet consumed meat broth?
The bhikṣu related the matter in detail, and the physician said,
"Noble One!..."
"This old substance is unfit to serve as medicine; you should take fresh meat, boil it, and drink the broth.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "First filter it with a cloth, and then drink it."
The illness still did not subside, so he informed the physician of this matter. The physician replied, "Take it without filtering.
He reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The physician’s prescription should be taken as directed; whether dry or moist, provided it possesses flavor, it should all be consumed without giving rise to doubt.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In all matters, whatever I have permitted for a sick person at improper times must not be done after the illness has been cured."
If anyone should do so, they shall incur an offense against the Dharma.

The fourth section, the Summary Verses, says:
Smoking pipes and dyed robes, Nasal tubes and water-drinking vessels.
The syringe is not a precious object; it is for eye medicine and for applying ointment to the spine.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“As the Blessed One has said:
‘I allow the bhikṣus to possess smoking pipes.
We do not know what kind of object it is that should be made.”
The Buddha said:
"With the exception of precious objects, all other items may be kept.
[He continued: "As the World-Honored One has said:"
Regarding the instruction, "Permit all bhikṣus to wear robes of dyed color," [the monks] did not know what things constituted such items.
The Buddha said:
"One may keep a [nose-cleansing] tool made from seven types of thread as one wishes.
Furthermore, although it was permitted for the bhikṣus to possess nose-pipe tubes, they did not know with what material they should be made.
The Buddha said,
"Except for precious materials.
Again, [the monks] were permitted to possess drinking vessels, but they did not know with what material they should be made.
The Buddha said, "Except for jewels. [The monks asked:
"Furthermore, you have permitted the bhikṣus to possess needle cases; we do not know with what material they should be made?"
The Buddha said, "Except for jewels.
[The monks asked,] "Furthermore, you have permitted the keeping of eye-medicine pestles and small medicine boxes; we do not know with what material they should be made?"
The Buddha said:
"With the exception of jewels,
all other items may be kept."
The fifth section, summarized in verse, says:
Medicine vessels and woolen rugs, footstools and purgatives—these a bhikṣu should not make;
one should select the robes of the deceased.
The setting was as before.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“As the Blessed One has said:”
"The Buddha has permitted the bhikṣus to possess containers for storing medicine.
What materials should be used?
The Buddha said:
“Except for various precious objects.
[The monks asked: “Furthermore, although it has been permitted for bhikṣus to possess woolen rugs (*kambala*), we do not know which ones are appropriate to possess?
The Buddha said:
"One may possess and maintain [a footstool] made of seven kinds of thread.
Furthermore, it is permitted for bhikṣus to possess a footstool for the purpose of washing their feet; what material should it be made of?"
The Buddha said:
"Except for jewels.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.
At that time, there was an elder who was afflicted with a grave illness; he went to a physician and asked, "Virtuous sir!
Please prescribe for me the medicine that is appropriate."
The physician replied,
"First consume oily substances to provoke the illness, and only then should one take the purgative.
Upon hearing this, the elder consumed ghee.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whom the elder had regularly supported; he came to the elder’s house to inquire after the sick man, asking, "Is your strength and well-being secure?
The man replied:
“Noble One! I am still ill;
the physician has prescribed that I first take clarified butter and afterwards take a purgative.
At that time, the bhikṣu replied to the householder:
"I am skilled in medical arts; you have medicine intended as payment for a physician, so you should give it to me. I have a purgative that I can give to you.
Having heard this, the householder replied, "Excellent!"
The bhikṣu took the medicine and gave it to him to take.
At that time, the elder’s dosage was excessive, so he sent a messenger in haste to the physician’s place to ask:
"O worthy sir!"
"The master of my household has not ceased taking medicine.
The physician asked,
"Who administered the medicine?"
The messenger replied,
"There is a bhikṣu. Upon hearing this,
the physician was filled with anger and resentment.
"You should go there and ask what medicine it is.
When he went back to the place where the bhikṣus were to inquire, the elder had already passed away.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus! You should not sell medicine.
If a bhikṣu is skilled in medical formulas, he should, out of a heart of compassion, provide medicine according to the illness.”
However, monks should not administer a purgative to another and then depart; they should personally observe [the patient] to ensure it does not exceed the proper limit.
If they must go elsewhere, they should entrust someone to watch over the patient before leaving, and furthermore, inform them, saying:
"If the purgative proves excessive, you should use such-and-such medicine as a remedy."
“If there is a bhikṣu who receives the value of a payment and subsequently gives medicine, or who accepts wages to work as a hired laborer, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a man who owed a debt to a householder; having been detained for seven or eight days, they entered into an agreement that he would repay it on a certain day.
Then the debtor thought to himself:
"The appointed date is drawing near, yet I have nothing to repay him; I ought to hide and evade him."
He further reflected:
"To abandon my home and flee is difficult; I shall instead kill him.
At that time, as the elder was near the Jeta Grove, he was killed by the debtor. Seeing that the man’s body was still clothed, the group of six monks said to one another:
"Now is the time for an abundance of rag-robes.
Having spoken these words, they immediately went together to take them.
At that moment, the householder’s kinsmen arrived and saw them; they reviled them with harsh words, saying:
"Noble one! To wear the robes of a great seer and yet commit such an unrighteous act is utterly base and contemptible.
The group of six replied:
"This was not killed by us; another enemy came and took his life. We are now taking discarded rags (pāṃsukūla); what fault is there in this?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!..."
One should not take up these discarded rags (pāṃsukūla) haphazardly; rather, if they are known by the community to be abandoned items, these robes may be taken.
Otherwise, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
