The Buddha said:
"Except for precious objects.
The setting and circumstances were as before.
At that time, the six bhikṣus themselves carried loads on their backs or held large bundles upon their shoulders.
At that time, some brahmins and householders, having seen this, mocked him, saying: "Venerable sir!
We are worldly people who, for the sake of our parents, wives, children, and kinsmen, seek out food and clothing and bear these burdens upon our bodies."
"For whose sake, O virtuous ones, have you exerted yourselves in this laborious task?
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!"
"One should not carry or bear large bundles on the head, back, shoulders, or waist.
Should anyone violate this, they shall incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The setting of the rule is the same as before.

At that time, there was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, gave birth to a son. The child’s countenance was upright and handsome, a sight for which people took delight. The father then held a birth feast for his son and entrusted him to various nurses to raise him.

As the son gradually grew up, he went forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma. During the first watch of the day, having put on his robes and taken up his alms bowl, he entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Suddenly he encountered his father, who asked him:
"Have you already gone forth?"
He replied, "I have left the household life.
His father said to him:

"This body of yours was brought forth by me; now that it has reached maturity, you ought to be concerned for my well-being in matters of both suffering and joy. Now that you have abandoned us to go forth into homelessness, who will provide for me?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“How could we possibly perform the affairs of householders?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Parents perform difficult deeds for their children and shoulder manifold sufferings; even if [the child] has gone forth into homelessness, they ought to provide for their parents.
At that time, he did not know what object he should give.
The Buddha said:
"One should provide for them from one's robes, bowl, and other belongings.
If there are no such items, one may request them from a donor at the appropriate time."
If it is difficult to obtain through begging, one should provide for them using the goods regularly acquired by the Saṃgha.
If there are no such goods, one should take half of the portion of food regularly consumed by the Saṃgha and use it to provide for them.
"If one who constantly begs for alms lives dependent on others, they should take half of the food sufficient to fill their own belly and give it to their parents.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.
At that time, there was a donor who established a dwelling within a village to provide for the community of monks, and an elderly bhikṣu resided there.
Once, this elderly bhikṣu went to the Jetavana Grove in order to pay homage to the caitya.
For the sake of profit, the six groups of bhikṣus established a regulation that they would take turns, always sending one person to stand outside the gate.
When it was Upānanda’s turn to be on duty, he went to the gate and stood there walking up and down. Seeing from afar that an elderly bhikṣu was approaching, he thought to himself:
“Who is this venerable elder?”
"I should go to him and offer my respects.
Having arrived, he asked, "Welcome!"
"Welcome! He then replied, "I now pay homage to the ācārya."
Upānanda then thought to himself:
"This is merely an old man who has gone forth; not only does he fail to recognize his two root preceptors, but he has never even known how to revere the Dharma."
He then greeted him, saying, "Welcome, old father!
He immediately led him into the Jeta Grove, providing him with refreshments and allowing him to rest for a while.
Then the elderly bhikṣu said: "Venerable Upānanda!
I must go out now."
At that time, he asked:
"Where do you wish to go? He replied:
"I shall go to pay my respects at the caitya and then return," but Upānanda again urged him to stay. He said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I did not intend beforehand to stay outside, so I left my three robes at my original location; therefore, I should not remain here for long.
Upānanda said, "Do not worry about these three robes; I shall give them to you, and you should maintain possession of them."
He then gave him a large woolen cloak (*kambala*) and a small woolen rug (*karpata*), which he took to serve as his three robes (*tricīvara*) and as lower garments.
After the afternoon meal, when the *gandī* was struck, all those who paid homage to the *caitya* gathered together.
An elder bhikṣu said, "Upānanda!..."
"I shall briefly leave my cell to pay homage to the caitya.
He replied, "Old man!"
"You have no three robes; how can you pay your respects?

He then took a small mat to serve as his lower garment (*antarvāsaka*), tied a coarse rope around his waist to bind it in place, and further used a woolen shawl with the fleece side out to serve as an *uttarāsaṅga*. He also used a heavy, thick woolen blanket with the fleece side out to serve as a *saṃghāṭī*.
Having done this, he replied: "O Mahallaka!
You may now pay your respects as you please."
When the elderly bhikṣu had finished putting on his robes, he immediately went outside the room. Seeing him, the other bhikṣus all said: "Old man!
Where did you get this ridiculous robe to wear?"
He replied, "I maintain these three robes exactly as prescribed by the Buddha; how can this be called 'playing'? The bhikṣu asked:
"Who gave you these three robes?
He replied, "The Venerable Upānanda!"
When the people heard this, they all said:
"Apart from these individuals, who else could commit such an evil deed?
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Long-haired garments have such faults as these.
You bhikṣus! You must not, under any circumstances, possess any long-haired material to serve as your three robes.”
"If there be any who violate this, they shall incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
As the Blessed One said:
"I decree that no bhikṣus shall keep long-haired triple robes (*tricīvara*)."

At that time, there were brahmins and householders of pure faith who offered coarse woolen blankets and other thick cloaks to the bhikṣus; however, the bhikṣus, having become doubtful, did not dare to accept them.
Those householders replied, "Noble One! If the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, had not appeared in the world, we would have regarded the non-Buddhist teachers as superior."

"Now that the World-Honored One has descended into this realm of birth, we have taken you, O Benevolent One, as our supreme field of merit. Having offered these meager things, we do not receive your acceptance; how could we be permitted to abandon the provisions for virtue and pass from this world to the next?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"You should accept it, regarding it as belonging to another, and use it while maintaining it as such.
If the wool is short, light, and thin, this item should be treated as a long robe (dīrghacīvara) and kept."
"Whatever items such as thick, large, or long-haired objects exist, one should always regard them as the property of their respective donors and keep them for use.
The seventh section, a summary verse, says:
"Hair and nail reliquaries (stūpas) may be made in a fresh white color."
One may place lamps wherever one wishes, provided that on one side there is a high eaves.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the place where the World-Honored One was and addressed him, saying:
"I now wish to construct a stūpa for the hair and nail-clippings of the Blessed One; I only pray that the Blessed One, out of compassion, will grant me permission.
The Blessed One replied, "You may do as you please."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will permit me to smear and polish the hair-and-nail stūpa with fresh white substances, and furthermore to offer worship by arranging rows of lamps at that very spot."
The Buddha said, "Do as you please.
The elder placed the lamp upon the steps, and the oil dripped down and defiled the stūpa. The Buddha said:
"One may arrange lamps in rows along the steps.
A dog ate the oil and knocked over the oil vessel; the householder said to the Buddha, "Please have lamp-stands made."
The Buddha said, "Do as you please.
When a cow came and gored it, the elder informed the Buddha:
"Please construct a lamp stand.
The Buddha said,
"It should be made."
"Placing lamps on all four sides would not provide sufficient illumination. The householder addressed the Buddha, saying, "I request that you allow for a high eaves.
The Buddha said:
"As you wish. The eighth son’s summary verse says:
"The gateways and eaves of the hall, as well as the foundations beneath the stūpas."
"Coated with red stone and purple mineral, these were all made according to circumstances.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I only pray that you will permit me to construct a doorway within the empty space between the hair-and-nail stūpa, further install a porch, and build a foundation for a tower; moreover, I shall smear its pillars with red stone and paint the walls of the tower with purple mineral."
The Buddha said, “As you wish.
The ninth son summarized the verse as follows:
One should not drive in stakes, nor climb upon a stūpa;
the use of gold and silver flowers is permitted, as is covering the top of a stūpa with a roof.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
When the community of bhikṣus was making offerings, they wished to hang flower garlands upon the stūpa; they immediately climbed up and drove nails into the stūpa to suspend the various garlands.
Then the brahmins and householders all said this:
"O Great Masters, you have long since removed the nails and thorns; for what reason do you now drive them back in?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not drive sharp spikes into a stūpa; whoever violates this incurs the offense of duṣkṛta."
"However, at the time of first constructing a stūpa, one should drive out auxiliary stakes to serve as ivory pegs.
Later, when it was time for offerings, some bhikṣus climbed to the very top of the stūpa to place oil lamps there. The Buddha said:
"One must not set up lamps upon the summit of the fragrance platform; whoever violates this incurs the offense of duṣkṛta (wrongdoing)."
At that time, the bhikṣus ascended the stūpa to install banners, canopies, and other articles of offering.
Thereupon, the brahmins and householders all criticized them,
saying, "They have defiled it by treading upon it."
The Buddha said:
"One should employ a layperson.
If there is no layperson, one should employ a śrāmaṇera."
If there is no śrāmaṇera present, the bhikṣus should first wash their feet with pure scented water or smear them with fragrant mud, making this reflection:
"I now do this desiring to make an offering to the Great Teacher."
"Only after that should one ascend the stūpa.
If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If the stūpa is tall and large, one should fasten a rope to the lower part of the parasol rings (*chattra*) and climb up by pulling upon it."

There were brahmins and householders who all came to the stūpa of hair and nails, each bringing flower garlands to offer as an act of worship. They did not remove the withered flowers, so that it could not remain clean.
The Buddha said: "Remove them."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now wish to offer a flower garland of gold and silver as an offering to the stūpa of hair and nails.
The Buddha said:
"Build it accordingly.
When birds nested on top of the stupa and defiled it with impurities, [the monks] wished to construct a protective shelter over it.
The Buddha said, "It should be built."
Furthermore, as the room was doorless, dark, and dilapidated, the Buddha said,
"Open the door as you please.
The tenth sub-section concludes with a summary verse:
Stūpas may be constructed of iron, as well as of gold, silver, and so forth;
the offering of banners and flags is permitted, and fragrant oil may also be used.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada requested of the World-Honored One, saying,
"I pray that you will permit me to construct an iron stūpa.
The Buddha said:
"Proceed accordingly," he replied. He further said,
"I wish to have it fashioned from gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, copper, and so forth."
The Buddha said, "It should be made.
[He continued,] "Although it has been made, the top of the stūpa is not yet well-adorned; I wish to offer worship by means of banners, flags, and various silken fabrics."
The Buddha said,
“It should be made.
At that time, they did not understand the ritual method for constructing the banner, so the Buddha said:
“There are four kinds of banners: namely, the lion banner, the ox banner, the garuḍa banner, and the nāga banner.
On the flags and streamers, he painted these four forms and further addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I now wish first to apply fragrant oil for rubbing, and next to prepare exquisite perfumed water using purple resin, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth, to wash the hair and nail stūpas. I only pray that you will grant me permission.”
The Buddha said,
"All may act according to their wishes.
The third section concludes.
The summary verse for the fourth section on miscellaneous rules (*nidāna*) states:
Door-bolts and their use in various places; Wetting the robes during defecation and urination;
Dyeing robes, damaging them, and identifying robes; Postponing the acquisition of robes, fruits, and the absence of purification.
The first sub-section is summarized in this verse:
Door-bells, leaning against the belt, and nets; Gathering rice for the community’s meal, Building private rooms within the monastery— Those who dwell there should make use of them.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the Blessed One has said:”
"One should install rings and knobs upon the door panels.
The bhikṣus did not know what materials should be used for this.
The Buddha said:
"Except for precious materials, other substances may be used.
As the Blessed One said:
"A bhikṣu should make a shoulder-strap (kaṭicāpaka)."
“I do not know what materials should be used.
The Buddha said,
“Any one of the seven kinds of thread may be used.”
“As the World-Honored One has said,
‘I allow the keeping of nets,’ what materials should be used for them?”
The Buddha said:
"One may use *māo*, *kuài*, *má*, or *máng* grasses for all such purposes.
The World-Honored One further said:
"Allowing for window screens—
what materials should be used?
The Buddha said:
"Except for precious items, all others may be used.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

In this city, there was a householder who conceived deep faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem; being of virtuous disposition, he subsequently married a daughter from among the naked ascetics (nirgranthas). The householder said to her:

"O Worthy One! The Unsurpassed Compassionate Father is my Great Teacher, whom I constantly honor, as well as the Sangha, the supreme field of merit; you should likewise provide them with robes, food, and drink."
At that time, the bhikṣus regularly followed the monastic order and went to this house every day to receive their food.
On one occasion, the elder encountered some other business and had to go to another village; he said to his wife, "I now have a matter that requires me to go to that village."
"Just as when I was alive, you should always provide offerings at the places of the Buddha and the Sangha,
and never let them be in want. He replied, "Noble son!"
"I shall act according to your instructions.
Then that householder went to the bhikṣu and said,
"Noble One!..."

"I now have business that requires me to go to another village; I only wish that the Saṃgha would always take their turn according to seniority and partake of a meal at my home. They replied, "So be it."
At that time, the bhikṣus deliberated among themselves, saying:
"That householder’s wife previously lacked faith; those who rely on the sequence of the Saṃgha must arrive early.
When the householder’s wife saw the bhikṣus arriving, she spoke with resentment, saying:
"Why have you venerable ones arrived so early at dawn, when we have not yet prepared the food and the seats have not even been spread?

Then the bhikṣus said to one another, "That householder’s wife has long been known for her lack of faith; we have already seen her anger since our early arrival today. Tomorrow, we should go to her residence at midday."
Then, at dawn on the following morning, the householder’s wife prepared food, arranged seats, and waited for the bhikṣus. At that time, the Saṃgha arrived only when midday had come.
The woman said, “Noble ones!”
"Do I have no other business and do nothing but this?
I have already prepared the food and arranged the seats early in the morning; for what reason have you gentlemen come only at midday?"
Then the bhikṣus said to one another:

"We came early and were already scolded; having arrived at midday, we have been rebuked once more. Since begging for alms is our constant practice, we should instead go from house to house to provide for ourselves, rather than going to that lay household to eat."
Then, when that householder had finished his business and returned home, he asked his wife,
"O virtuous lady!
Do those noble ones come to eat regularly?"
He replied, "We accepted food here for only the first two days; we have not come again since.
The householder reflected:
"It must be my wife who, manifesting signs of stinginess, has caused the noble ones not to come to receive food.
At that time, as the bhikṣus were going on their alms-round from house to house, they entered the gate of the elder's residence; having seen them, the elder asked: "Noble ones!"
"Virtuous ones, why do you not come regularly to receive food?
They replied, "Householder!"
"We were originally mendicants who lived by begging; we need only carry our alms bowls to travel and obtain sufficient sustenance.
He replied, "Noble ones!"
"It is only that my wife has conceived a mind of stinginess.
However, the rice in my field has ripened anew this year; you may take as much as you wish to satisfy your midday meal.
The bhikṣu replied:
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one maintains the intention that it belongs to the Saṃgha and holds it as such, there is no offense."
Furthermore, there was an elder who constructed a separate dwelling for the bhikṣus within the Jeta Grove; inside that dwelling, he provided many beds, mats, and various articles of sustenance.
At that time, the bhikṣus took turns guarding the property, placing the items belonging to individual rooms among the communal goods.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The property of an individual room may be used according to its location."
Furthermore, regarding the mixing of gains with communal property, the Buddha said:
"They should not be mixed; those who reside in separate quarters should be permitted to use them.
The second sub-section is summarized in a verse:
"Whatever materials are required for each location, and whatever tools, food, lamps,
and oil are needed by those engaged in construction, shall be used according to the application of the donor.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was an elder who built a separate room within an old monastery; in that room, he provided many beds and mats, and all necessary provisions were abundant and complete.
At that time, the bhikṣus took personal items and mixed them with the communal property. The Buddha said:
"One should utilize [the property] according to the residents; furthermore, all offerings and gains should not be commingled, but should be used according to their original application."
At that time, when the bhikṣus were distributing communal property, they were unwilling to share it with those residing in separate rooms. The Buddha said:
"Even for those who occupy separate rooms, the communal benefits must be shared."
At that time, the bhikṣus appointed an administrator, but because he saw that there was a separate room, he did not dispatch him. The Buddha said:
"He should be dispatched according to the order of seniority.
In this city, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms, and he exhorted that donor to take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts.
On another occasion, he taught that donor the seven meritorious actions involving material things and praised their benefits.
The donor replied, "I too am capable of performing them; what deeds should I do?"
He replied, "One should construct a dwelling place for the Saṃgha.
The donor then said:
"I possess wealth and wish to perform meritorious deeds, yet I have no one to assist me.
The bhikṣu said, "You may bring it here; I can assist you in its execution."
Then that donor presented the materials and requested that they be used for construction.
The bhikṣu took the materials and placed them in his own room, but did not have the construction carried out.
The donor thought to himself:
"I shall go for a moment to see whether the newly constructed dwelling has been completed.
When the donor arrived, he did not see any place under construction and said, "Noble One!"
"Why have you not engaged in construction for so long?
The bhikṣu replied, "The tools required for construction are what I need; since these items are entirely absent, how can the work be undertaken?"
The donor replied, "How is it that the items I have given are not sufficient for use?
The bhikṣu replied:
"This item already belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions; who would dare to damage or use it?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“O donor, listen; you should take this object and make it into utensils.
At that time, while going on his alms round, the bhikṣu arrived at the donor’s house. Seeing him from afar, the elder spoke these words: “Noble One!”
"Since you, O Benevolent One, go daily on alms rounds throughout the town, who will look after the monastery I have built?
The bhikṣu replied,
"How could I bear to build a monastery for someone else while remaining hungry?"
The householder replied,
"Why do you not take and eat the food I have offered?
They answered:
"This item already belongs to the Saṃgha of the four quarters; the Buddha has not yet permitted its use.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the donor permits it, it should be used."
They then prepared exquisite and delicious food and drink, eating and drinking according to their own desires.
The Buddha said, "It should not be like this; you should eat coarse food.
When they were eating coarse food, they lacked the strength to supervise [the distribution]. The Buddha said:
"As is the constant custom of the Saṃgha.
When a bhikṣu eats, he should store his utensils within a dark room; furthermore, he must carry oil for lamps as he goes from house to house to beg.
Then that donor, seeing him again seeking oil, asked: "Noble One!
What do you intend to do?"
He answered with the facts of the matter.
The householder replied,
"Why do you not use some goods?"
He answered in full as before, and the Buddha said:
"If the donor has given permission, there is no offense when using it.
He then kept the lamp lit throughout the entire night, and the Buddha said:
"One should not leave a lamp burning throughout the night; once the items have been gathered, it may be extinguished.
One should understand that this applies to ointments for the feet and other such articles; the management of these requisites should be conducted according to the principles set forth above."
The third section, summarized in verse, says:
Causing rain to fall upon the property of the Saṃgha; sharing beds at midnight;
small seats according to seniority; and the spreading of mats is all likewise.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The six bhikṣus of the group, having put on their saṃghāṭī robes and gone outside, each left them placed in the open air, causing them to become ruined by the rain.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"The bedding and furnishings of the Saṃgha must not be allowed to be damaged by the summer rains; those who fail to collect and store them shall incur a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, the bhikṣus wore the saṃghāṭī robe while washing, dyeing, and making bowls, which caused the robes to be damaged. The Buddha said:
"If one wears the communal robe while dyeing it or making a bowl, one incurs the offense of duṣkṛta."

The group of six bhikṣus were traveling through the human realm when they came upon a village. In that village there was a monastic residence; they did not enter the monastery until after the first watch of the night had passed, at which point they went to their friends and acquaintances to relieve their fatigue.
The group of six monks said:
"Venerable sirs! The Great Teacher’s True Dharma currently abides in the world; why do you not rely upon his instructions?"
"Do not let yourselves feel regret later; you may assign me bedding according to your seniority.

At that time, the resident monks gathered all the small seats, beds, and mats belonging to the Saṃgha at midnight and divided them among themselves in one place. The group of six bhikṣus took their bedding and slept wherever they pleased; having finished providing for themselves, dawn soon broke.
At that time, the group of six monks said to the other bhikṣus, "Gather up your bedding; we wish to set out on our journey. The host replied:
"The Elder sought only one night for his own physical comfort, yet he caused the entire assembly to contract jaundice.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not occupy the monastic bedding during the night; rather, one may stay for one night according to the company of friends."
"If you stay longer, you may be given [a bed] according to your seniority; otherwise, you will incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a certain village. In that village there was a dwelling place, and having entered the monastery, they saw old beds and mats. Thereupon, the group of six, along with their disciples, each lay down to sleep upon the large beds.
However, these six groups were all elderly, and no one was ever able to move them; the other senior monks simply lay down wherever they found space upon the ground.
When dawn had broken, he went to the Jetavana Grove; seeing him, the bhikṣus said, "Welcome! Welcome!"
"Have you been able to travel with ease and find peace?
He replied, "How could there be any peace? Having lain upon the ground all night long, I have not known a moment's rest."
He replied, "Venerable sir!
In which room did you sleep last night?"
He then related these matters in detail to the others.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"As for large beds, seats, and other rugs or cushions, they should be distributed from the senior monk (sthavira) downward according to the order of seniority."
The fourth section, summarized in verse, says:
Regarding the places for excrement and urine, walking meditation, and not disturbing others,
washing the feet and wiping the shoes, and the cauldron and ladle— do not seize them for use.
The setting was as before.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus frequently came and went from the latrines and urinals to perform walking meditation, while conversing together, giving instructions, reciting texts, and engaging in various forms of frivolous play.
Seeing another bhikṣu about to enter, he then obstructed him, saying:
"Do not enter for now; I am the elder.
Thus, he intentionally caused delay and made the other person feel vexed.
At that time, the bhikṣus gave rise to feelings of aversion and contempt, and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"One should not walk back and forth or linger for a long time in places for defecation and urination to cause annoyance to others; whoever violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group, by the water jars at the place for washing feet, drove others away, saying:
"We are the elders; it is right that we use [the water] first."
The Buddha said:
"At the place for washing one's feet, if someone is already there and their task is not yet finished, one should not forcibly call them to rise; to do so constitutes an offense against the Dharma."
At that time, a bhikṣu had already entered to urinate when the group of six arrived behind him and said,
"We are old! The Buddha said:
"One who arrives first may enter immediately; this place does not follow the order of seniority.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who, while halfway through washing their feet, were approached by the group of six who said to them:
"We are seniors; you should yield to us."
The Buddha said: "It should not be so.
Generally, one who serves as an elder must recognize the propriety of the occasion; although he is entitled to precedence, if the matter is not yet concluded, he should not be asked to rise."
"If you cause it to be used, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a cloth for wiping his shoes; he intended to use half of it, but the Group of Six saw it and seized it, saying: "We are old!"
The Buddha said:
"One should not take based on seniority; one must wait until the other has finished using it. To snatch it away while they have not yet finished is an offense against the Dharma.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who were boiling medicine in a cauldron when it was not yet half-boiled, and the group of six bhikṣus snatched it away from them. They replied:
"I am old! This should be used first.
He poured it onto the ground and took the cauldron for himself.
The Buddha said:
"It is not permissible to rely on seniority; one must wait until the preceding matter is completed before proceeding.
Should one fail to follow this, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The monks of the Mahāsāṃghika school had already begun stirring the medicinal broth with an iron ladle when the group of six monks seized it from them. The Buddha said:
"This should not be done. Should anyone violate this, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The fifth section, summarized in verse, says:
Dyeing pots and water flasks, monastic bowls and drinking vessels,
knives, whetstones, and items for the nose, bed supports, and not inquiring about seniority.
The setting was as before.

There were certain bhikṣus who were using the Saṃgha’s dyeing vessels, jars, cauldrons, and other utensils to boil dye; when the task was nearly half-finished, the group of six [monks] said to them, "We should have used these first."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not take precedence based on seniority; one must wait until the others have finished using it.
If anyone forcibly seizes it, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had already taken up the communal bowl and had not yet finished his meal. The group of six [bhikṣus] said to him, "We are the elders; you should give it to us.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"When the other has finished eating, one should not take [the food] by force.
If one should take it by force intentionally, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharma-āpatti).
The same applies to drinking vessels and utensils; this should be understood accordingly."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had shaved his hair until it was half-finished when the group of six approached and seized his razor. The Buddha said:
"If the shaving is not yet complete, one should not take [the razor] and use it."
"The whetstone for the knife should be understood to follow the same principle as above.

When the small nail-clippers were used to cut only half [of the nails], and the nose-tweezers were still in use and not yet finished, as well as the items for supporting the bed, they were taken away while he was lying down. He reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"None of these items shall be taken back according to the number of years; one may only take them back once that person's business is concluded."
"If one does not comply, one shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The sixth section is summarized in a verse:
"Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe, when marking the lines and sewing it properly,"
One should not seize dyed liquids, miscellaneous items, and the like when they are being used.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, the great assembly possessed *kaṭhina* cloth.

There was a bhikṣu who was using this cloth to sew a saṃghāṭī and other robes; when he had finished only half of the garment, the group of six monks came along and saw him, whereupon they forcibly seized it, saying:
"We are the senior elders; by right, we should use it first."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If another person's use is not yet finished, you must not take it away abruptly; you may only take it once that person's business is concluded."
"If one seizes [the work] in such a manner, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma; thus it should be understood.
While the monks of the group of six were using the marked lines for sewing when only half was finished, they seized it. The Buddha said:
"One must wait until it is completed before taking it; he who takes it before completion incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"If one uses dye, a knife, a needle, a shaving cloth, or a sitting block, none of these should be confiscated;
this should be understood according to the preceding [rules]. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna*, Volume Four; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna*, Volume Five.
The Seventh Section, the Summary Verse, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree, says:
A non-Buddhist falsely claims ownership of a robe; making a mark on it, or giving it away at the time of death.
"There are five kinds of friends; having attained the Dharma, one should practice it alone.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.

Then, King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha, having heard the sublime Dharma and realized the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya), together with a multitude of eighty thousand devaputras, as well as more than a hundred thousand elders, householders, and brahmins from the kingdom of Magadha, established a solemn decree within the great assembly. He beat the drum to proclaim his command, universally announcing to all the people of the nation:
"No one shall ever commit theft.
Should anyone violate this, they shall be expelled from the country; all their household property and treasures shall be granted entirely to those who were robbed."
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the *Kumāra-sūtra* for King Prasenajit of Kośala. Once the king had been tamed, the Buddha also established a strict regulation throughout the kingdom:

"Within my realm, no one shall commit theft. Should anyone violate this, their life shall be taken; all the family property, storehouses, and wealth belonging to the offender shall be given entirely to the victim."
At that time, the bandits all fled and took up positions in camps between the two kingdoms.
There were merchants from the kingdom of Magadha who were traveling together toward the kingdom of Kośala.
Having reached that realm, the caravan leader said to his companions, "I am now safe;
you may return. Once the followers had departed, the bandits saw from afar that there was no one to protect them and proceeded to plunder them together.
At that time, all the merchants fled toward the kingdom of Kośala to seek refuge with King Prasenajit.
Having arrived at the king’s presence, they stepped forward and addressed him, saying:
“Great King, you should know that in this realm there was formerly much trade; however, because of these bandits, our merchant caravans no longer come.”
At that time, King Prasenajit commanded his great general named Virūḍhaka:
"You must go at once to capture those bandits and bring back both them and their stolen goods to appear before me."
At that time, the great general, leading his fourfold army—consisting of brave troops, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—proceeded to the location of the enemy camp in the wilderness forest.
There, the various bands of thieves had gathered in the perilous woods, laid down their weapons, and were distributing the plunder they had obtained.

At that time, when the general saw the bandits from afar, he deployed his troops in a complete circle around them on all four sides. As soon as the battle drums resounded, the bandits were struck with terror; some fled, some suffered injury, some were killed, and others were captured alive. Having recovered the stolen property along with the bandit leaders, he returned to the King’s presence and addressed the Great King, saying:
“These are those bandits and their plundered goods.”
Then King Prasenajit said to the people,
"Each of you may take back your own original belongings.

Once the merchants and traders had recognized their goods, the various non-Buddhist practitioners also took their own property, including their robes dyed with red ochre, as well as the robes and bowls belonging to the bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus arrived later at the king’s place, and the king said,
"Virtuous ones, you too should identify your robes and bowls.
The bhikṣus replied:
"There is no robe or bowl of mine among these goods.
The king said,
"Have you not already been plundered by bandits?"
He replied, "I,
too, have been robbed by bandits.
The king said:
"If there is no one else, you should summon that non-Buddhist ascetic and bring him along with the garment he claims.
When the non-Buddhist ascetic heard the king’s summons, he took the garment and came at once.
When the bhikṣu saw the robes, he spoke thus:
"This is my saṃghāṭī; this is my saṃkakṣikā.
The king said to the non-Buddhist:
"He is but a petty thief, while you are a great thief, for you have forcibly claimed another's garment.
He remained silent and offered no reply.
The King said:
“Noble One! Do you have some means of identifying your robes so that I may know which belong to the non-Buddhists and which belong to the bhikṣus?”
The bhikṣu replied,
"My robe is neutral (avyākṛta).
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu’s robes and requisites should be marked for identification.
Not knowing how to do so,
the Buddha said:
"One should hold [the object] only after it has been purified by making a knot or a mark with ink, and provided there is some other sign of identification.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son. His wife died, and he took a second wife; before long, she too gave birth to a son.
The second son was troubled by his mother and, longing for the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, desired to go forth; having gone forth, he traveled through the human world.
Later, when his father encountered a grave illness and knew for certain that he would die, he commanded his eldest son:
"All my wealth should be divided into three parts."
The son, having received his father’s command, immediately divided [the property] into three parts.
He then informed his son, saying:
"This portion is yours to use for the family estate; one portion belongs to me to provide for the funeral rites; and the remaining portion is for the son who has gone forth."
He then sighed to himself:
"All that is accumulated must disperse; all that is lofty will surely fall.
All meetings end in separation; all who have life return to death."
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away.

When the son who had left the household life heard that his father had died, he went at once to his brother’s place; they met with hearts full of affection, and after both had wailed together and finished their inquiries after one another's welfare, [the narrative continues].
The elder brother then said:
"On the day our father passed away, he left a final testament stating that one portion of his wealth should be set aside for you to take.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
“As the Blessed One has said:
‘After death, this non-Dharmic wealth shall be given to him.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"When any householder is about to pass away, they have a mind that clings [to worldly things]; such donated wealth should be accepted, and one should not harbor doubts regarding the portion of wealth allotted to the father."
Having received the wealth, they shall offer it as an act of worship to the Triple Gem.
Those who have left the household life will have no lingering attachment at the time of their death; if they say, "I shall give this after my death," [the recipient] may take it.
"Such wealth as this should not be accepted. The setting of the occasion was the same as before.
There were two bhikṣus who were close friends; they lived together in harmony, finding great pleasure in their conversation.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu was traveling through the human realm, teaching and transforming others according to circumstances; he left behind his clothing, as well as tooth-sticks and powdered earth, in his original cell and other places such as his walking path.
At that time, after his friend had collected [the items], he became suspicious and went at once to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense in collecting them.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of friends."
What are the five? First, mutual affection;
second, joy in the heart; third, being like a teacher or elder; fourth, gaining their favor; and fifth, their hearts feeling delight and pleasure upon hearing of one's use of wealth.
"These five kinds may be permitted for collection and use.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

At that time, there was an elder who, not long after marrying his wife, gave birth to a daughter. When she had grown up, she renounced worldly ties and went forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, as it was a period of famine and alms were difficult to obtain, she went from door to door begging for food until she gradually reached her father’s house. When her father saw his daughter coming, he went forward and asked, “Noble lady!
"How, then, shall you sustain your life now?

He replied to his father, "Begging for alms by visiting every door is truly difficult; though I have endured great hardship, it does not satisfy my hunger, and the fire of starvation is so intense that it is very hard to endure."
Upon hearing these words, the father was deeply distressed and displeased, and he said to his daughter:
"If you remain at home and do not go forth into homelessness, even though I may lack affection for you, I shall still provide for your needs;
from this day forward, you may come to my house every day to receive food."
Having accepted the invitation, on another day he again arrived at his father’s house with a companion to receive the offered meal.
His father said to his daughter, “I do not have the means now to provide for two people; you should come alone to take the food.”
The daughter replied to her father, "The World-Honored One does not permit a single woman to travel alone; had the Buddha permitted it, we would not have encountered such suffering.
Then the bhikṣuṇī reported all these matters in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha of the circumstances. The Buddha said:

"At a time when there is famine and it is difficult to obtain food through begging such that one cannot sustain oneself, it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to request permission from the community to travel back and forth to her parents' home."

One should beg in this manner: having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, once the formal announcement has been completed and the community of nuns has assembled, the nun who is begging for the Dharma first prostrates to the Saṃgha in order from the senior-most seat. Standing before the head of the assembly with palms joined in reverence and squatting down, she should beg as follows:
"May the venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha listen!..."
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now encounter a time of famine when food and drink are difficult to obtain; without food and drink, I am unable to survive.
I, [Name], now request from the community of bhikṣuṇīs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for residing and traveling among my own kinsmen.
"I pray that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha will perform for me, [Name], the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding visiting and residing with my relatives; may those who are compassionate please show compassion.

The second and third [proposals] should be stated in this same manner, and the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) should be performed accordingly, as explained in the *Ekottara-śata* (The One Hundred and One).

If a bhikṣuṇī has had the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed by the community authorizing her to associate with her lay relatives, this bhikṣuṇī may go alone without offense; she may go to the homes of her kinsmen and eat as she pleases.
Furthermore, one should not go when it is a time of abundance; if one goes alone, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The eighth sub-section’s summary verse says:
Taking another’s robe on credit and going away, as well as acting as a broker for others.
One should not purchase clothing by overpricing or underpricing it; one should pay the price with two or three [coins].
The setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who purchased a garment on credit from a layperson; having taken it to the monastery, he subsequently passed away.
At that time, the owner of the robe, having heard the news, went hurriedly to the monastery and asked the people there,
"Where is the bhikṣu so-and-so now? The bhikṣus replied:
"He has already died.
The owner of the robe said, "He borrowed this robe from me on credit; you must now return its value."
The bhikṣu replied, "You may go now;
go to that cemetery and ask for the price of the robe as you please.
The owner of the robe replied:
"Divide all robes and alms bowls among yourselves and send him into the forest to collect his debt from the corpse! How can these sons of the Śākyas deceive people?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When a bhikṣu has died, the price for his robes and alms bowls should be returned."

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who obtained a costly robe on credit from a layperson; even after that bhikṣu had passed away, the owner of the robe came to the monastery and asked, "Where is the bhikṣu so-and-so now?"
He replied, "He has already passed away.
The owner of the robe said:
"The person took a robe from me on credit. Then the bhikṣus returned the original robe to him.
The owner of the robe replied, "The item he took was a robe of great value, yet this one he returns here is completely worthless."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should use whatever items are currently available to serve as the price for the robes."
"You should say to him:
'That person has already died; this object is currently in my possession. I now return it to you; you should feel joy.
At that time, two householders were engaged in a transaction together, and one of them asked:
"What is the price of this robe?
The owner of the robe replied, "Twenty kārṣāpaṇas."
The buyer said, "I shall now pay you ten kārṣāpaṇas. At that time,
Upānanda arrived at that place, and those two men thought to themselves:
"The Great Bhikṣus are decisive in their speech; we should request that they determine its price.
The two men together asked Upānanda:
"Venerable One!..."
"What is the value of these garments?
At that time, Upānanda asked a man in private:
"Do you wish to buy these clothes?"
"Are you going to sell your robe?
He replied, "I am buying it."
Upānanda replied, "The value of this robe is twenty kārṣāpaṇas.
He then asked a second time:
"Do you wish to sell your robe?
He replied, "I am selling it."
Upānanda replied, "This robe is worth forty kārṣāpaṇas. The two of them engaged in trade;
he demanded forty for selling it, yet paid only twenty for buying it, which led to a dispute.
The buyer said, "I heard from the market broker that its value was twenty [units].
The owner of the garment spoke again:
"I heard from the market person that it was worth forty.
They said to one another, "The two of us were listening to the appraisal at the same place, yet the prices differ; this must surely be that man intentionally causing discord."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"In general, bhikṣus should not determine the price for others who are laypeople, nor should they arbitrarily discuss the value of goods at marketplaces according to the custom of haggling."
"If anyone violates this, they shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, when the bhikṣus wished to purchase clothing and offered various prices, a layperson replied:
"I am but a minor merchant, whereas you are great merchants indeed."
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not negotiate the price; if bhikṣus wish to purchase clothing, they should have a layperson pay the purchase price."
"If there are no laypeople present, one may personally pay the price for two or three [fruits]; if one pays for more than that, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
The ninth sub-section is summarized in verse as follows:
"Appointing someone to repair fruit trees; four kinds of things should not be divided."
"When the fruit is ripe and present before you, do not engage in idle chatter while observing it.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then King Bimbisāra offered a grove of one thousand *āmra* trees to the Saṃgha.
At that time, although the bhikṣus took the fruit for food, they did not have anyone guard it; consequently, the trees were broken down and the grove fell into ruin.
When King Bimbisāra saw the forest thus devastated, he asked his attendants:
"Whose garden trees are these mango groves?"

The minister replied, “This was originally a thousand *āmra* trees that Your Majesty previously bestowed upon the community of bhikṣus. After the monks had eaten, they failed to look after them; consequently, they were destroyed and have fallen into this state of ruin, for the noble ones did not repair them.”
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not abandon the monastery grounds; the Saṃgha should appoint a gardener to repair them."

Then the park keeper erected fences and distributed the various fruit trees among the people; beneath the roots of the trees, they would chew tooth-sticks, rinse their mouths, wash their hands and faces, bathe their feet, and launder their clothes.
At that time, once the forest trees had been irrigated, their branches and leaves flourished and their fruits ripened in abundance.
A great many visiting bhikṣus arrived and said to the resident monks, "The fine fruits have newly ripened; you should bestow some upon us."
The resident monks replied, "We have already divided [the food]; how can you, Venerable Sir, obtain any to eat? He answered:
"This is the portion of the *ācārya*; this is the portion of the *upādhyāya*; this is the portion of one who is like an *upādhyāya*; this is the portion of one who is like an *ācārya*.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of items that must not be divided."

What are the four? First, the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions; second, the property of the stūpa; third, the medicine for the sick belonging to the community; and fourth, the assets and property of the monastery.
"Whoever violates this shall incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
These fruits should be distributed among the Saṃgha.
At that time, some thieves came to steal the fruits, whereupon the World-Honored One said:
“The assembly should appoint a person to guard the garden.
Once appointed, he was exclusively occupied with guarding it and consequently lacked food. The Buddha said:
“Appoint another person specifically for this; after that person has finished their morning meal, they should replace him and provide him with food.”
As the Blessed One said,
"Distribute the *āmra* fruits to the community of monks," the park keeper then distributed them equally, but some of the fruits contained insects.
The Buddha said:
“You should examine them carefully; set aside those that contain insects, and only after performing the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) should you consume them.
When the bhikṣus were purifying their fruit, they made loud noises and clamored in jest, spitting saliva that splattered and defiled the fruit. The Buddha said:
"One must not engage in idle chatter; one should remain in noble silence and practice contemplation.
Should one be noisy and boisterous, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The summary verse for the tenth section says:
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should not take [food] oneself; it is not to be eaten.
Exceptions are made for those who are ill, for those within a defined boundary (*sīmā*), and for those who have witnessed the plowing.
As the Blessed One said:
"The *āmra* fruit should be distributed to the Saṃgha.
Not knowing who should be responsible for the distribution,
the Buddha said:
"Have a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) go. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should have a *śrāmaṇera* go.
If there is no *śrāmaṇera*, the bhikṣu should first perform the rite of making it permissible (*kappiya-karaṇa*) and then receive it; he may then use it himself."
As the Blessed One said:
"Appoint a park-keeper to guard [the fruit].
However, as soon as the attendant and the novice had departed, various birds came and pecked at and damaged the fruit. The Buddha said:
"One should cover it with tree leaves.
When the attendants and novices have finished their work and return, you should point it out to them.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took turns being appointed as gardeners; they selected the finest *āmra* fruits, carried them back to their residence, and after receiving them, ate them.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another,
"We have not seen such excellent fruit being distributed for a long time. They replied:
“There is nothing that can be brought [to you].
Everything has been selected by the group of six; they take what is good to their own quarters and, having had others hand it over, eat it all themselves.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take [food] for oneself and eat it; if anyone does so, they shall incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus selected the best portions for themselves, causing others to hand them over, and as they gave this to one and that to another, a great commotion ensued. The Buddha said:
"One should not select [the food] for oneself and eat it."
If one eats it, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if, when the digestive heat is weak, one takes what is cooked; or if the digestive heat is strong, one may eat what is raw.
The setting was as before.
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a certain village where there was a monastery. Having entered the monastery, they did not see a single person.
The resident bhikṣus had previously gone to their daytime walking grounds, so the monastery was entirely empty.
At that time, the visiting bhikṣus said to one another,
"Since this empty monastery has no bhikṣus, how can we reside here in a place that lacks the boundaries [of a formal monastery]?"
"We shall now establish a boundary together.
First, they established a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*).
At that time, resident bhikṣus arrived, and the guests said to them:
"Welcome! Welcome, Venerable One!
Please come here; I shall relieve you of your fatigue."
The host replied, "Venerable one!
Why do you instead dispel our fatigue?"
"I am the host; I shall go for a while to a quiet place during the day.
The guest then said, "I wish to establish a boundary, yet I have already established a small boundary here first."
The host replied, "I have already established a boundary here.
Both parties were in doubt as to which of the two prior boundaries should be accepted.
"Or should it be taken later?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should take the preceding boundary; the subsequent binding will not be established."
Whenever a bhikṣu arrives at another dwelling place, he should remain there for seven or eight days; if no one comes to him during that time, they should together establish a boundary (sīmā).
Should it be otherwise than this, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣu was dwelling in an araṇya hermitage when two plowmen engaged in a quarrel, eventually striking one another with their hands and bodies.
At that time, these two men took the bhikṣu as their witness.
Then the two of them led each other together to the king's presence, each presenting their own case and stating that there was a witness.
He had the bhikṣu summoned.
Once the bhikṣu had arrived, the king questioned him himself, saying:
"What is the situation regarding this matter?"
The bhikṣu replied: "Great King!
If you can establish a solemn covenant for yourself as one does a Wheel-Turning Monarch (cakravartin), I shall report this to the King."
The king agreed with his proposal.
The bhikṣu replied,
“These two combatants, harboring mutual resentment toward one another, both employ fists and clubs.”
When the king had heard this, he punished both of them. The bhikṣu said,
"Great King, why do you inflict punishment?"
"Just now you established a vow, like a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) traveling through the world to transform beings.
The King asked, "How does a Wheel-Turning King travel and transform beings?"
He replied: "A Wheel-Turning King merely ceases what is unbeneficial and causes what is beneficial to be practiced.
The king said:
"If this is the case, both of you have committed an offense; let each be given a light punishment, and both shall be released.
At that time, the two men each gave rise to resentment.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If there is fighting, a bhikṣu should not remain standing by the side watching it.
If he sees those engaged in a dispute, he should quickly leave; if he does not leave, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
The summary verse for the fifth section of the Nidāna states:
Making offerings to an image of the Bodhisattva; Auspicious communal meals;
Dwelling on grass cushions during a great assembly; And summoning the Saṃgha by beating a large drum.
The first section, summarized in verse, says:
It is permitted to make images of Bodhisattvas, And five kinds of banners are also allowed;
One may place a sacred image upon a seat, And iron poles may be used as one desires.
The setting is as before.

When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, personally presides at the head of the assembly as the senior elder (*sthavira*), there is a solemn majesty and the multitude is all strictly disciplined; when the World-Honored One is not present, that supreme state is absent.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to create an image of Jambudvīpa; I only pray that you will grant me permission."
The Buddha said,
"It should be made.
When they wished to install banners and canopies, the Buddha said:
"Act as you wish.
At that time, the elder did not know what kind of banner he should have made.
The Buddha said:
“There are five kinds of banners:
namely, the lion banner, the makara banner, the nāga banner, the garuḍa banner, and the bull-king banner.
The householder further requested that a seat be made for the image of Jambudvīpa, to which the Buddha said:
"It may be made.
They then fashioned an iron pole to suspend banners and streamers, and the Buddha said,
"It should be made."
The second section, summarized in verse, says:
One should make offerings to images of the Bodhisattva, And likewise fashion various necklaces and ornaments,
Scented ointments and carriages, As well as parasols, canopies, banners, and streamers.
The setting was as before.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Was it not when the Buddha was a bodhisattva that he extensively made offerings?"
The Buddha said, "So be it. [The king] said,
"I now wish to perform a随心供养 (suīxīn gòngyǎng) as an image of Jambudvīpa."
The Buddha said, "One should do so. [The interlocutor asked:
"When the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, did he wear various necklaces and ornaments?"
The Buddha said, "So it is.
[The king said,] "I now wish to fashion various necklaces for the image of Jambudvīpa."
The Buddha said, "Do as you wish, with the sole exception of anklets and earrings; for all else, you may make them as you please.
[The laywoman said,] "I now wish to prepare ground incense, ointment incense, and cloths to wipe the Buddha’s hands and feet."
The Buddha said, "It should be made.
[The king asked,] "When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he would enter or exit riding in a palanquin or a chariot; I now wish to have a sedan chair made."
The Buddha said,
"It should be made. He spoke again:
"When he was a bodhisattva, he always carried a parasol and followed with banners and streamers; I now wish to provide a parasol for this image and to create various banners.
The Buddha said, "You should do so."
“The Bodhisattva, while living at home, always wears flower garlands and necklaces as ornaments; I too shall now create an image adorned with these.
The Buddha said, “I permit the making of all such various articles of adornment.”
The third section, summarized in verse, says:
Auspiciousness and offerings, Garlands and incense boxes;
When the great assembly gathers, Open the gates by day and close them at night.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, the entire great assembly honored and made offerings to him with auspicious rites."
"If the Buddha permits it, I shall perform auspicious rites and offer worship before an image of Śākyamuni in Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha said, "You may do as you wish."
“I now wish to further create a crest-garland and various incense boxes as offerings for the Jambūdvīpa image.
The Buddha said, “You should do so.”
The householder said,
"I shall adorn the temple buildings with images of Jambudvīpa.
Then the bhikṣus painted the temple, using various fragrant muds, flower garlands, burning incense, powdered incense, and playing various drums and music, making extensive offerings.
At that time, when the multitude saw this marvel, they were struck with unprecedented wonder and said to one another, "This dwelling place is most wonderfully adorned.
When the bhikṣus saw the people making such a commotion, they closed their doors during the day; upon seeing this, the laypeople gave rise to criticism and disdain, saying:
"This obstructs the arising of wholesome states.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is music and performance for the purpose of making offerings, one should keep the gates open during the day and close them at night."
The fourth section, summarized in verse, says:
When the great assembly gathers for a meal, In the month of Vaiśākha,
At the incense altar after five or six years— On these occasions, one should hold a Great Assembly.
At that time, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was preparing the offerings, a great multitude of the seven assemblies of disciples, including many bhikṣus, gathered together.
Upon seeing this, the householder was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"As the World-Honored One has said:..."
“Bhikṣus! There are five kinds of timely giving. What are the five?
First, providing gifts and assistance to those who have arrived as guests and to those about to depart;
second, providing gifts and assistance to the sick and to those who attend to them;
third, providing gifts and assistance during years of famine and while traveling on perilous paths.
Fourth, when one obtains new grain, new fruit, or the arrival of a new season, one should first provide for those who uphold the precepts and possess virtue, and only thereafter eat them oneself.

Fifth, when encountering wind, rain, cold, or snow, one should take cakes, congee, parched grain, and various syrups to offer to the Saṃgha, so that the Noble Ones do not have to endure hardships while traveling, but may dwell in peace and comfort after receiving my offerings of food and drink.
"I now see these bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have come from afar to this place, exhausted by the journey."
"If the Buddha would grant me permission, I shall prepare a great assembly for his sake.
He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, there are five kinds of timely giving, as explained in detail above.

Observing that a great assembly of bodhisattvas had gathered from all directions to make offerings, and seeing that those traveling the roads were exhausted by their hardships, [the king] thought: "If the Buddha would permit it, I shall provide these offerings."
The Buddha said, "You may do as you wish.
The elder then established a great unrestricted assembly (pañcavārṣika).
At that time, the elder addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I shall now further arrange a great assembly.
The Buddha said:
"It should be done. The householder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"On what month and day was the Bodhisattva born?"
The Buddha told the householder:
"On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha is my birthday.
I now wish to hold a great festival for my birthday."
The Buddha said, "It should be made. [The king] said,
"I now wish to construct a fragrant dais for the image of Jambudvīpa."
The Buddha said,
“It should be made.
[The interlocutor asked,] “World-Honored One, when you were a bodhisattva, how many years did it take for you to shave off your topknot?”
The Buddha said,
"Five years. [The king replied,] "I now wish to hold a great quinquennial assembly."
The Buddha said,
“It should be made.
[The interlocutor asked,] “World-Honored One, at what age did the Bodhisattva re-establish his uṣṇīṣa?”
The Buddha said: "Six years.
The rest is as previously stated.
“World-Honored One, I wish to perform a great assembly for the Buddha in honor of the image of Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha said, “You should do so.”
The fifth section, summarized in verse, says:
For the great assembly, one should prepare a seat of grass; one should not sit in a disorderly manner;
one should strike the *gandī* drum to announce the time so that all may know it.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was hosting a great assembly, people from all six great cities gathered there like clouds.
At that time, many bhikṣus also arrived, and because of this, the mats and cushions were entirely insufficient.
The Buddha said, "Householder!..."
"One should tie up a bundle of grass and sit upon it for meals at any time.
After the bhikṣus had finished eating, they departed without putting the bundle away. When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"After a bhikṣu has finished eating, he should collect the grass bundle and place it aside before departing as he pleases. However, if it has been used during a Buddha-pūjā assembly, it must be discarded."

At that time, the bhikṣus did not sit according to seniority, but sat in a confused jumble, disregarding the proper order. This caused those serving the food to delay for a long time, and sometimes when the meal was finished, others would still arrive, causing them to miss their allotted time. The Buddha said:
"One should announce that the time has arrived."
Although he announced that the time had arrived, the assembly was so noisy that they did not hear him. The World-Honored One said, "You should strike the *gandī*.
Still, they did not hear it, and the Buddha said:
"One should blow the conch shell and strike the drum.
However, as this was not heard everywhere, the Buddha said,
"Strike the great bell and drum."

The Buddha ordered the drum to be beaten; after it had been struck three times, it was then beaten in a long roll. There were those who were ill and those in charge of administrative affairs who were in need of food. The Buddha said:

"One should wait until the sick have received their food and the administrators have finished eating, and only then beat the long roll. If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The sixth section, summarized in verse, says:
Gather the Sangha by sounding the great drum; When the offerings are finished, remove the banners and streamers.
If many precious treasures are obtained, Distribute them all accordingly.
As the Blessed One said:
"The *gandī* should be struck and the pair of conchs blown.
Although they acted accordingly, it was still not heard everywhere. The Buddha said:
"One should beat the great drum so that its sound is heard everywhere, for when it is time for the great assembly, those from far and near will all gather.
Although the assembly had concluded, the people still did not disperse; the World-Honored One said:
"The banners and streamers set out for the offerings should be removed; once the multitude sees this, they will naturally disperse."
When this assembly was held, the community of bhikṣus obtained a great deal of precious wealth and did not know what to do with it.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding those entitled to receive it, from the senior-most elder down to the lowest-ranking monk, distribute it equally according to the Dharma, in accordance with their respective seniority."
At that time, the bhikṣus were still in a state of commotion. The Buddha said:

"If the assembly is large, one portion should be given to a thousand people for them to divide among themselves; or again, it may be a hundred, or twenty, or even ten people who form one portion, and are thus permitted to take their own share."
Upāli said to the Buddha:
“If one person among a group of ten dies, who is entitled to receive that deceased person’s share?
The Buddha said:
"If the distribution of robes has already been completed among ten people, the deceased's share should enter the Saṃgha.
If it has not yet been distributed, the nine remaining people shall receive it together; this principle applies to larger numbers as well."
The *Nidāna* is concluded.
