Chapter Two: The Summary Verses (Uddāna) for the Major Section on the Mūlakas state:
The first concerns confession and apology; The second concerns the fixed assignment of objects.
Third, the Requisites and Robes; the summary verse for the *Mūlakalpa* (Mukha-dhāraṇī) states:
In the section on the initial general summary of the individual gates:
"Apology, grass, and within the field; combined exemptions, King Bimbisāra."
Dog meat, cups, sugarcane, Sugar, ghee, roots, and so forth are permitted.
The summary verse for the first section says:
Apologizing to one who is not fully ordained, And observing the appearance of a novice.
The rules for *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs* are such that when they perform legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) for one another, they are all valid.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the *bhikṣus* divided into two factions to deliberate on the principles of the Dharma, which led to the outbreak of disputes; therein, the junior *bhikṣus* rebuked the seniors.
At that time, the great bhikṣu retreated into his cell, his mind filled with resentment and anger, thinking:
"How can such a lowly and insignificant creature insult me?
Because he was thus tormented by the fire of wrath, his life ended thereupon and he was reborn among the venomous snakes.
At that time, the young bhikṣu felt remorse in his heart, thinking:
"I have done what is unwholesome; how could it be right for me to scold and reprimand the elder bhikṣu? I should now go to him and beg for forgiveness."

Having formed this thought, he went to that place together with the bhikṣus. Seeing that the door was closed, he opened it with an object and reached the place where the bhikṣu was; wishing to offer his prostrations, he said:
"Venerable One!..."
"I pray that you will grant me your forgiveness.
He then saw a venomous snake, full of malice, poised to bite.
At that moment, the World-Honored One, through the power of great compassion, came to that place and addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
“You should now pay homage at his feet and beg him for forgiveness.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How can I be expected to prostrate at the feet of this snake?
The World-Honored One replied,
"You should perform the prostration while conceiving the thought that he is the body of a bhikṣu from a former life."
Then that bhikṣu prostrated himself before the snake.
The World-Honored One said to him: "Worthy one!
"You should grant me your pardon.
He then spoke the Dharma of three phrases to the venomous snake, saying: "O noble one!"

"You have already practiced pure conduct under me and should have been reborn in the heavens; however, because you were consumed and harmed by the fire of anger, you have been born among poisonous snakes.
O noble one, you should know this!"
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are devoid of self; nirvāṇa is peace and bliss.
You should give rise to pure faith toward me; by virtue of this merit, you shall abandon the realm of animals and be reborn in a happy destination."
Then that venomous snake thought to himself:
"I should not now, having personally heard three phrases of Dharma from the World-Honored One, continue to consume food and nourish this useless body."
The fires of hunger among the various classes of animals are most intense; because they did not eat, they immediately passed away.
Due to having conceived pure faith in the Blessed One, at the end of their lives there, they were reborn in the heavens.
Whenever a being is first born in the heavens, whether male or female, it is the natural law that three thoughts arise: "Where did I die?
Where have I now been born?"
"By what karmic conditions have I come here?
He then observed for himself that he had cast off his snake body to be born in this heavenly realm due to having conceived pure faith toward the Buddha.
At that time, the devaputra thought to himself:
"Now, I ought not to fail to go to the Buddha's presence to pay homage and make offerings; I should go to the Buddha's presence to repay his kindness and serve him."

Then that devaputra immediately adorned himself with exquisite necklaces of the seven precious gems, earrings, and armlets; his radiance was magnificent and brilliant. Taking celestial flowers—blue utpala flowers, red padma flowers, and white puṇḍarīka flowers—he approached the Buddha after midnight had passed. He scattered these celestial flowers before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
By the power of this devaputra’s majestic radiance, the Jeta Grove was illuminated with universal light.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing the differences in that devaputra’s inclinations, latent tendencies, and faculties, preached the Dharma for him.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the devaputra immediately attained the fruit of stream-entry while still on his seat. Having attained the fruit, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"That which I have now realized could not have been accomplished by my parents or others," and so forth, as detailed elsewhere.

By virtue of the power of the World-Honored One’s benevolence and compassion, you have drawn me out from the three evil realms and established me in the abodes of devas and humans. You have brought an end to the cycle of birth and death; the great ocean of blood and tears has been entirely dried up; the great mountain of bodily bones has now been transcended; and the twenty peaks of the mountain of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* accumulated since beginningless time have been shattered with the vajra-pestle of wisdom, whereby I have realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
"Bhagavān! Today I take refuge in the Triple Gem; may you bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall maintain the utmost pure faith toward the Triple Gem."
Then that deva-son prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and suddenly vanished, returning to his original celestial palace.

At that time, as the bhikṣus were practicing diligent cultivation and tranquil meditation with alert minds during the first and last watches of the night, they saw the Jetavana grove radiating brilliant light and all thought to themselves:
"Is this Brahmā, Śakra, the various devas, or the Four Great Kings? Or perhaps a powerful deva-son who has come to the World-Honored One's presence to pay his respects?"
Having formed this thought, he went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and reported the foregoing matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"It was neither the Brahma King nor even a Great Powerful Deva who came to my presence to pay their respects."
"Do you recall that when there was a great venomous snake, I taught him the Dharma in three phrases?
They replied to the Buddha,
"We saw it."
The World-Honored One said:
"Having passed away, he was reborn in the heavens and came to where I was.
I preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained the vision of the Truth (dṛṣṭi) and returned to his celestial palace."
"For this reason, the light shines everywhere. The World-Honored One said,

"Because there is such a fault in intolerance, monks, if you have anger or disputes, you should quickly repent and apologize to one another, practicing mutual forbearance, so as not to incur such transgressions at a later time."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had just been rebuked; he immediately went to him to ask for forgiveness, but [the other] instead increased his anger and replied:
"Look at this! It causes me the greatest distress."
The Buddha said:
"One should not immediately seek confession upon being newly rebuked with anger; rather, one should wait for that person’s agitation to subside before seeking forgiveness.
In this city, there were two bhikṣus who, while discussing the meaning of the Dharma together, became angry and resentful, and the junior bhikṣu rebuked the elder.
At that time, an elderly bhikṣu entered his cell and remained there; having given rise to extreme malice, he passed away and was reborn among poisonous snakes.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should go to where that venomous snake is biting, and at my command, proclaim these words:"
"May you be free from illness! he replied, "O noble one!"
"You have already gone forth within my True Dharma and Discipline; you ought to realize at least one of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Because of the intense hatred you harbored in a previous life, you were born as a venomous snake; therefore, you should grant him your forgiveness."
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to where the venomous snake was and said to him:
“O worthy one! The Buddha inquires after your health.”
He further spoke these words:
"You have already gone forth in my True Dharma and Discipline; you ought to realize one of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Because of the intense hatred you harbored in a previous life, you were born among poisonous snakes; therefore, you should show forbearance toward him."
At that time, the venomous snake was inside the room, hissing and making sounds, unable to remain still.
The World-Honored One again commanded the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should go to where that venomous snake is biting and convey my words to it, as explained at length previously."
When Maudgalyāyana had arrived, the venomous snake briefly poked its head out from the gap in the door-panel and then withdrew back inside.
The World-Honored One again commanded the Venerable Śāriputra:
"You should go to that place where the venomous snake bit and convey my words to it, just as was said before."
When Śāriputra had arrived, that venomous snake exposed half its body between the door panels and then retracted back into the room.
At that time, the Blessed One went into the room himself and said to the snake: "Noble one!
"You have already gone forth in my True Dharma and Discipline; you ought to realize one of the four fruits of the śramaṇa, yet you have not attained even one.
Because of the weight of your anger in a previous life, you were born among the biting venomous snakes; therefore, you should grant him your forgiveness."
The snake then emerged from its dwelling and coiled its body before the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to that bhikṣu,
"You should seek forgiveness from this venomous snake that bit you."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How should I perform the rite of repentance?"
The Buddha said,
"You should pay homage at his two feet. He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Since he has fallen into the realm of animals, how can I now pay homage at his feet?
The World-Honored One replied:
"You must visualize that bhikṣu’s previous life before you and only then prostrate at his feet.
When the bhikṣu had formed this thought, he prostrated at his feet; the snake then covered the bhikṣu’s head with its hood as a gesture of repentance.
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! It is because of anger that such faults arise. Therefore, if bhikṣus harbor mutual resentment, they should quickly offer an apology."
"If one has become angry in the afternoon, one should seek an apology in the morning; yet when the other person offers an apology (*kṣamā*), their anger increases even further. The Buddha said:
"One should first extend a greeting, and only afterwards request forgiveness."
He still did not accept it, so the Buddha said,
"You should accept it.
When he reached a place near him, he did not pay his respects, so the Buddha said:
"When one arrives at the place of the preceptor, one should immediately pay respects; the preceptor should respond by saying, 'Free from illness.
If this is not done, both parties incur an offense."

Furthermore, there were two bhikṣus who, while discussing the meaning of the Dharma, became resentful and angry toward one another. At that time, the younger one rebuked the elder; the younger bhikṣu, realizing his own conduct was improper, prostrated at the elder’s feet and requested his forgiveness.
The elder bhikṣu remained silent; the junior one thought to himself:
"Since he is so extremely angry that he will not tolerate me, I shall wait until his anger has subsided before going to apologize."

At that time, the elderly bhikṣu went into his old room and remained there harboring resentment. When the junior bhikṣu arrived at that room, he grasped [the elder’s] feet, prostrated with his head, and said:
“Venerable Sir!”
"I beg you to grant me your forbearance.
He then gave rise to great anger and said to the others,
"Venerable sirs!"
"Please observe this person who has come specifically to harass me.
The youth then thought:
"Since the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has sent me to offer an apology, I should abide in a state of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit."
"However, since this bhikṣu showed no joy upon seeing me approach, why should I seek his forgiveness?
Thinking thus, he did not go forward to offer his salutations.

Later, at another time, while that elderly bhikṣu was walking back and forth and conversing with other bhikṣus on the path of practice, a young bhikṣu approached that area intending to pay respects to someone else. Seeing him, the others said to the elder:
"Venerable One!..."
"This person's precepts are pure; why do you not ask for his forgiveness?
The elder replied, "He harbors ill intent, yet he has come merely to pay you homage."
Then the elderly bhikṣu said to those standing nearby, "You have witnessed with your own eyes that he bows only to you and not to me; this proves beyond doubt that this man harbors evil intentions."
Then a bystander said to the junior monk, "This man's precepts are pure; why do you not pay him homage?
At that time, the junior bhikṣu related the preceding events in detail.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Whenever those engaged in a dispute come into each other’s presence, they should perform a respectful salutation.
The other should respond by saying:”
If one says, "I am free from illness," without acting accordingly, both parties incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
One should simply join the palms and pay respectful homage.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"When one is receiving the precepts, the recipient says these words:
'Venerable sir!'"
"One should not grant me the full ordination (upasampadā).
At that time, the bhikṣus forcibly conferred the ordination upon him; do you know whether this person has successfully achieved the status of a fully ordained monk?
The Buddha said:
"Upāli! It does not constitute a valid undertaking.
If even when the words have already been spoken it is called 'renouncing the precepts,' how much more so when at the very moment of undertaking them could it be called 'properly undertaken'?"
As the Blessed One has said:
"A śrāmaṇera who has reached twenty years of age should receive full ordination (upasampadā).
Yet, this śrāmaṇera does not know how many years he has reached.
At that time, the bhikṣus also gave rise to doubts and did not confer full ordination upon him; meanwhile, that man remained there with guarded intent.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should examine his demeanor."
At that time, the bhikṣus exposed his body, looking at his private parts and his armpits, which caused him to feel shame.
The World-Honored One said:
"You may hang your water flask, alms bowl, bag, or other garments upon a high ivory peg or a bamboo rack, and then say to him:"
"You should now take those robes and bowl and bring them here.
As he was about to lift his hand, he should observe the length of the hair on his armpits.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If, when śrāmaṇeras are receiving the full precepts, the community of bhikṣus then performs the bhikṣuṇī karmavācanā for them to receive the upasaṃpadā, would they be said to have received it?"
The Buddha said:
"The full ordination is accomplished, yet the bhikṣus incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The second section is summarized in a verse:
A brief explanation from the *Grasthānagrāmaka-vinaya-saṃkṣepa*: Generating the thought [of confession] constitutes the *poṣadha*;
there is no fault in being bound by bandits; six exemptions regarding monastic offenses.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus were traveling together with a caravan of merchants. Upon reaching the day of the poṣadha, they saw a secluded spot of soft grass and said to one another, "Venerable sirs!..."
"This is a fine, soft grassy spot; let us perform the *poṣadha* ceremony here.
They then sat together to conduct the *poṣadha*.
By the time the rite was concluded, the courageous merchants had all passed by.
At that time, the bhikṣus followed behind and were all plundered by bandits.
Upon entering the monastery, the resident bhikṣus saw these newcomers and immediately asked,
"Welcome, Venerable Ones!"
"Are you practicing the conduct of peace and happiness? He replied,
"How could there be any peace and happiness?"
"I have been robbed by bandits and now barely survive.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"One should not perform the poṣadha ceremony out of a desire for soft grass or level ground; one must follow one's traveling companions until reaching a village or town before performing the poṣadha."
As the Blessed One has said:
"The *poṣadha* (confession and purification) is to be performed only when one is near a village or town.
At that time, some bhikṣus had already entered the village while others remained outside it, and they thought to themselves:
"I am now living apart; shall I perform the *poṣadha* or not?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who have entered the village should assemble in one place and perform the *poṣadha*."
Regarding those outside the village: they must leave the vicinity of the village and assemble in one place for the purpose of the *poṣadha* ceremony.
The *poṣadha* should not be performed until the bhikṣus have assembled; if it is not so assembled, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
Furthermore, while the bhikṣus were traveling on the road together with a caravan of merchants, when the day for the Poṣadha ceremony arrived, the bhikṣus said to the merchants:
"O worthy ones!..."
“Stay for a while;
I now wish to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony.
The merchant replied:
"There is danger from bandits here; you must come quickly, for I cannot remain.
Then the bhikṣus traveled along with their companions, saying these words: "Stay here! Stay here!"
When dawn finally broke, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not fail to perform the poṣadha until the day has ended; rather, one should perform the poṣadha together while traveling along the road."
While they were traveling on the road, they performed the *poṣadha* ceremony together. At that time, the merchants all raised voices of derision and said:
"Noble ones! We remain silent out of fear of bandits; for what reason do you raise such loud voices?"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the *poṣadha* in detail; it should be performed briefly.
However, those merchants still harbored criticism, so the World-Honored One told them:
"One should maintain them through mental recollection.
There are six matters to be maintained through mental recollection:

the relinquishing of the three robes, the formal distribution of the three robes, the relinquishing of extra robes, special invitations, the observance of the Uposatha, and the invitation ceremony (Pravāraṇā)."
It should be stated as follows:
"Today is the fourteenth day for the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha; I, the bhikṣu [name], shall also perform the Poṣadha on the fourteenth day.
I, the bhikṣu [name], declare myself to be pure regarding all obstructing dharmas."

For now, I shall observe the Poṣadha; if at a later time I encounter a harmonious assembly, I shall join that harmonious assembly in observing the Poṣadha, in order to fulfill the entire collection of precepts.
Thus he spoke three times.
If one reaches this day and it is the time for the *poṣadha* ceremony, yet fails to perform it, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside when they were captured by bandits. The bandits said to one another:
“You all may now purify yourselves among the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus, knowing that those bandits intended to commit murder, said to them:
“For what reason do you wish to harm us?”
The robbers said:

"You bhikṣus are all well-acquainted with the king, the great ministers, the elders, and the merchants; they hold deep feelings of affection, faith, and respect for you. You should inform them that we will derive no benefit from them, and for this reason, they must be cleared away."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu within the assembly who, having committed a deliberate lie, thought to himself:
"I am now being killed; dying with this transgression upon me, I shall surely be reborn in an evil realm."
He called the other bhikṣus to a secluded place to confess the offense he had committed.
When the robbers saw them, they said,
"Venerable sirs, where do you intend to go?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am performing a small amount of monastic ritual.
Then the bandits spoke again:
"Do you wish to flee? You should simply remain here; you ought not to go elsewhere.
Those two bhikṣus then confessed their offenses in the presence of the bandits:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. Regarding this offense that I have committed, I now come before the Venerable one from a state of purity and disclose and confess it all; I do not conceal it."
"By confessing and declaring one's offenses, one attains peace and happiness; by not confessing and declaring one's offenses, one lacks peace and happiness.
A second and third time, he spoke thus.
At that time, when the bandits saw that they had confessed their sins, they asked:
"Virtuous ones, did you not tell a deliberate lie? They replied:
“I shall not do so. “If it is thus, you may depart as you please; take care not to tell anyone that we have met here.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt regret in his heart.
"I have confessed my offense to a layperson.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, all those who are thieves are persons of high standing in dangerous places; for you to confess your offenses to them is called a 'proper confession'."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human realm who was captured by bandits.
The bandits said to one another, "Gentlemen, you should now purify yourselves of these bhikṣus."
At that time, the bhikṣus, knowing that the bandits intended to harm them, said to the bandits:
"For what reason do you wish to harm us?
The bandits replied as they had before, up to the point of saying, "It is for this purpose that we must purify [the meat]."
The bhikṣu replied,
"If you will simply release me, I shall never speak of you.
At that time, the thief spoke these words:

“Only after we have made a solemn covenant shall we release you. Every month on the fifteenth day, when the great assembly gathers and there is something to be proclaimed, you must expound upon the Dharma for our sake in detail; then we shall release you.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu within the assembly who had mastered the recitation of the precepts; he then gave a detailed exposition of the Prātimokṣa until its conclusion.
The leader of the bandits said to him, "Venerable sir, you should depart, and wherever you go, please be careful not to speak of me."
When the bhikṣus had thus been spared, they later felt doubt, thinking:
"We recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra in the presence of bandits.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whoever among you is a nobleman of the forest or wilderness, speak up; this would be well said.
The setting was as before.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were traveling through the human settlements in the country of Vaṅga, they were seized by bandits. The bandits said to one another:
"You all may now purify yourselves among the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was one among the bandits who had previously been a bhikṣu living nearby; he said to his companions, "Why trouble yourselves by killing these?"
"You should bind them quickly with grass roots and stalks, so that they may die of hunger and thirst from self-starvation.
Thereupon, those bandits bound the bhikṣus with grass and departed, abandoning them there.
At that time, King Udayana of Vatsa went out for a hunt and encountered him; he said to his attendants, "Is this a deer or a bear?"
The rider galloped forward to observe and saw the bhikṣu, asking,
"What kind of person are you?
The bhikṣu replied:
"He is one who has gone forth. "In which class?
"He is a son of the Śākyas."
"What is it that causes you to stay here? He replied,
"I have been bound by bandits."
“By what is it bound? He replied, “By living grass.”
The king asked,
"Why do you not pull it out? He replied:
“The Blessed One has prescribed this training rule for me: ‘If a bhikṣu destroys living plants or grasses, he commits a pāyattika offense.
The king immediately dismounted from his vehicle, personally untied them, and having bestowed three robes upon each, he departed.
At that time, the bhikṣus became suspicious and thought,
"We have described his transgressions to the king.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus! If there should be such a kṣatriya king, consecrated by coronation, who explains the characteristics of offenses, this is a correct explanation.
They then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"May one confess one's offenses in the presence of another who has also committed an offense?
The Buddha said:

"One must not confess one's offenses in the presence of another who has also committed an offense; however, if there are unavoidable circumstances, there is no offense in confessing in their presence."
"However, one should not confess one's transgression to another person who has committed the same offense.
The setting and circumstances were as before.

There was a bhikṣu who was deeply conscientious, firmly upheld the prohibitions, and took delight in the training rules (śikṣāpada). Suddenly, at one time, he committed the first of the formal offenses (saṃghāvaśeṣa). He immediately felt remorse and was filled with shame; his complexion grew pale and emaciated, and he gradually fell ill.
Another bhikṣu came to inquire after him, saying:
"Venerable sir,
why is your body so pale and emaciated?"
"What illness or suffering do you have?
He remained silent and did not answer.
Later, when a bhikṣu with whom he shared a close friendship came to inquire, he then related the matter in full, and the friend replied:
"Venerable one! If this is indeed so, I shall now inform the bhikṣus on your behalf. He replied:
"If you report this, I shall take my own life; it would be better for me to go to another country before I recount his crimes.
Then those two departed together, and midway along the road, one of them passed away.
At that time, the companion bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The person for whose sake I am here has now passed away; I should no longer remain here.
He then returned to his original location.
The bhikṣus saw him and said to him:
“Welcome, Venerable One!
Have you been traveling in peace and well-being?”
"Where is my companion from days past now?
he cried out, weeping as he said,
"That man has died."
As he spoke these words, he sighed:
"Although I know that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, how long will it be before that bhikṣu—who died while bearing his transgressions—is released from his fall into hell?"
"Because of this, I remember it with profound sorrow.
Then the bhikṣus reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"That son of the Śākyas has emerged from his transgression."
He addressed the bhikṣus:

"In all cases of transgression, I declare that it arises from the mind; it cannot be removed by means of punishment. Therefore, I authorize that one who possesses such a nature of shame and modesty must confess their offense before a single person."

At that time, among the bhikṣus, there were those who were experts in the Sūtras, those who were experts in the Vinaya, and those who were experts in the Abhidharma, who committed offenses against the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.
They went before the assembly and recounted their transgressions. Upon seeing them, others spoke thus:
"These great virtuous ones are the very path to the sublime; yet because they committed these offenses, they have reached such a state. How, then, will the other bhikṣus fare?"
They reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should go to another place and confess your offenses.
These bhikṣus likewise passed away as before, and the Buddha said:
"One should confess before a single person.

Furthermore, if there is another person of great merit, such as a leading elder (sthavira) at the head of the assembly, one should likewise confess one's transgressions before that single individual."
The third section, summarized in verse, says:
Those exempted should be released; Digging canals and sending the assembly on their way;
From one day up to four *yojanas*; Skin and flesh are both impure.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Ānanda was on duty by turn when King Prasenajit of Kośala came to that place, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Ānanda briefly expounded the Dharma within the holy teaching. The king said:
"Venerable One!
I have no other business; please explain it to me in detail."
Then Ānanda spoke it again in brief, and the king spoke once more, saying:
"Noble One! I have no other business;
I pray that you will explain it at length."
Thus he spoke up to three times, and Ānanda replied:
"Great King! Although you have no business, I have other matters."
The King said, "Venerable Sir,
what task is there to be done?"
He replied, "Great King!
I am the temple steward; I must conduct an inspection."
The king then thought to himself, "This is my concern.
He immediately paid his respects, took his leave, and went to where the Buddha was. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am a Kṣatriya, a great king consecrated by coronation; however, whatever task I ought to perform, that I shall do.

Whether it be what the queen ought to do, or what the crown prince, the ministers, the various generals, the officials, or the common people ought to do—each must perform their respective duties according to their station."
“The World-Honored One is the unsurpassed Dharma King; we only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant exemption from this matter for those who ought to be exempt.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
Then King Prasenajit rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!"
"I now grant permission that those who ought to be exempted should not be appointed as administrators of monastic affairs.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know who were the persons who ought to be exempted.
The World-Honored One declared:
"Those who understand the Sūtras, understand the Vinaya, and understand the Abhidharma—these should be exempt.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having merely read and recited two or three chapters of the Sūtras, immediately began to claim for themselves: [that they understood them].
"I am a holder of the sūtras; I too ought to be exempt from managing monastic affairs.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Only one who has mastered the entire collection of sūtras shall be exempt from administrative duties."
Furthermore, there were those who upheld only a single *pārājika* rule and then declared of themselves:
"I am one who upholds the Vinaya; I too should be exempt.
The World-Honored One said:
"Only by thoroughly upholding the Vinaya-piṭaka can one be exempt from administrative duties.
Furthermore, there were those who had read only one or two minor treatises and would then say of themselves, "I am an upholder of the Abhidharma; you should also release me."
The World-Honored One replied:
"Only by mastering the sections of the *dhāraṇī-śāstras* can one be exempt from the various duties.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.

At that time, King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kośala faced a rebellion on his borders. The king dispatched a general with troops to suppress it, but he was defeated by the enemy and returned with his army in retreat. This happened as many as three times, until he was finally subdued and returned to his own country.
Then the chief minister addressed the king, saying:
"The rebel forces are powerful and their generals have been unsuccessful; unless Your Majesty personally leads the campaign to punish them, there will be no way to bring them to submission."
Then King Prasenajit beat the drum to proclaim his command to all people:
"All those within the kingdom who are skilled in wielding the sword may join the expedition.

At that time, the king personally arrayed the fourfold army to punish that rebellious vassal; however, the latter held firm and remained there, for his city relied on its natural defenses and was difficult to subdue by force.
At that time, the minister spoke again to the king, saying:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada possesses great merit and is protected by devas; if he should come here, we might perhaps be subdued."
At that time, the king dispatched a messenger to tell the elder:
"I have a minor matter for which I wish to see you.
Accepting this command, the elder immediately went to the king's army.
At that time, the bandits had not yet been subdued, and much time had passed.
The king asked the elder,
"Do you not have thoughts of returning home?"
He then addressed the King, saying, "I truly have no mind to concern myself with that family; I merely have a private desire to see the assembly of monks.
At that time, King Prasenajit issued an edict to the officer on guard:
“Regarding those noble ones, you should not grant them an audience; rather, find a means to send them here, for I wish to see them.
When the minister on guard saw the king’s command, he thought to himself:
“How can I now refuse to grant them an audience so that the Ārya may come into the presence of the king?”
At that time, an old minister said to his colleagues,
"I shall devise a stratagem so that the assembly of noble ones will come to the king’s army of their own accord, rather than it being we who issue them the command."

Not far from here is an old garden belonging to the former king Brahmadatta, which has been completely ruined; [the king] will falsely claim to be restoring it by dredging the channels and excavating the temple grounds, using this as a pretext so that he will come there of his own accord.
The minister in charge, leading his various attendants, entered the Jeta Grove and proceeded to lay out lines with cords within the monastery to divert the channels for the passage of water.
The bhikṣus asked him, "O worthy one!"
"What are you doing? He replied, "Noble One!"
"The Son of Heaven has issued an edict, desiring that we repair the old royal gardens and clear the drainage channels within the Jeta Grove.
The bhikṣus said, "How can you destroy the stūpas containing the hair and nail relics of the Buddha?"
He replied: "This is the King’s command; what can be done now?
I have no second head—whom else could I refuse the royal decree?"
The assembly then said to him, "Please pause for a moment; we shall go to the king ourselves to deliberate together. The bhikṣu asked:
"I wish now to go there; will I return on the same day?
The minister replied, "No;
it will not be possible even to return within seven days."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are monks who have important communal business, I now permit them to remain for up to forty nights while maintaining their formal observance before departing."
The assembly of bhikṣus did not know how to maintain the formal observance.
The World-Honored One told them:
"First spread out the mats and seats, then strike the *gandi*; announce the matter at hand to inform the assembly."
Once the assembly has gathered, one should encourage and exhort a bhikṣu who is so inclined, saying:
"Are you able to remain on behalf of the Saṃgha for forty nights while traveling outside the boundary?"
He should reply, "I am able. Then,
after one bhikṣu has first made the formal announcement (jñapti), the others should perform the ritual act (karman) to formally undertake [the object] and depart.
Then the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One:
"Is it permissible to maintain the observance for one night while traveling outside the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted. He further asked:
"May one, having undertaken the observance for two nights, three nights, or even up to ten nights, or twenty nights, or thirty nights, or forty nights, go outside the boundary?"
The Buddha said,
“It is obtained.
He addressed the World-Honored One again:
“Is it permissible to maintain the *dhāraṇī* [of the robe] beyond forty nights while traveling outside the boundary?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permissible.”
"One must spend more than half [of the time] residing within the boundary.
As the Blessed One said: "One may maintain [the observance] for one night."
"Against whom should it be performed?
The Buddha said:
"It should be performed against one person; even for up to seven nights, it is always performed against one person."
"If one exceeds this, one should receive it before the Saṃgha.
As the Blessed One has said, "The hide is not pure"; is the meat pure?
The Buddha said:
“If the skin is impure, the flesh is likewise impure; even the sinews and bones are all impure.
The fourth section concludes with a summary verse:
King Bimbisāra’s bed was given as an offering; the property of the king’s mother entered the Saṅgha.
Crows, cranes, vultures, and eagles—monks should not eat [their meat].

At that time, in Rājagṛha, the kingdom of Magadha, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra, having been subverted by his extremely evil advisor Devadatta, unjustly took the life of his father, King Bimbisāra, a righteous and noble monarch.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru was filled with remorse; seeing his father’s bed and seat, his tears flowed freely.
A minister reported, "In the past, the former king had deep faith in the Noble Assembly; he ought to have offered this bed and seat to the Saṃgha."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to deliver his father’s bed to the monastery where the monks resided.
When the bhikṣus had accepted the bed, they spread it out beneath the porch of the gatehouse.
On one occasion, the king went to the monastery and saw his father’s bed beneath the porch; he wept even more bitterly.
At that time, a minister said to him:
"O Noble One!..."
"Your Majesty originally did not wish to see this bed; it was for this specific purpose that we brought it to offer as a gift. Why have you spread it out beneath the gate?
This causes the King to see it once more, increasing his sorrow and tears."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not place the king’s bedding at the entrance.
They then spread it beneath the veranda, where the same faults as before arose; the Buddha said:
"One should not spread it out on the veranda.
He then placed the bed inside the room.
Those who lacked faith then began to criticize and slander him:
"The former king's bed has already been sold by the bhikṣus for food and drink.
The World-Honored One said,
"On the eighth or fifteenth day of the month, it should be spread out under the eaves of the corridor."
Those who lacked faith saw this and slandered him again, saying:
"This is not the bed upon which the former king lay; the monks have already sold the bed on which the king lay and used it together for food and drink."
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is appropriate to clearly write the characters upon the bed; this is the bed bestowed by King Bimbisāra."
As it was with this bed, so too was it with the gifts bestowed by King Prasenajit for his mother; the detailed account is the same as this.
The setting is the same as before.
During the night, hail suddenly fell, causing great harm to birds and beasts. All these people went out at night and carried back home all the various kinds of birds and beasts that were fit to eat.

At that time, the six bhikṣus were by nature fond of eating much and sleeping long; having risen in the early morning, they would gaze in the four directions, and if they saw smoke rising from a house or flocks of birds soaring over a field, they would immediately go to those places to seek food and drink.

At that time, seeing a vulture flying down from the sky, they immediately informed one another and went together to that place; they gathered various dead crows, ravens, egrets, owls, and eagles, and carried them back on their shoulders.
At that time, some brahmins and householders saw him and asked,
"Ācārya, what use have you for these things? He replied:
"I wish to eat. He asked again, "Why do you eat that which is not fit to be eaten?"
He replied, "Since that which ought to be eaten cannot be found when sought, how could one fail to eat from this very thing?
Because he was thus reviled and disparaged, he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus should not eat the flesh of crows, owls, white cranes, eagles, vultures, and similar species; should they eat such, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhaṅga*, Fascicle Six. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhaṅga*, Fascicle Seven.
The Fifth Sub-section, a Summary Verse, states: One should not eat dog meat,
nor the flesh of birds or beasts that feed on corpses.
Nor should one eat animals with cloven hooves, nor should one eat monkeys.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
It was a year of famine, and many laypeople were eating dog meat in great quantities.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the group of six bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food; wherever they went, people all said to them, "Noble ones!..."
"You may go; there is truly not a single thing worthy of being offered as a gift.
Inside the house was a place where food was being prepared, and when the group of six saw it, they asked the people there, "What kind of food is this being cooked in the pot in your house?"
He replied, "Dog meat. He asked:
"Virtuous ones, do you eat dog meat? They replied, "We do."
The group of six replied, "We have gone forth under the patronage of your honors; you should therefore give us a portion of the food you eat.
They then handed it over, and the six bhikṣus accepted the meat and departed.
At that time, having caught the scent of the meat, a pack of dogs gathered around, barking and following along.
When the lay devotees saw this, they said:
"Noble ones!..."
"Why are you being pursued by a pack of dogs?
He replied, "What I am carrying is dog meat."
He asked, "Virtuous one, do you eat dog meat? He replied:
"I am eating. Because of this, he was criticized and disparaged.
He reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Monks, you should not eat dogs, nor owls, nor any birds or beasts that feed on corpses; none of these should be eaten.
Should anyone eat them, they commit an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
The setting was as before.

At that time, there were thieves who stole a superior horse from the stable of King Prasenajit of Kośala. They led it into a dark forest, where they took its life; having severed its head and tail, they carried away the flesh and departed.

The six bhikṣus were by nature gluttonous; at dawn, they looked all around and observed the four directions, seeing from afar that various vultures and crows were flying down from the sky toward a dark forest. Thereupon, they informed one another and went together to that place, where they saw discarded horse-tails, heads, and hooves.
They then said to one another: "Upānanda!..."
"I now have an abundance of refuse-rags," he said, and they proceeded to collect them together.
At that time, the stable-hand arrived following their tracks and asked the group of six: "Where have you been?"
"What you are wearing is the robe of a Great Sage; how can you still commit such evil deeds? He asked, "What have I done?"
He replied, "The noble ones and others stole and killed the horse from the king's stable.
He reported this, saying:
"This was not killed by us; it was stolen by a thief who killed it and took the meat, leaving the head, hooves, and tail on the ground before departing.
We have taken them as discarded refuse."
The horse owner remarked with derision,
"This is truly a desirable piece of discarded refuse.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus, you must not eat any animals with cloven hooves, such as foxes, minks, and their like.
Should anyone eat them, they commit an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).”
At that time, a monkey climbed a branch and leaped far out, suddenly falling to the ground and dying on the spot.
When the group of six saw this, they took it back to their residence and placed it inside a cauldron to cook it themselves.
At that time, there was a woman who had lost her son; following his tracks, she entered the Jeta Grove and saw the six groups of monks boiling that monkey in a large cauldron.
Upon seeing this, the woman beat her breast and cried out: "Alas!
My son is being boiled here!"
At that time, the group of six monks plucked out the hands of a monkey and showed them to the women;
the women cried out, "Alas!
These are the hands of our children!"
Next, he gouged out her feet, whereupon the woman cried out: "Alas!
These are my son's feet!"
Next, she raised up its head, and the woman spoke again: "Alas!
This is my son's head."
He then raised its tail and asked the woman,
"Does your son also have a tail? The woman replied:
"How can you, sirs, eat the flesh of a monkey?
They replied, "If it is not your child, what fault is there in our eating it?"
When the people heard this, they immediately began to criticize and disparage [the monks], and they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!
Since the appearance of a monkey resembles that of a human form, bhikṣus should likewise not eat it."
"If anyone eats it, they shall incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The sixth section, the summary verse, says:
"Small cups, the corners of robes, and faults regarding skins, leaves, and so forth."
"With the exception of iron, you may use other materials as you please.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted by a grave illness and oppressed by suffering; he went to a physician and said:
“O Wise One! Please prescribe for me a medicine that is appropriate.
The physician replied:
"There is a mild medicinal enema that may be used; the illness will be quickly cured.
He said, "O worthy one!"
"The World-Honored One has not yet granted permission.
He replied, "Your Great Master takes compassion as his foundation; there is no doubt that he will grant permission on account of this matter."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When a physician prescribes an enema, you should prepare it as you wish.
They used small cups for the enema and then discarded the medicine. The Buddha said:
"One should not perform the lower pouring with a cup.
He used a corner of his robe [to receive the medicine], and discarded the medicine as before. The Buddha said:
"One should not use a corner of one's robe."
He also poured [the medicine] using a piece of hide and then discarded the medicine again.
The Buddha said, "One should not use a piece of hide. He then wrapped it with leaves. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done; rather, a tube should be made.
He then used iron to make it, heating it until it was hard and rigid. The Buddha said:
"With the exception of iron alone, you may make them as you wish from materials such as lapis lazuli, copper, and so forth."
The seventh chapter, the summary verse, says:
Sugarcane, curd, meat, and sesame; four distinct types of medicine;
hempseed and turnip porridge; and one should eat porridges made from roots and the like.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"May the seven-day medicine also be used as a lifetime medicine?
The Buddha said:

"It is so. Just as with sugarcane: its substance is a *kālābhojana* (food for the appropriate time), its juice is a *yāmika-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for a watch of the night), its sugar is a *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for seven days), and its ash may be used for as long as one lives. Upāli!"

Curd is categorized as a seasonal medicine; fermented grain juice is collected for further use; clarified butter is for seven days; once burnt curd has turned to ash, it is for the duration of one's life.
Upāli! Meat is a seasonal medicine; fat is for seven days; once burnt meat has turned to ash, it is for the duration of one's life, to be taken according to the specific circumstances.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, afflicted by the suffering of illness, went to a physician and asked:
"O worthy one! I am currently beset by illness; please prescribe a remedy for me."
The physician replied, "Venerable One,
you should eat hemp porridge."
The bhikṣu said, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it; how can I eat?
The physician answered as before.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I permit the physician’s prescription for eating sesame porridge; likewise, whether it be the roots, stems, flowers, leaves, or seeds of the turnip, all of which remove wind-related ailments, you should prepare them as porridge and eat them."
The eighth section, summarized in verse, says:
It is permitted to drink molasses syrup; it may be taken as a seven-day medicine.
If one intends to perform five types of service, one should share [the benefit] with others who would assist them.

At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm when he arrived at a certain village. There was a householder there whose karmic conditions from past lives made him one who should be transformed and delivered by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the elder’s time for conversion had arrived, went to his residence.
Thereupon, the elder prepared and spread out a wide and spacious seat for the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One took his seat. The elder, having prostrated at his feet, sat to one side.

Then the World-Honored One, observing the elder’s inclinations, latent tendencies, and the distinctions of his faculties, preached the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden him. By means of the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom, he caused the elder to shatter the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having attained the fruit, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"That which I have now realized was not created by my ancestors or parents, nor by the king, nor by the devas, nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor by friends or kinsmen."
"By relying on the power of the Blessed One, the Great Teacher, he spoke thus at length, until the man took the three refuges and his mind was filled with pure faith.
At that time, as the Blessed One preached the essentials of the Dharma for that householder, the day drew to a close; the Buddha and the great assembly were all left without food.
The householder said to the Buddha,
“I now wish to prepare non-seasonal gruel.
The Buddha said:
"You may do as you wish.
He then went to prepare molasses syrup and other drinks to offer to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus, finding it too sweet, were unable to drink much of it. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Grapes, pomegranates, oranges, citrons, and the like should be crushed by rubbing them with the hands and filtered through a cloth; one should drink them after stirring them so that they are not thick or turbid.
Then the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it permissible to keep molasses syrup for seven days?"
The Buddha said: "It may be obtained.
To what extent should one drink? Until it becomes clear, as long as it has not turned sour and its substance has not changed, you may drink it as you please."
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. A certain householder invited the Venerable Ānanda to his home for a meal.

At that moment, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was afflicted with a serious illness; having heard of this, the World-Honored One went to the householder’s residence with his attendant Ānanda to inquire after his suffering.

At that time, the elder prepared a seat for the Buddha; once the World-Honored One had taken his seat and finished expounding the essential Dharma for the elder, he wished to rise from his seat and depart.
Then the elder entreated the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will have compassion on me and accept my meal now."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Then Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"Previously, an elder had already invited me for a meal."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“One should relinquish a previous invitation to give it to other bhikṣus. There are five matters that are accomplished through mental attention alone: namely, the distribution of robes, the formal possession of robes, the poṣadha ceremony, the pravāraṇā ceremony, and accepting an invitation from a donor.”
The setting was as before.

At that time, it was a year of famine, and it was difficult for the community of bhikṣus to obtain almsfood. There were devout brahmins and householders who invited elder bhikṣus to their homes to eat.
At that time, the bhikṣus accepted only one invitation and declined all others.
The World-Honored One told them:
"In years of scarcity when food and drink are difficult to obtain, you should accept any invitations as they arise."
"After you have eaten yourself, you should all eat together with the other bhikṣus.
Even those who had not been invited went to that house, and the donor said to them:
"Venerable sirs, you are not the people whom I invited."
He then did not give him any food. The World-Honored One said:
"One who has accepted an invitation should first eat two or three mouthfuls as a token of acceptance, and then speak these words:
'Householder!'"
"These bhikṣus find it difficult to obtain alms; I shall divert this food and give it to them.
You may rejoice in this.
Thus, two or three times, whatever food one obtains should be diverted and offered to others, while the last portion should be eaten by oneself until satisfied.
The ninth section, summarized in verse, says:
The physician’s instruction to take ghee, oil, and other residual touches;
as well as the permission to take medicinal compounds; and setting aside ten [types of food] for the clean kitchen.
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣu was afflicted with a serious illness and consulted a physician.
The physician replied:
"You should take ghee; your illness will then be cured.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "The physician’s prescription should be followed as he directs; you should take it accordingly."
At that time, a sick bhikṣu was about to consume ghee during the night, but there was no one to hand it to him. The Buddha said:
"He should take it himself and consume it; if ghee is difficult to obtain, he may consume oil."
Since oil was even more difficult to obtain, its use was consequently discontinued.
At that time, another bhikṣu had some leftover, defiled ghee and oil, and he said:
"I have ghee and oil, but they are leftover and defiled."
"If the Buddha permits it, you should take and consume it.
[The monk] reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For one who is ill and lacks resources, even if it is leftover or touched by others, there is no offense in consuming it."
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the Blessed One has said:
‘You, O bhikṣus, should carry a vessel for holding medicine.’”
As for what was said [in that passage], how is its meaning to be understood?
The Buddha replied:
“With the exception of the four precious substances, all other items may be possessed.”
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī and addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are ten kinds of grounds upon which one should not establish a pure kitchen (kalpi-kutī). They are: an open space, a gateway house, a lower room, the area under a eaves, a warm hall, a bathing chamber, the residence of a government official, the vicinity of a caitya, the home of a non-Buddhist practitioner, the house of a layperson, and within a nunnery."
"If one cooks food [in such a place], in all cases it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one constructs a single room together as a pure kitchen (*kalpiya-kuti*), once the ritual has been performed, does the entire area—above, below, and on the sides—all become pure?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
"If the great assembly collectively grants permission to designate a certain place as a pure kitchen, then everything within its boundaries—above, below, and on all four sides—becomes pure."
The tenth chapter, a summary verse, says:
Roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits—these all should be soaked in mild wine, stirred with water, and consumed; furthermore, other types of food are permitted.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had ordained the sons of the Śākyas, those men were all accustomed to drinking wine; because they had ceased drinking, their complexions became sallow and haggard.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:

"Whatever materials are used for making wine—namely roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth—all should be ground into a powder and wrapped in white cloth. This may then be soaked in a weak, non-intoxicating wine that does not cause intoxication; do not let the vessel be filled to the brim, but seal it with a lid."
Afterwards, pour clear water into it and stir it to drink; alternatively, grind together malt, tree bark, and various fragrant medicinal herbs into a powder, wrap it in cloth, and [place it within].
Tie a staff crosswise and suspend it inside a new jar of freshly brewed wine so that it does not touch the liquor; after one or two nights have passed, stir it with water and use it.
Regarding these two types [of fermented liquids], whether consumed at the proper time or otherwise, there is no offense in drinking them as desired.
In this way, it can cause the thirst for alcohol to cease. You bhikṣus!
Those who take me as their teacher should not drink alcohol; they should not give it, nor take it, nor even place a drop of alcohol on the tip of a blade of grass into their mouths.
“As the Blessed One has said,
‘The bhikṣu Śāṭī should be given different food,’ how should it be given?”
The Buddha said:
"The dung and urine of a newborn calf, along with the ashes of the following trees:
first, the Bodhi tree; second, the *kapittha*; third, the *aśvattha*; fourth, the *udumbara* tree; fifth, the *nyagrodha*, which enters into the earth."
"Mix the soil from four finger-widths below with [the other materials] in one place, stir them together, and use as needed.
[The question was asked: "Who should take [this soil]?
The Buddha said:
"Let those who have faith and respect take it, and let those who have faith and respect give it back.
The summary verse for the second section on specific rules (*mukha-dvāra*) states:
Regarding items designated for a fixed purpose and places with owners, one must inquire about Kosala.
Having been dispatched in advance by the image [of the Buddha], she greatly reduced the assembly of nuns.
The first son’s summary verse says:
One should not move designated items; do not pick up goods left behind by thieves.
The charnel ground is likewise; whatever is permitted should be collected there.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder of great wealth who constructed a dwelling and offered it to the Saṃgha, providing bedding, mats, and various personal requisites, all of which he presented as offerings.
There were some bhikṣus staying there who said to one another:
"Venerable friends!

Since our bedding and requisites are so abundant, we fear they would be greatly damaged if we were to pack them up and move them. We should instead distribute all our surplus belongings to the community of bhikṣus."
They acted according to their deliberation, distributing all remaining goods to the local Saṃgha.
At that time, a wandering bhikṣu who was begging for alms arrived there; the resident monks then relieved him of his fatigue, whereupon the visiting bhikṣu asked:
"Venerable ones!..."
"Is there perhaps any other extra bedding and furniture? He replied,
"There is no surplus here."
The visiting bhikṣus lay uncomfortably upon broken beds throughout the night until dawn, when they took their keys and went to the local monastery’s chief, who was a layman.
Having arrived there, he took his seat and immediately expounded the essential points of the Dharma to the householder, praising the seven types of meritorious actions involving material things.
The householder replied,
"I have already performed these meritorious actions."
The bhikṣu replied, "In your dwelling, bedding and furniture are still lacking; last night I slept on a broken bed and suffered great hardship."
The original owner of the monastery replied, "I have offered many bedding materials and requisites to the community; have the bhikṣus not taken my donated goods elsewhere?"
The bhikṣu asked, "Do you recognize the lock and key? He replied:
"I recognize it.
He then went with the householder to observe it.
Upon arriving at the residence, the householder asked the resident bhikṣus:
"I have offered many bedding materials and requisites to the great assembly; where are they all now?
At that time, the bhikṣus fully answered the donor regarding these matters.
The elder said, "You should bring it here;
I originally intended in my heart to give this dwelling place as a gift.
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take items from this location to give to another residence; rather, one should use them according to their designated place.
If one gives them privately, one must pay the full price."
"If one does not return, one shall incur a grave offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting and circumstances were as before.
The group of six bhikṣus was traveling through the human world together with a caravan of merchants.
At that time, all the traveling merchants were plundered by bandits; however, those bandits did not take all the goods but abandoned some and departed.
Then the six bhikṣus followed behind the bandits, and seeing the abandoned items, they said to one another: "Nanda and Upananda!..."
"How wonderful! These rag-robes are so abundant; let us take them together.
They immediately took the garments.
When the owner arrived and saw the group of six holding the clothes, he rebuked them, saying:

"What I possess, which even thieves did not seize, you, O virtuous one, have stolen again! Venerable sir, wearing the robes of a Great Sage, you have committed this evil deed. He asked, "What have I done?"
He replied, "You have stolen my robe. The bhikṣu said:
“Bandits have robbed you of your robes and abandoned them as they departed; we shall take them, regarding them as ‘refuse rags’ (pāṃśukūla).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should not accept items abandoned by bandits after robbing a caravan. If one takes such items, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).”

Furthermore, there was a caravan leader who had been robbed by bandits; regarding the remainder of his goods that he had not fully carried away, the householders said to him, "Venerable sir, take whatever you please."
The bhikṣu did not take it, and the World-Honored One said:
"If you are permitted to do so, you should take it.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the six bhikṣus went to a cold forest, a place where corpses were left, and there they saw clothes, parasols, and firewood.
They said to one another: "Nanda and Upananda!..."
"There are many discarded objects (pāṃśukūla) that we may take together.
Later, when the caṇḍālas who guard the charnel grounds arrived there, they thought to themselves:
"Who has plundered this cemetery?"
At that time, after seven or eight days had passed, the group of six monks said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda! The cemetery should surely abound with discarded rags; we should go there together to collect those items."
Having arrived there, the caṇḍāla immediately seized him and said,
"Ācārya! All the royal corvée duties are located at the deep maśāna (cremation ground)."
"How is it that you, venerable sirs, have stolen property belonging to others?
He reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You bhikṣus!"
"One must not take clothing, canopies, firewood, or grass from a *śmaśāna* (charnel ground) that is under the control of others.
Should anyone take such things, they commit a grave offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Furthermore, there were those in other places who managed the charnel grounds; having conceived faith and reverence, they said to the bhikṣus:
"Take the robe as you please.
He did not dare to take it and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If he permits it, you should take it as you please."
The second section, summarized in verse, says:
One should not take property belonging to a temple with an owner; a bhikṣu should not [take it], nor should one who is tending to the sick;
one should not urge another to discard their dharma-robes.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The group of six bhikṣus were traveling along a road with a caravan of carts when, suddenly midway, one of the cart axles broke.
At that time, the merchant leader discarded this broken axle and departed, having substituted it with another axle.
The six bhikṣus then took the broken axle and buried it upright at a crossroads, saying to one another:
"This should be named 'The Holy Lord Axle'."
Having established it, he abandoned it and departed.
At that time, there was an elder who made offerings of food as a sacrifice, and other people also made vows there, saying:
"If you can fulfill my requests, I shall build a hall for the World-Honored One."
Together with a company of one hundred and eight Brahmins, they came daily to hold assemblies.
Having made this prayer and attained their desired goal, they immediately constructed a hall and a temple at that site.
At that time, various caravans passing through this place all offered garments, cotton cloth, wool, and other items as gifts to the Celestial Lord.

When the group of six monks returned and saw that temple, they observed it was bustling with merchants and crowded with wagons and horses; there was an abundance of wealth and provisions far exceeding the usual.
They said to one another, "The Celestial Lord of the Axle has an extraordinary abundance of clothing and goods; we should take them now."
At that time, the temple guardian saw him taking the objects and said,
"Venerable One! I am constantly performing repairs here."
"How is it that you gentlemen have taken the cotton garments from a shrine belonging to a deity?
The group of six replied, "You have long been poor and lowly; where could you possibly possess such a celestial temple?"
"This was originally established by us; we broke off this axle to fashion it into a divine image, yet you do not understand its origins and have needlessly developed a sense of possessive attachment.
Then Upānanda struck the axle with his fist and pulled it out with his hand.
The people said, "Whether it was the Venerable One who made them or someone else, we rely on these to sustain our lives; why then should you seize all our clothing and provisions?"
At that time, the lay devotees all raised voices of reproach and suspicion.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One must not arbitrarily take clothing, wealth, cotton, wool, or other such items belonging to a temple dedicated to a deity that has an owner. Should anyone take them, they shall incur a grave offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"There are other celestial shrines from which you may take as you please.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to take anything and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If others have given permission, then you should take it."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu afflicted by the suffering of illness. As the Blessed One had said:
"One should cause a sick bhikṣu to cultivate meritorious deeds within the Saṃgha."
Then the attendant said to the patient,
"You should offer a small gift to the Sangha.
The patient replied:
"I have nothing at all; I should now offer my three robes to you.
At that time, the attendant who was nursing the sick person took the robes and offered them to the Saṃgha. Having accepted them, they sold them and divided the proceeds among themselves.
When a bhikṣu recovered from his illness, he found himself lacking the three robes. He reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"One should not urge a sick bhikṣu to give away his three robes to others; to urge another to relinquish them constitutes an offense against the Dharma."
However, it is not appropriate for the Saṃgha to accept these three robes; even if they were accepted, they should not be distributed, and should be returned upon seeing that they are missing.
If anyone should distribute them, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
The third section, summarized in verse, says:
Regarding objects, one must inquire of the donor; The benefits for the community may be divided equally.
For the two great [divisions], they should be shared equally; For the remaining groups, there should be additions or subtractions.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who provided food for both the community of monks and the community of nuns, and further offered wealth and goods as alms to both communities.
The bhikṣus did not know how they should divide the items.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"You should ask the donor; divide them according to his instructions."
The setting was as before.
At that time, sixty bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a certain village.
There, an elder who had long cherished right faith invited the bhikṣus to his home for a meal.
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"Those bhikṣus each offered me a single robe as a gift.
Before he had finished eating, sixty bhikṣuṇīs came to beg for alms, and the people said to them:
"There are bhikṣus at the house of a certain elder who are currently receiving offerings; you may go there.
The nuns then went to that place and also received their food.
The elder thought to himself:
"I should now distribute these robes by giving them to everyone;
I ought to proceed from the eldest.
At that time, the elder placed sixty pieces of fine cotton cloth before the senior monk (upādhyāya), but the bhikṣus did not know how to divide them among themselves.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is property belonging to the two assemblies; it should be divided equally between them.
The circumstances were the same as before.
There was a householder who prepared a meal for the two assemblies and bestowed material goods as offerings. At that time, the bhikṣus divided these equally with the śrāmaṇeras.
Thereupon, those who were fully ordained (upasaṃpanna) became resentful and said:
"What we require are the three robes, yet those śrāmaṇeras are satisfied with just two garments—a saṃkakṣikā worn over the shoulders and a single lower robe."
"How can I share this with her equally? He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should divide it equally. For śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, one-third should be given; for śikṣamāṇās, one-half should be given; and for those wishing to receive the full ordination, likewise one-half should be given. It should be understood in this way."
The fourth section, summarized in verse, says:
The cotton cloth of Kosala, The Buddha’s son because of eating parched grain,
The case of Śrīgupta, And an extensive discussion on construction matters.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, was traveling through the human settlements of the country of Kośala when he arrived at a certain village.
There, a householder invited the Buddha, the Saṃgha, and their regular followers to his home for a meal.

At that time, sixty bhikṣuṇīs who were traveling through the human realm also arrived at this village; they went from house to house begging for food and reached the house of the elder, where they too were invited to receive a meal.

At that time, after the elder had made offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, he placed one thousand two hundred and fifty pieces of white cotton cloth before the presiding elder; the bhikṣus did not know how they should divide these donated items.
At that time, sixty nuns spoke thus:
"We previously received half of the donated goods; we should now likewise receive half.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus should not divide the alms-offering with bhikṣuṇīs by calculating the number of people so that it is exactly half for each.

Furthermore, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal. When the time arrived and the bhikṣus went to the meal, the World-Honored One alone did not go to the invitation; instead, he sent a messenger to request food and remained within the monastery.
The Buddha has five reasons for not accepting an invitation to a meal, as explained in detail elsewhere; however, he now wished to establish a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for his disciples.

At that time, the householder, out of respect for the elders, served them with *upadaṃśa* (side dishes) accompanied by fresh butter and cakes cooked with butter; to those of middle age, he served cakes cooked with oil; and as for those of lower rank, he gave them oil-cake dregs and vegetables cooked with oil-cake dregs.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula personally took the bowl of food from the World-Honored One and carried it to the Buddha’s presence; having prostrated at His feet, he sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas to greet those who bring food with kind words of inquiry: "Did those bhikṣus obtain fine food?"
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Saṃgha has obtained excellent food and drink; it is most abundant.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Why is your body so emaciated now? Then Rāhula spoke this verse:
"Consuming oil provides strength; ghee brings sufficient radiance."
"With hemp dregs and leafy vegetables, how could one possess physical beauty and strength?
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "I asked you why your body was so emaciated; why did you answer me with matters concerning food?"
Rāhula reported all these matters in detail to the Blessed One, and the Buddha asked:
"Who is the senior elder (sthavira) of the Saṃgha? He replied:
"This is my upādhyāya. The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"Your teacher Śāriputra, this is bad food and cannot be called good food; why do you not observe the food of the middle and lower seats?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish the rules of conduct for the Sthavira of the Saṃgha.
As a Sthavira, upon first seeing the food-distributor approach, he should first instruct [the assembly] to kneel with palms joined and chant 'Three Pātrakaḍas'."
The Elder should then say:
"You may proceed with impartiality.
At that time, when they see the arrival of fine vegetables, cakes, and other such things, if they all speak these words [of partiality], it will result in negligence and failure.
The World-Honored One said:
"When first distributing the salt, you must immediately announce:
'It may be distributed equally.'"
"There is no need for further elaboration.
Should anyone violate what has been prescribed, they shall incur an *āpatti* of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard the Blessed One declare that it was not "proper food," used his finger to pick out and spit out the food he had consumed.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“The food received by Śāriputra was then vomited up.
The Blessed One replied:
"O bhikṣus! It is not only today that I loathed his food and he vomited it up; in a past life as well, I loathed his food and he already spat it out then."
"You should now listen!
In the past, there was a brahmin who was constantly engaged in recitation; he traveled through the human world with a young brahmin boy and arrived at a certain village."
He then set this boy down outside the village by the edge of a pond and said to him:
"Stay here for a short while; I shall enter the village to beg for some parched grain."
The youth then remained there.
At that time, a man of the caṇḍāla caste came to the edge of the pond and sat by the water to eat some parched grain.
When the youth saw him, he said to him:
“O Noble One! You might kindly grant me a small amount of roasted grain.
He then replied to the youth:
"One may sew leaves into a vessel.
He then immediately sewed the leaves.
At that time, the Caṇḍāla gave him some parched grain flour.
At that time, seeing that the flour was moist and oily, the youth immediately asked him,
"Why is this flour so moist and oily? He replied:
"The vessel of oil contained parched grain, and because of this, it has become moist.
At that moment, the youth went to eat the grain.
Then, the brahmin returned from the village and said to the youth:
"You may now enter this village to beg for some parched grain and cakes.
The youth replied, "I have already eaten my parched grain."
He then asked, "Where did you obtain it? He replied:
"It was obtained from a candāla.
The brāhmaṇa said, "This is an impure and wicked person; why did you take flour from him?"
At that time, the brahmin felt contempt and disdain.
Thereupon, the boy immediately spat out the flour.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor any other thoughts; the one who was chanting and reciting as a Brahmin at that time was none other than myself.

Your father has already completed half the work on the monastery when he unfortunately passed away; you should carry out the remaining construction.”
He then said, "Ācārya! The monastery is exceedingly vast and magnificent;
