The Buddha said: "Construct it as small as you wish according to your means.
However, once a stūpa has been built, that which is small may be enlarged, but that which is large must not be reduced."
"If there are laypeople capable of performing great works, it is well; if they are unable to manage it, the bhikṣus should encourage and assist in its construction.
Regarding a stūpa pinnacle that has become old and dilapidated, the Buddha said:

If a clay image of the Buddha becomes damaged or decayed, and a bhikṣu feels hesitant and dares not repair it, the Buddha said:

"Not so," the layman replied. "The Great Master is currently causing a schism in the Saṃgha; no longer following his instructions, they have gathered separately."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs also obtained wealth and profit. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs should not separately form a wheel-like circuit."
"If there is one who acts as an agent in this schism, it is a preparatory act for causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and they shall incur a sthūlātyaya offense.
The Buddha said:

"Whatever material gains are obtained by the community of bhikṣus should also be divided and given to the community of bhikṣuṇīs; he who does not give them shall incur a transgression of the Dharma (dharmātikrama)."
The seventh son’s summary verse says:
One should appoint a person to distribute goods; The Elder should determine the value accordingly.
One must not hastily pay the price, Nor demand a price when returning a robe.
At that time, the business of the great assembly was concluded and much wealth had been acquired. The community of bhikṣus did not know how to dispose of these goods.
The Buddha said:
"You should appoint a distributor of goods; they should be appointed in this manner."
Once the assembly has gathered, one should first ask:
"You, [Name]! Are you able to act as the distributor of robes for the Sangha?"
He replies, "I can. Then,
one bhikṣu should perform the formal procedure (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name], wishes to serve as the distributor of property for the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu [Name] to act as the distributor of property for the assembly."
"Thus it is announced.
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) should be performed according to this announcement.
At that time, the person distributing the robes shall prepare the seating, strike the *gandī* bell, and after making the formal announcement, assemble the Saṃgha to sell the robes obtained.
The bhikṣus did not know who should sell the robe.
The Buddha said:
"The Sāṃghika elder should determine the price of the robe."
At that time, the Elder set the price for the robes too high, and no one else would buy them. The Buddha said:
"When first setting the price for the robes, you should choose a moderate amount; do not let it be too expensive or too cheap, and give it to them immediately upon the initial setting."
The Buddha said, "One should not wait until the price has reached its maximum before giving it.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, seeing others making assessments of the price, increased the value of the robes; when it came time to give them, they spoke as follows:
“I have no need for robes; I wish to increase the price of the robes for the sake of the great assembly.
The Buddha said:
“If the assembly sells robes, those who do not purchase them should not intentionally increase their price.”
"If one intentionally increases the price, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
At that time, the group of six monks obtained robes by increasing the price and immediately put them on.
When they saw [the owners] demanding the full value, they returned the original robes. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear the robe until the price has been paid in full.
If one wears the robe before the price has been paid, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The eighth sub-section is summarized in a verse:
The monastery significantly reduced its storeys; those who would wear [the robes] should use them when fear has subsided, and otherwise follow the *Saṃghāṭī* according to the regulations.
As the World-Honored One said:
"A bhikṣu’s monastery should have five stories; the incense altar should have seven stories, and the gate tower should also have seven stories.
A bhikṣuṇī’s monastery should have three stories; both the incense altar and the gate house should each have five stories."
Because it was so heavy, it subsequently collapsed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The upper story should be removed."
Because it was still falling into ruin, it should gradually be left as it is until it becomes fit to serve as a boundary marker.

After the Blessed One had manifested great supernormal powers, people of faith—even those from remote regions—built monasteries; once the bhikṣus resided there, they were subsequently subjected to fear and alarm.
At that time, all the bhikṣus fled in various directions. Some bandits arrived and seized all their robes and bowls, leaving the bhikṣus without clothing.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The bedding and requisites of the Saṅgha must not be lost; if one must go, they should be taken along."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, seeing that the occasion for fear had arrived, took a saṃghāṭī robe and departed together with the other bhikṣus.
When evening fell, an elder bhikṣu said to him:
"Venerable one, you have a saṃghāṭī robe; as I am advanced in years, it is my turn according to seniority. You should give it to me."
He immediately took it and gave it to him; the other took it and lay down.
When dawn had broken, he said:
"Venerable one!..."
"You may take this robe and go.
The junior monk replied, "If it must be worn,
then it shall follow the custom for senior monks."
“Even if one has not reached the required age, if they possess the necessary fortitude for the practice, they may take this *saṃghāṭī* robe with them.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“Those who wish to take it away should indeed use it.”
Later, when the fear had subsided, the bhikṣu said to him, "This is the property of the Saṃgha; why did you use it alone? He replied:
"Buddhism allows me to enjoy [these things].
The Buddha said,
"In times of fear, I permit you to temporarily use the bedding and furniture belonging to the Saṃgha."
"Since the fear has been dispelled, you should act according to the usual custom.
The ninth son’s summary verse says:
"If there is a great assembly, beat the drum to gather the Sangha."
The assembly was divided into groups for their respective duties; the supervisor first took his meal.
At that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada requested of the World-Honored One:
"I wish to establish a great Dharma assembly in the Jetavana Grove; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The Buddha said, "Now is indeed the right time.

On the day the assembly was convened, the bhikṣus from the six great cities all gathered together; as the multitude was so vast, they consequently missed the proper time for their meal. The Buddha said:
"One should strike the *gandi*.
Although they struck the *gandi*, the assembly was so noisy that it could not be heard. The Buddha said:
"One should beat a large drum."
Upon hearing the sound of the drum, they should assemble at the dining hall; the bhikṣus should then sit in order according to their seniority.
However, while the food was being distributed, before it had reached the end of the line, the sun passed the meridian, and many of the bhikṣus were left without food.
The Buddha said:

"If the assembly is large, one must measure the number and establish separate lines of distribution; food and drink should be placed before each head of the line so that they may be served simultaneously."
However, when laypeople were distributing cakes and fruit, they could not do so with impartiality. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should be appointed to oversee the distribution of the cakes and fruit.

Once he had been appointed, he would accept the items and distribute them, observing carefully to ensure they reached everyone. Yet, this bhikṣu would wait until the assembly had finished eating, thereby missing his own meal. The Buddha said:
"If the overseer takes his portion first from the meal for the fast-day, there is no fault in eating it.
The tenth sub-section, a summary verse, says:
"In the presence of the community of nuns, one should always provide an empty seat."
"Wait for other bhikṣus; do not increase the price out of solitary suffering.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then there were many bhikṣuṇīs who, while traveling through the countryside, arrived at a certain village.
At that time, there was an elder in that village who, with a heart of reverence and faith, invited the community of bhikṣuṇīs to his home for a meal.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā personally served as the presiding elder (upādhyāyī).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who lived on alms; traveling among the people with a caravan of merchants, he arrived at this village and went from door to door begging for food.
Then a villager said to him: "Noble one!..."
"There are several bhikṣuṇīs staying at the house of a householder, receiving his offerings; you may go there now to receive food.
Having heard this, he went to that place, and the bhikṣuṇī said to him:
"Venerable Sir!"
When the assembly has finished eating, one who is able to offer prayers of blessing (*paritta*) and preach the Dharma should occupy the seat of honor.
If one is unable to do so, one may sit to one side and depart once the meal is concluded.
Then that bhikṣu thought to himself with a sigh:
"If I wait until after the meal is finished to preach the Dharma before departing, time will be delayed and I fear I shall miss the caravan."
He then finished his meal at the side of the road and departed, gradually arriving at Śrāvastī.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they said to him, "Welcome!"
Welcome, Venerable One!
Have you been traveling in comfort and well-being?
He replied, "How could there be peace and happiness when one is deeply humiliated by a bhikṣuṇī? He asked:
“What was the intention?
he asked, and they then told him everything in detail.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If there is one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī, that bhikṣu should take the place of honor; he should first receive the water and receive the food. Likewise, whether it be two, three, or even many bhikṣuṇīs, if a single bhikṣu is the leader of the assembly, he should first receive the water and receive the food."

In any place where bhikṣuṇīs eat, one seat must be reserved at the head for the senior-most member; even if a śrāmaṇerī arrives later, she shall take that seat and eat, for she belongs to the higher assembly.
"If it is not done thus, the bhikṣuṇīs will incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

At that time, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had held a great assembly at the Jetavana Grove, he gave away his wife, concubines, sons, and daughters entirely to the Saṃgha; the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should ask the householder.
After they had asked him, the householder replied:
"You should sell it according to its appraised value.
The bhikṣus agreed upon the appraisal.

At that time, the group of six [monks] vied with one another to bid up the price. A certain woman, destitute and suffering, seeing that the price was being raised, became filled with grief and fear, and said to the elder:
“I am solitary and distressed; do not abandon me!
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Women who are solitary and distressed are by nature full of sorrow and fear. You bhikṣus!...”
One should not purchase at an increased price;
if one increases the price, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
One should accept the payment as discussed, in accordance with the donor’s respectful faith and pure intention.
The summary verse for the third section of the Mūlakas states:
Requisites, robes, and ignorance; if appointed, one does not use them as a layperson;
while performing the rite, a gift from a householder; a razor and a stūpa.
Biscuits, curd, leaves for receiving water, And matters such as washing the bowl;
These one thousand and two verses Should be known as summarizing the essentials.
The first sub-section summary verse says:
The thirteen types of requisites are to be formally recorded by name and maintained;
all other surplus robes should be entrusted to others and properly categorized.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling through the human realm when one of them suddenly fell ill; lacking medicine, he subsequently passed away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, I authorize all bhikṣus to keep a robe for the purpose of purchasing medicine."
"If one encounters illness, it may be sold to provide for medicine.
As the Blessed One said:
"I ordain that bhikṣus shall possess robes for the value of medicine."
When the bhikṣus had received [the money], they washed, dyed, and kept it as their own property; subsequently, when they purchased medicine, they could not obtain the full value.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wash or dye clothing intended for the price of medicine."
"One should keep new cotton cloth and retain its fringes.
In the Western lands, one keeps a pair of white cotton cloths; in this region, this corresponds to one bolt of silk. Then the Venerable Upāli said to the Buddha:
"As the Blessed One has said:"
"Regarding the statement that 'the bhikṣus maintain the three robes, yet the World-Honored One has further permitted the keeping of a robe for the value of medicine,' we do not know what this means.
The Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to possess thirteen types of requisites and robes.
The bhikṣus did not know which were these thirteen requisites and robes.

The Buddha said: "First, the saṃghāṭī; second, the uttarāsaṅga; third, the antarvāsaka; fourth, the niṣīdana; fifth, the lower robe (śāṭī); sixth, the secondary lower robe; seventh, the saṃkakṣikā; eighth, the secondary saṃkakṣikā; ninth, the face-cloth; tenth, the body-cloth; eleventh, the wound-covering cloth; twelfth, the shaving-cloth; thirteenth, the medicine-money cloth."
"This is called the thirteen types of requisite robes.
Then the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Blessed One has said:"
"Regarding the statement, 'A bhikṣu should possess thirteen types of requisite robes,' how should one maintain them?
The Buddha said:
"One should formally accept each individual robe by reciting its name separately, speaking as follows before a single bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir, please attend to me!'"
"This saṃghāṭī robe I now formally accept; it has been made into a finished garment and is for my use.
Recite this three times.
Other robes should be formally accepted in accordance with this. For a robe purchased with medicinal funds, one should add: "It is for my use on account of illness."
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Beyond these thirteen robes, there are further garments; I do not know what to do with them.
The Buddha said:
"One should maintain the entrustment with respect to one's preceptor and instructor; it should be distinguished in this manner.
One should speak thus to a single bhikṣu:
'Venerable one, please attend!'"
I, the bhikṣu [Name], possess this extra robe which has not yet been formally designated;
it is appropriate that it be so designated. I now designate it before the Venerable One, entrusting it to my Upādhyāya as the custodian; I now hold it.
Thus it was said three times. The second section, the summary verse, states:
"Those who, out of delusion, do not understand the Tripiṭaka—these twelve individuals;
when they have lost their sanity and returned to their original state, their reproaches should be recorded."
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"How many kinds of persons should not be addressed with reproach or have their words disregarded?
The Buddha said:
“There are twelve kinds of persons. What are the twelve? First, the foolish;

second, the deluded; third, the unclear; fourth, the unskilled; fifth, the shameless; sixth, those with faults; seventh, those dwelling outside the boundaries; eighth, those who have been expelled; ninth, those whose speech lacks coherence; tenth, those who have abandoned their dignified demeanor; eleventh, those who have lost their original nature; and twelfth, those undergoing training.”
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of people should be rebuked?"
The Buddha said: "There are three kinds:
first, abiding in one's original nature; second, speaking with sequential order; and third, not abandoning dignified deportment."
“What is meant by ‘foolish’?
The Buddha said:
“A fool is one who thinks evil thoughts, speaks evil words, performs evil deeds, and speaks of things that are difficult to relinquish.”
“What is delusion? The Buddha said,
“It refers to not upholding the Sūtras, not upholding the Vinaya, and not upholding the Mātṛkās.”
"Lacking clarity" refers to not clearly understanding the textual teachings of the Three Piṭakas.
"Lacking skillfulness" refers to being unskilled in the principles of the Three Piṭakas.
"Lacking a sense of shame" refers to committing any one of the four defeats (*pārājika*).
Regarding the phrase "having flaws or gaps in the precepts," this refers to either newly engaging in strife or having existing enmity.
Regarding the phrase "outside the boundary," this refers to those residing outside the boundary.

Regarding the term "abandoned," this refers to the Saṃgha performing an act of abandonment by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
To speak "without sequence" means to engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
To "abandon dignified deportment" means to leave one's original seat.
To "lose one's fundamental nature" means to perform improper actions and to lack knowledge of how to practice the various rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).

"Regarding the term 'one who undergoes training' (śikṣādattaka), this refers to a person who has committed a grave offense but does not conceal it; the community performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to grant them the status of one undergoing training.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When a person who has lost their original nature is subjected to the *karma* of censure (*pravrājana-karman*), there is no need to take their objections into account; if they object, the censure is not valid."
"If this person were to return to their original nature, would they be subject to censure?
The Buddha said, "They would be subject to censure."
The third section, summarized in verse, says:
If twelve persons are appointed, this speech constitutes a formal reprimand;
If, at the time of receiving [the precepts], one says, "I am a layperson," this does not constitute full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Blessed One has said:
'If, while the formal ritual (karmavācanā) is being performed for a person, that person is permitted to voice an objection.'"
Regarding those who say, "The assembly has appointed twelve kinds of persons to speak these words:
'Venerable sirs, you should not appoint me,' should these words be recorded?"
The Buddha said:
"Both must be recorded.
As for my statement that 'words do not constitute a formal censure,' I made that remark based on the time when I administer disciplinary measures according to the actual conduct."
“World-Honored One!
Suppose, at the time of receiving full ordination, that person says of themselves: ‘I am a layperson.’”
"Can this person successfully receive full ordination?

The Buddha said, "If one has already received full ordination and then declares oneself to be a layperson, one still loses that ordination; how much more so when it is at the very time of receiving it!"
All of these cases are based on the premise that one possesses a mind when relinquishing the precepts.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka*, Scroll Eight; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka*, Scroll Nine.
The Fourth Section, the Summary Verse, states:
Do not use the five kinds of fat; Explain the precepts according to the circumstances.
Because Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa opened the way for the rice gruel, the King’s fields should be accepted by the Saṅgha.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
As the World-Honored One had said:

Regarding the statement, "There are five kinds of impure leather footwear that should not be worn," at that time the group of six bhikṣus used five kinds of impure fats and ointments to smear their leather footwear.
At that time, King Prasenajit’s elephant, smelling the odor of fat, became terrified and bolted away;
thereupon the group of six monks said, "Why do you not seize this elephant?"
He replied, "I cannot uphold it. The bhikṣu said:
"I can hold it for you. "If you gentlemen can hold it for me, I shall now pay you the price of the cakes and fruit.
At that moment, the six members of the group moved downwind, and the elephant immediately stopped; the men then reported this.
“Venerable sirs! Do you understand the vidyā-mantras?
We were unable to restrain the herd of elephants as they fled in terror; how did you manage to make the elephants stop?”
The group of six replied, "We truly do not understand how to recite or maintain vidyā-mantras; we merely used elephant fat to smear upon our leather sandals.
"Noble ones! [he said.]
"If the King's fine elephant has been injured, is it not because you, O virtuous ones, have performed an unbeneficial act?
Thus they were filled with mutual disdain and contempt.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"O Bhikṣus! You should not use the fat or grease of a superior elephant to smear upon leather footwear; whoever does so incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
As it is with a superior elephant, so it is with superior horses, lions, tigers, leopards, and the like—it is entirely improper."
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
King Bimbisāra went to the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, and said: "Venerable Ānanda!..."
"Is this not indeed the day for hearing the Dharma, and furthermore, the time for the *poṣadha*?
May I hear it? He replied, "Great King!"
"You should know that the *poṣadha* is an activity to be performed collectively by the bhikṣus; it is not appropriate for laypeople to attend.
The king then rose and departed.
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing [the situation] yet asked Ānanda:
"Why did the king come and depart immediately without listening to the Dharma?
He then answered in full.
The Buddha said:

"You have committed a great error; had the King been made to hear this Prātimokṣa earlier, he would certainly have conceived even greater faith and reverence. Having given rise to pure faith, he would have become the foremost among those who possess it."
"Therefore, I now permit you to preach this to kings, ministers, and others who possess pure faith and the aspiration to hear it.
The Buddha said, "Furthermore,
even if there is someone who is noble and honorable yet lacks respectful faith, you should still preach it to such a person."
"If there is a poor person, one should also preach for them; however, if they are both impoverished and lack respectful faith or the desire to hear the precepts, one should not preach for them.
At that time, the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.

The Venerable said that the bhikṣu Koṇāgamana-Śatakoṭi had been nourished on gruel since childhood; after he went forth, however, he no longer obtained gruel, and his body became emaciated, jaundiced, and weak.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"For what reason do you say that the body of Koṇāgamana, the Buddha of Twenty Koṭis, was extremely withered, pale, emaciated, and devoid of strength?"
Then Ānanda informed the Buddha of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣu Piṇḍola Bharadvāja to eat gruel at his own discretion."
Then Ānanda, transmitting the Buddha’s instruction, said to those bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One has permitted you to eat gruel at your own convenience. They then replied:
"Is this addressed to the great assembly as a whole,
or to me alone? He replied:
"Only you alone," he said to Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja,
"because of this cause and condition, my fellow practitioners of the holy life have ridiculed me."

"You say that Koṇāgamana, having now gone forth, has gained much; yet formerly in Campā he was peerlessly wealthy, renouncing seven elephant-kings to become a monastic, and even at this present time he seeks nothing more than thin gruel."
“World-Honored One, if you would grant permission for the great assembly to eat gruel on my account, I too shall partake.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Now, because I have spoken with Koṇāgamana as the foremost, I permit the entire great assembly to eat gruel.”
At that time, many brahmins and lay devotees of pure faith brought excellent gruel as offerings to the bhikṣus.
When King Bimbisāra heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to eat gruel at their pleasure, he offered a thousand acres of fertile land to the Great Assembly.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept fields, and they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"For the sake of the Saṃgha, you should accept fields; the fruits and produce harvested there shall be used by the community."
The fifth section, summarized in verse, says:
Laypeople and novices, etc., must never sit together;
if there is a reason for difficulty, those under training may stay in the same place without fault.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. The Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One:
"Is it appropriate for bhikṣus to sit on the same mat as laypeople?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted. However, if there are unavoidable circumstances, sitting together with them constitutes no offense."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May I sit on the same seat as a śrāmaṇera?
The Buddha said:
"It is not appropriate.

If one gives [alms] to a minor, a paṇḍaka, one who has defiled a bhikṣuṇī, one who has committed the five ānantarya crimes, a follower of an external path, one who has gone over to an external path, one who dwells as a thief, one who dwells separately, or one with whom communal residence is not shared—these also are not permitted to sit on the same seat."
"If there are unavoidable circumstances, sitting on the same seat with them is not an offense.
He asked again:
"Is it permissible to sit on the same mat with one who is under training (śikṣamāṇā)?"
The Buddha said: "It should not be so.
However, if there are unavoidable circumstances, you may sit together as you wish."
“May one sit together with a layperson on a single wooden bed?
The Buddha said, “It should not.”
If there are unavoidable circumstances, one may sit together with them at will.

This applies even to those with whom one does not share a common residence; in all such cases, it is improper to sit together except when there are unavoidable circumstances, in which case sitting together is not an offense.
If one sits on the same bed, it is explained at length as before; however, if one uses a folded woolen rug or mat as a screen, there is no offense in sitting [with them].
The sixth sub-section, summarized in verse, says:
"While [the other] is acting, do not make them rise; sit according to seniority; and [use] a dyeing basin."
"You should all protect the monastery grounds; do not burn timber intended for construction.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣus were sitting on small stools, performing tasks such as washing, dyeing, sewing robes, and repairing their alms bowls.
At that time, the six bhikṣus pushed up from their own seats, causing others to be interrupted.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"When a bhikṣu is engaged in such tasks as washing or dyeing, one should not cause him to rise; he who causes another to rise incurs a duṣkṛta offense."

Wherever the six groups of bhikṣus went, they relied upon their status as senior elders to push others aside and force them to rise. When those bhikṣus refused to rise, they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should sit according to the order of seniority and in accordance with one's rank."
As the Blessed One said,
"One should sit according to seniority," yet when the group of six bhikṣus saw others eating, they arrived after them and caused those others to rise.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If that bhikṣu is in the midst of eating, the elder who arrives later shall not require him to rise."
"If one causes another to rise, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); one may sit and eat in any place.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Blessed One has said:..."
"One should not cause a bhikṣu who is eating his proper meal to rise.
[The question was asked: "To what extent is it called 'mealtime'?
The Buddha said:
"Even down to receiving salt or receiving food leaves, it is in all cases improper to rise.
As the Blessed One said:
"A bhikṣu should not rise while receiving food."
Regarding the phrase "the six groups of bhikṣus," because they went toward the place where the senior monks were seated, they received food first.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not go first to sit at the head of the senior monks in order to receive food; whoever does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
"All bhikṣus should be well-acquainted with the order of seating.
Regarding the jars for storing dye and various basins belonging to the Saṃgha, one bhikṣu first took a robe to dye it, whereupon the group of six bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"Venerable one!..."
"I am older, so it is right that I should use it first.
He poured out the dye and forcibly took it for his own use, causing the other bhikṣu’s affairs to be left unfinished and neglected.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"However, regarding the vessels and dyeing basins used by the Saṃgha for boiling and dyeing, one must not forcibly seize them while another is currently using them; they should only be taken once the task is finished.
Anyone who takes them before this is completed incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing)."
As the Blessed One said:
"When a dye-vessel is soiled, it should not be taken up.

At that time, the group of six [monks] would stain the vessel with the dye-liquid as soon as they had dyed a small piece of cloth; intending to keep the vessel for themselves, they obstructed others from using it. The Buddha said:

"If it is only when the entire garment is dyed within that it is called 'stained,' one should not create an obstacle by retaining even a small portion; anyone who violates this incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense."
The setting was as before.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada constructed a wooden fence to enclose the Jeta Grove.
Some laypeople then broke down the wooden fence and stole the wood and grass. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Have them guarded. Once they had been made to guard [the wood] and had abandoned it and fled, no one gathered it, and it all rotted away.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those pieces that are ruined and useless may be brought to the monastic kitchen to serve as firewood; the remainder that is still usable should be taken and given to the laborers.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, regarding whatever wood was suitable for their construction work, all broke and burned it to use for boiling and dyeing.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu must not burn the materials for construction; one must use various types of wood.
Should anyone violate this, they shall incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
The seventh chapter, summarized in verse, says:
Regarding the goods offered by a householder, one should inquire and then set them aside;
do not neglect others' belongings wherever they may be, and only after washing one's body should one enter the monastery.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"If the Buddha would grant me permission, I now wish to offer the Jeta Grove once again to the Saṃgha."
The Buddha told the householder,
"Do as you wish. Thereupon,
the householder adorned all the trees within the Jeta Grove that had male voices with the garments and ornaments of men.
Regarding the "women's voice trees," they were fashioned in the attire of women and elaborately adorned.

Having likewise decorated the monastery courtyard, the walking paths, the gatehouses, the interior of the bathhouse, the communal dining hall, the infirmary, and the regular refectory, he then offered them all to the Saṃgha.
At that time, the bhikṣus received these robes but did not know what to do with them.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, who said:
"You should ask the householder."
Having gone there and asked, the householder replied,
"The object should belong to whoever it was given to.
The Buddha said:
“The trees that produced the voices of men and women, and even all the clothing throughout the monastery, were each placed in chests and boxes and stored away according to their respective locations.
If, at a later time, a great assembly is held within the Jeta Grove, they shall again be arranged and decorated in those same places as before.”
That which is on the walls should be used for painting the walls.
If it is in the warming hall, one should purchase firewood to provide fuel for heating.
That which is in the bathhouse is for the purpose of bathing; that which is in the water-storage hall is for the use of the community.
Regarding the use of drinks for proper or improper times: if they are kept in the infirmary, they should be provided as a fine meal for offerings.

However, if they are located near the monastery courtyard, or in front of a pavilion or eaves, or at a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), or near the entrance, they should be divided among the *saṃgha* present there.
"If it is within the courtyard of the monastery, it belongs for the use of the Saṃgha of the four directions.
At that time, the bhikṣus constructed a meditation hall for severing delusions and practicing dhyāna, wherein they cultivated various wholesome qualities.
At that time, the group of six monks came to this hall and called out to others, saying,
"I am the senior [monk].
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not act according to seniority in this regard, nor cause other bhikṣus to rise up abruptly.
Should anyone cause them to rise, they shall all incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

At that time, the bhikṣus rose from their seats and went away for a short while to walk in meditation; the group of six [monks] then came and sat in their places, causing others to interrupt their affairs. The Buddha said:

"One should not sit down hastily upon another's seat. When you, bhikṣus, wish to practice walking meditation (caṅkrama), you should first leave a mark at the sitting place using a decorative sash or a saṃkakṣikā, and only then proceed with the walking meditation."

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was beating his leather shoes against the pillars of the cloisters and courtyards. Another bhikṣu, seeing this, felt disdain and shame, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I shall now establish the rules for the proper conduct of those traveling on the path."

Whenever bhikṣus are traveling on a road and wish to enter a monastery, they should go to any place where there is water. Having set down their robes and bowls and shaken out their garments, they should next bathe their bodies, down to their hands and feet, washing away dust and grime. They should then refill the water jar with clean water, wipe their leather sandals with a coarse cloth, and finally put on their robes. With a composed and dignified demeanor, they should enter the monastery walking slowly.
The eighth section, summarized in verse, says:
Razors and tweezers, once used, should not be kept;
When the business of defecation or urination is finished, It is not appropriate to remain inside the dwelling.
As the Blessed One said:
"Razors and tweezers should be kept as personal requisites.

The group of six bhikṣus took the razor and tweezers belonging to the Saṃgha for themselves; once they had finished shaving their hair, others took them and did not return them, to which [the group of six] replied:
"I shall need it again at a later time.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, once you have finished using a communal knife, you should not leave it behind."
"Just as with knives, it should be understood that the same applies to stone tweezers, small knives, and footrests.
After the six bhikṣus had entered the restroom and finished their business, they remained inside the room. When others wished to enter, they intentionally blocked them, saying: "Do not enter!"
"I shall go later to urinate again.
Thus, he troubled others and caused them to feel resentment and shame.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"If one has finished urinating, one should not remain there for long; if one stays longer, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. Likewise, if one intentionally causes annoyance to others at the place for defecation, one incurs an offense as well."
The ninth section, summarized in verse, says:
Circumambulating the stūpas, extensively displaying the various holy sites;
drinking turbid water as appropriate, and discerning it if it is salty.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to provide adornments for the stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata; if the Buddha permits, I shall construct it."
The Buddha told the householder,
"Do as you wish. The householder did not know how to proceed.
The Buddha said:

"From the time he descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born in Jambudvīpa, through his guidance of sentient beings until his parinirvāṇa, you should construct the sites of his previous lives and sacred traces as you wish."
At that time, as the bhikṣus were traveling along the road, they encountered turbid water and, suspecting it, did not drink it. The Buddha said:
"If one’s reflection can be seen in the water, it may be used for drinking; if the reflection cannot be seen, it must be given to you by someone else to drink.
If the water is extremely turbid, you should take *kataka* fruit or grape fruit and throw them into it until it clears, or you may put flour into the water."
The bhikṣus then threw scattered flour [into the water], whereupon the Buddha said, "One should instead form it into balls with water and throw them in.
At that time, there was salt water which caused some to doubt and refrain from drinking; the Buddha said:
"If it is fit for use as salt, accept it and then drink;
if it is not fit, take it yourself and drink, without harboring any doubt.
The tenth sub-section concludes with this summary verse:
Rice, curd, and the like are not defiling, and may likewise be poured into a jar;
as for the five types of jars used for washing the feet, to what extent can they be called "pure for the mouth"?
When receiving a stream of water with leaves or the hands, there is much doubt regarding its flowing into the bowl.
Carrying provisions while crossing a river, even if touched by others, does not constitute an offense.
When washing the bowl, one should be mindful; if touched by another, one must inquire before accepting it.
Regarding the exchanging of food, carrying provisions, and so forth, these are all prohibited unless there is no difficulty.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There were some brahmins and householders who, not far from Jetavana Grove, held a banquet within a fragrant garden; they had discarded various leftover foods into a well.
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to obtain water for use; they filtered it through a strainer, and within the water-strainer they saw grains of rice.
The bhikṣus became doubtful and did not use it.
Furthermore, they also harbored doubts regarding water jars used for storage and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It does not become impure by that circumstance alone.
If it is filtered, it becomes pure; you should not discard the water."
Furthermore, while the bhikṣus were drawing water from a pond, they saw someone washing vessels for ghee and jars for curd.
Another bhikṣu was also washing an oily bowl there with his hands; the grease floated upon the water, drifting and bobbing, while the dregs from the curd jar sank down piece by piece.
At that time, the bhikṣu, being doubtful, did not dare to use it; he reported the matter to the Buddha, who said:
"It was not he who could have made the water impure. Since it has been filtered, it is pure; there is no offense in using it."

At that time, as the bhikṣus were traveling along the road, water was extremely difficult to find. Upon reaching a waterwheel where they wished to take some water, they suspected it was impure; because of this lack of water, they suffered extreme exhaustion and distress before finally entering the monastery.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You may take the water; first you should examine it, rinse your mouth, and then drink as you please."
"Or if one does not dare to drink it even at improper times, the Buddha said:
'One may drink it even at improper times.
However, one should not store it in a bottle. The Buddha said: [One may do so.]
"It should be stored.

At that time, as the bhikṣus were traveling on a road, they found no water available. Fearing that the spring water from a crumbling cliff might be unsafe, they dared not drink it and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"You should observe it and then drink."
Or, fearing it might be the improper time, they did not dare to drink; the Buddha said, "It should be drunk at the improper time.
They did not dare to refill the flask; the Buddha said:
"It should be added.
At that time, the bhikṣus saw the muddy floodwaters and, fearing it was impure, did not dare to drink.
The Buddha said, "Even if the water is turbid, you may observe it and drink as you please."
Or if one does not dare to drink even at improper times, the Buddha said:
"There is no offense in drinking and using [the water] whether at the proper time or the improper time; there is likewise no offense in adding it to the water jar for storage."
While traveling on the road, he saw a leather bag containing water with some fragments of curd inside; suspecting it might be impure, he did not dare to drink it.
The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"Whether it is the proper time or not, you may drink and use it as you please."
"O bhikṣus, those things which I have permitted during times of emergency must all be prohibited when there is no such emergency.
Should you continue to use them, you will all incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a cowherd settlement. Unable to find water, they used buttermilk to wash their feet; however, having developed doubts about its propriety, they did not use it.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In places where there is no water, if you are given buttermilk, you should use it to wash your feet.
Thereupon, they went again to the cowherds' quarters and borrowed vessels and containers, intending to fetch water.
A bhikṣu borrowed a vessel for ghee or oil; fearing it was improper, he did not dare to use it, and thus his needs were left unmet.
The Buddha said:

"You bhikṣus should know that there are five kinds of vessels: [the one used by householders, the one used by renunciants, the one used for both, the one used for medicine, and the one used for food]."
First is the vessel for excrement, second is the vessel for urine, third is the vessel for wine, fourth is the oil jar, and fifth is the butter jar.
The first three vessels should not be used to store other substances; should they ever be so used, the contents must be discarded at a distance.

The latter two jars should be purified by burning with fire, or by scrubbing with saline soil, or by washing with cow dung; once thus purified, they may be used to store water and may be used for drinking at any time, whether during the proper hour or otherwise, as one pleases.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who drank a non-timely beverage; a greasy odor then emerged from his throat, and he felt remorse. The World-Honored One said to him:
"First wash your hands thoroughly, then rinse your mouth and lips; only after rinsing your mouth may you drink the beverage."
As the Blessed One said,
"Rinse the mouth clean," the bhikṣus then used salt earth to rub their lips, which caused them to become chapped and cracked. The Buddha said,
"One should use cow dung to wash the mouth and lips clean."
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said,
‘The mouth should be purified,’ to what extent is it called purified?”
The Buddha said:
"How could a mouth that is stained by defilement ever be made free of stain?
One should crush it with clean cow dung or rub the lips with soap mixed with water to remove the oily odor of food."
Furthermore, one should rinse the mouth two or three times with two or three handfuls of water; this is what is called purification.
Whenever any bhikṣu drinks or eats, whether at the proper time or otherwise, he should do so in this manner before consuming anything.
"If it were otherwise, every sip and swallow would constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, during the improper time (*akāla*), took a vessel in his hand and poured water toward his mouth; an ant had previously entered the vessel and, upon emerging, stung him.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not drink water by pouring it directly from a vessel into the mouth. First, wash your hands thoroughly and rinse your mouth cleanly; only then should you pour the water from the vessel and drink while supporting it with your hand."
Furthermore, a bhikṣu should make a container for holding water-jars (*kuṇḍikā*). At that time, he did not know with what material it should be made.
The Buddha said:
"One should use wooden boards or bricks and stones to place the water jar so that insects do not enter."
As the Blessed One said:
"First rinse your hands and then drink water.
When traveling on the road, if there is only a small amount of water, the Buddha said:
"You may drink from within the leaves.
Seeing that there were no green leaves for anyone to pluck and offer, the Buddha said,
"Take fallen, withered, yellow leaves yourself and drink the water."

At times, when fallen leaves could not be found even after searching, they would take water in their hands against the branches to drink; at other times, when leaves still attached to their stalks were even more difficult to obtain, the Buddha said:
"One should go to a secluded place, rinse one's mouth thoroughly, and then pour water from a vessel into the mouth to drink as desired."
The details regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited have been explained extensively as before.

At that time, the Venerable Kṣemavatī harbored doubts whenever he encountered anything; for this reason, people of the time came to call him "The Doubting Kṣemavatī. Seeing the water from his jar pouring down, he thought to himself:
"Others pour water in a continuous stream into their bowls; is this not an act of impure contact?"
He then refused to accept it.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"All flowing substances naturally move downward and cannot flow upward; these should be used, and you must not harbor doubts or suspicions. In doing so, there is no offense."
"In the same way, milk, curd, fermented grain-drink, and so forth, should be understood according to this principle.
...乃至佛言： "Do not give rise to doubt."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling along a road with a caravan of merchants. He had some śrāmaṇeras carry his provisions for the journey while he followed behind. When they paused and were about to depart, the śrāmaṇeras said to the bhikṣu, "Please hold these up for us."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to lift it up. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should lift it up for them.
They replied again:
"Please hold it down for me.
The bhikṣu felt doubtful and did not hold it down for him. The Buddha said:
"You should hold it down for him."
Later, as the śrāmaṇera was carrying his provisions along the road, he became exhausted from the heavy burden and said to the bhikṣu:
"Please carry this for me for a moment while I rest."
The bhikṣu was unwilling to do so, whereupon the Buddha said:
"You may tie it with a cord and have a śrāmaṇera hold the cord; you may carry it for him to allow him a moment's rest.
Later, he became doubtful.
"I shall untie it with my own hands.
He then did not dare to eat it. The Buddha said, "Eating it is entirely without offense."

At that time, the bhikṣus traveled along the same route as a caravan of merchants. Suddenly, they were plundered by bandits who seized the merchants' goods; the śrāmaṇeras abandoned their provisions and fled, and the bhikṣus likewise abandoned the road provisions and departed.
At a later time, he said to the śrāmaṇera,
"You should now go and fetch those provisions for the journey.
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"Are you now wishing for the bandits to kill me?
I cannot go; you may take it yourself.
The bhikṣu, having become suspicious, also did not go to fetch it; as his provisions for the journey were exhausted, he was consequently unable to proceed on his way.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should take it yourself.
Having brought it back himself, he felt doubt and did not eat it. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One may eat it without offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a śrāmaṇera carry provisions for the journey as they wished to cross a river; not knowing what to do, he asked the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should ask the śrāmaṇera:
'Can you carry my provisions and cross [the river] yourself?
If he replies:"
"I can only cross by myself; I have no strength to carry provisions.
The bhikṣu should assist him in carrying [the provisions] across the river.
If the śrāmaṇera says:
"If one lacks the strength to cross oneself, how can one have leisure to carry provisions?
A bhikṣu may do well if he is able to carry both that śrāmaṇera and the provisions for the journey;
if not, he should first ferry the provisions across and then carry the śrāmaṇera.
At that time, the bhikṣus became doubtful and did not eat. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should eat; there is no offense.
As the World-Honored One has said:
“Bhikṣus should eat from their alms bowls.
A certain bhikṣu, while washing his bowl, noticed a crack and feared he had committed an offense. The Buddha said:
“You should wash it thoroughly two or three times with care; even if there is a crack, there is no offense.”

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, while washing his bowl, saw grains of rice in its crevices. Suspecting that they were unfit for consumption, he informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"You should remove them with a blade of grass or a stalk, rinse the bowl three times with water, and then use it as you please."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who used an old, seasoned bowl to hold hot liquid; as he did so, a greasy film emerged, floated to the surface, and congealed. Feeling doubtful, he did not eat it.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should remove the grease on top; it is fit to be eaten."

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, having washed his bowl, set it aside in one place; when he washed and used it again on the third day, it subsequently broke. He then became suspicious, thinking, "The bowl has not been fired properly."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Wash it and you may eat.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, having returned from begging for alms, set down his bowl and went out; another bhikṣu, also returning from begging for alms, immediately placed his own bowl upon that bowl.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they became suspicious and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If there is someone to serve the food, one should receive it before eating;
however, if there is no one present, one may take the best portion for oneself, and eating in this way does not constitute an offense."
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has returned from begging for alms and sets down his bowl before going out, if a layperson comes along and happens to touch it, he should ask:
"Do you have any expectation regarding this food?"
If one says: "I saw a fly, or I saw a blade of grass or a leaf, and I brushed it away," then one may accept and eat [the food]. If one says:
"One who has the expectation that this food will be touched [by another] should divide it and receive it before eating. At that time,
there was a bhikṣu who, having returned from begging for alms, placed his bowl in one spot.
Furthermore, there was a śrāmaṇera who arrived after [the bhikṣus] had finished begging for alms; he then took the rice from his own bowl and placed it into the bowls of the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus became suspicious and consequently refrained from eating. The Buddha said:
"The area where the rice has been placed in the bowl should be cleared away extensively; you may eat as you please."
As the Blessed One has said:
"Whenever bhikṣus travel on a journey, they should carry provisions.
Since there were neither laypeople nor śrāmaṇeras present, the Buddha said:
"One should encourage the donor to give.
If there is no donor, one should take it oneself; later, upon seeing a layperson, one may exchange it with them for food.
If there is no one to exchange it with, divide it into two portions and say to the layperson:"
"Take one portion," he said.
Once it was in his hand, he should say to him:
"Take my food and take my portion; let us exchange them and eat."
"This, moreover, is difficult to obtain. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"On the first day, one must abstain from food; if it reaches the next day, one may receive and eat it if someone offers it."
If there is no one to give [alms], one may take for oneself a portion the size of a closed fist and eat it.
On the third day, if again there is no one to give, one may eat two fistfuls.
On the fourth day, if once more there is no one to give, one may take as much as desired to eat until satisfied; in doing so, there is no offense.
Later, when their provisions for the journey were exhausted, they saw ripe fruit fallen on the ground. The Buddha said:
"You should take it, perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), receive it, and then eat it.
If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) is difficult to find, you should eat it even if you have not performed the ritual of purification or received it."
"There is also no one to give it," [the monks said]. The Buddha said:
"You should take it yourself; maintain the thought that you are in Uttarakuru and eat it.
Regarding fruit on a tree that has ripened but not yet fallen to the ground, the Buddha said:
"You should climb a tree and shake it so that [the fruit] falls, then take and eat it yourselves.
O Bhikṣus! As for the aforementioned permissions, they are all granted on account of difficult circumstances."
"If there is no occasion of difficulty, all such acts must be strictly prohibited and severed.
Should anyone violate this, they shall all incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The summary verse for the fourth section of the *Mūlakalpa* states:
Sharing fields is improper; giving while naked or while fixed on an object;
[the rules on] monastic robes, names, and returning; sugarcane, fruit, and the *saṃkakṣikā* (side-covering garment).
The summary verse of the first section says:
Sharing fields and assisting one another, / Taking boats and carts as they please;
/ The crow-beaked fly has no shame, / Yet the *caitya* truly possesses few desires.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Bimbisāra bestowed a thousand mu of land upon the Saṃgha; although the bhikṣus constantly consumed its produce, they neglected it and did not look after it, until the fertile fields were eventually overrun with weeds and rushes.
At that time, King Kṛkin, while out on a journey, saw this and asked:
"Whose field is this where both grass and reeds grow together?
The minister replied:
"This was a thousand-acre field that the Great King offered as a gift to the Saṅgha; they harvested the grain from it but did not use it for repairs, and because of this, it has fallen into ruin.
The King said, "How could the Saṅgha not have distributed portions to others?"
He replied, "I will not give it.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should share it with laypeople according to their respective portions.
At that time, the bhikṣus gave all their field crops to the cultivators and did not take a portion for themselves. The Buddha said:
"One should take a portion in accordance with the laws of the king."
They then took their respective portions.
However, once the laborers had received their shares, they abandoned the grain and departed.
The Buddha said, "You should transport the rice and bring it into the monastery."
At that time, the laborers first took their own portions and afterwards took the portion belonging to the monastery. The Buddha said:
"First take the portion belonging to the monastery; only then take your own portion.
Although they brought it later, thieves still stole it. The Buddha said:
"You must guard it and not allow thieves or robbers to seize it.
When transporting it inside, they loaded only the portion for the Saṃgha; as the cart was about to overturn, they called out to the bhikṣus, wishing them to provide assistance.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw this monastic carriage, they did not dare to touch it.
The Buddha said, "You should assist one another.
A sick bhikṣu was traveling along the road, and the charioteer addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"Noble One, you may ride in this carriage.
The bhikṣu felt doubt and did not dare to ride; the Buddha said:
"Simply avoid the carriage shafts; you may ride away without committing an offense.
Furthermore, he transported his goods by boat, but when the boat ran aground in shallow water, the boatman said:
"Noble One!..."
"I pray that you will assist me in pushing this boat.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to assist him with the monastic boat. The Buddha said, "You should indeed push it."
At that time, the bhikṣus traveled by land and became extremely exhausted; then the boatman said to the bhikṣus, "You may come aboard the ship together."
At that time, the bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to board the boat.
The Buddha said, "Except for the area where the rudder is located, you may board the boat as you please.
On another occasion, when they were carrying their portions on a shoulder-pole and wished to rest for a moment, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I wish to rest for a moment and come here to set down my load.
The bhikṣu felt doubtful and did not dare to set it down for him. The Buddha said:
"You should set it down for him."
Furthermore, there was a porter who, becoming exhausted along the way, wished to rest and said to the bhikṣus, "Lift my burden for me for a moment so that I may relieve my fatigue.
Those bhikṣus hesitated and did not lift it. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Having tied the load with a rope and made him hold the rope, only then should you lift the load.
Alternatively, if he were to abandon the load halfway and flee, and a thief were to come and take the load away, the Buddha said:
"You should carry it yourself and proceed."
The bhikṣus did not know whom to send to take it away.
The Buddha said:
"One should send a layperson; if there is no such person, one may have a śrāmaṇera do so; if there is no such person either, the bhikṣu himself should collect it."
The bhikṣus, being doubtful, did not dare to eat because it had been touched by their own hands.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should eat; there is no offense."

Since many fires were lit beneath the large cauldrons and pots of the Saṃgha, the butter and curd boiled over and spilled outside. Fearing that they might be wasted or discarded if there were no *karmadāna* (attendant), the Buddha said:
"At such a time, one should not allow the *karmadāna* to leave. If there is a pressing reason that necessitates his going outside, the bhikṣu should immediately remove the firewood."
If the boiling does not cease, you should stir it with a ladle.
When decocting medicine, if the liquid boils over, you should understand that the procedure is similar to this. You bhikṣus!
"What has been permitted by me due to difficult circumstances must be prohibited during times when no such difficulties exist.
Should any practitioner [violate this], they shall all incur an *āpatti-duṣkṛta*. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*, Fascicle Nine.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhaṣika, Volume Ten,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree;
the remainder of the first summary verse.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A great number of merchants invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to a grove where they prepared a grand feast; the merchants held up the food and stood in a line before the assembly.
While the merchants were traveling, a fire suddenly broke out; having seen it, they abandoned their food and fled.
It was then midday, and as there was no one to offer them food, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I do not know what to do."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"Those donors have already formed the intention to relinquish [the food]. You should take it for yourselves and eat it, regarding it as if it were from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru); you should not harbor any doubt."
At that time, a crow came to the side of the kitchen and pecked at the food. The bhikṣus, being doubtful, did not dare to eat it. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you remove the beak-like marks on all four sides before eating, there is no fault."
While the bhikṣu had not yet eaten, a crow came again and pecked at him; suspecting this as well, he did not dare to eat. He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you discard the food from around the beak's edge and then eat, there is no offense."
At that time, the Venerable Kṣepāvatī entered the latrine room and saw various flies feeding on filth; they then flew toward the kitchen and defiled the food and drink. He said to the bhikṣus:
"I just now saw these flies in the latrine, and they have flown back here to defile the rice and food."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they all refused to eat it. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"As for flying insects, whether they land on a clean place or an unclean one does not make them impure; you should eat them."

A bhikṣu, while dyeing his robes, saw several household vessels containing ghee and oil; thinking they were dye-jars, he lifted them with his hand. Upon examining them and realizing his mistake, he cast them away. The Buddha said:
"If one carries [a vessel] up to the upper story and has not yet reached halfway, one must set it down on the ground."
"If it exceeds half-full, you should lift it up and place it on a level spot.
Because he did not examine the jar carefully, it tilted and spilled the oil. The Buddha said:
"You should support it with an object so that it does not lean or tip over."
At that time, because the bhikṣu had previously touched it, he became doubtful and did not eat. The Buddha said:
"This is pure; you should eat it.
Generally, there are two kinds of cases where bhikṣus are free from the fault of having touched [food]:”
First, one is touched by a person lacking shame and remorse; second, one is touched by a person possessing shame and remorse who did not do so intentionally.
Because this person possessing shame and remorse acted through a lapse of mindfulness, both cases are pure and unoffensive.

There were many bhikṣus traveling through the four directions on pilgrimage to sacred sites (caityas). At that time, brāhmaṇas and householders entrusted to those bhikṣus various ointments, incense, powdered incense, flower garlands, and cotton cloths to be offered at the sacred sites.
When a bhikṣu encountered circumstances that did not accord with his expectations, he gave rise to a doubt,
wondering, "What should be done with this object?
The bhikṣus then reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The four great caityas are their fixed locations:
first, the place of birth; second, the place of attaining perfect enlightenment; third, the place of turning the wheel of Dharma; and fourth, the place of entering parinirvāṇa."
If the donor’s original intention was to offer [the gift] to other caityas, this does not contradict these four locations.
However, if there are obstructing conditions regarding these four, then these four may mutually communicate with one another, but it should not be [offered] to other places.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"There are two bhikṣus who have fallen into mutual estrangement and slander one another with various discordant words. Between these two, which one is to be trusted?"
"Who should not be trusted?
The Buddha said:

"One who trusts those who uphold the precepts should trust both when they uphold the precepts; one who trusts those who are learned should trust both when they are learned; one who trusts those with few desires should trust both when they have few desires, and one who trusts those with extremely few desires [should trust both when they have extremely few desires]."
“Both are extremely free from desire; whom should one believe?
The Buddha said, “It is impossible that two who are both extremely free from desire would give rise to discord, using various different words to slander and revile one another.”
The second section, summarized in verse, says:
One should not allow those who dwell as thieves, eunuchs, and so forth,
nor even those under training, to cast voting sticks to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Then the Venerable Upāli requested the Blessed One, saying:
"If one who dwells as a thief (a person living in a state of schism) is made to cast a voting tally (*śalākā*), does this constitute a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“It is not accomplished.
[The questioner asked: “If one uses the five kinds of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs) up to those who are living apart (*pṛthag-vāsī*) as the counters for voting, does it constitute a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“It is not accomplished.
“If one who has committed the four pārājika offenses were to cast the voting tally (*śalākā*), would this constitute a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“It is not accomplished.
“If one uses a person under training (śikṣamāṇa) to cast the voting sticks (śalākā), does this constitute a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“It is not established.
The third section, summarized in verse, says:
Not to go naked while wearing robes; not to enter the kitchen while facing the rain.
"It is appropriate to patch and mend; by applying mud, merit increases for a long time.
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group lay down upon the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha while naked, stretching out their limbs and trampling it until it was crushed.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not sleep naked upon the communal bedding; one who sleeps naked shall incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
"Whatever bedding cloths belong to the Saṃgha should be protected with a cover, or one should take a five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭhina*) and use it with careful observation, enjoying it slowly.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus wore the Saṃgha’s bedding cloths while walking about in exposed areas; they were soaked by the rain and consequently damaged.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wear a monastic robe or cloak while walking about in the open air during rain. If one does so, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus took the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha and went into the kitchen, where it was damaged by smoke.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not take the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha and go into the kitchen; if one uses it for such a purpose, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who entered the room for defecation and urination while wearing his monastic bedding. A bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not enter the chamber for defecation and urination wearing the monastic bedding used for lying down; one who wears it there incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."

At that time, the bhikṣus saw that the bedding and robes belonging to the Saṃgha were being torn and damaged, so they discarded them together. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not discard them; if a robe is about to tear, you should sew it with long threads to reinforce it."

If a hole is seen, it should be patched; if it is rotted on the inside, two layers of cloth should be folded together. If it is completely decayed and beyond repair, one should make it into a lamp wick, or else chop it into pieces, mix it with cow dung to make mud, and use it to fill the holes in pillars or to plaster walls.
When used in this manner, it causes the field of merit offered by the donor to increase spontaneously.
If the three robes are torn or worn out, the procedure is the same as this.
The fourth section is summarized in a verse:
Regarding the giving of fixed items, one must not consume them elsewhere;
if anyone should take them away, they must be returned at their value.
[This was spoken when] the Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was an elder who constructed a monastery, providing it with all necessary requisites in full abundance.

The elder then invited other bhikṣus to serve as administrators of this monastery. However, these bhikṣus had many disciples residing in other monasteries, who came to this monastery in order to pay their respects and visit them.
At that time, the preceptor said to his disciples:
"The elder who built this monastery has invited me to serve as its overseer; you all should wait until after the meal is finished before departing."
The disciple said to his teacher:
"Upādhyāya! If there is surely food, please give some to me to take away so that we may eat together there."
He replied, "As you wish.

They then took the rice, or brought oil for lamps, or carried leather sandals; some held garments and canopies, while others carried firewood, roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs—all of which they took away until, before long, all their provisions were exhausted.
At that time, the other bhikṣus in this monastery all went to the house of the donor who had built the monastery and spoke these words:
"Do you know, O Householder?
All the requisites currently within your monastery are now lacking."
At that time, the elder replied:
"There are not many bhikṣus residing within the monastery; how can you say that the monastic requisites have all been exhausted in such a short time?"
Then the bhikṣus related the preceding circumstances in detail to the donor.
The elder said, "How could I give them to those bhikṣus from the other monastery?
The elder felt resentment and displeasure.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"A bhikṣu should not dwell in another location, nor should he take the food of this monastery to another place; furthermore, he should not use the property of this monastery to provide for another location."

Regarding rice, oil for lamps, and even flowers and fruits, if it was the donor’s original intention that these were provided solely for those residing at this specific monastery and not for others, then anyone who comes to eat from them must be compensated for the value of the items consumed.
The fifth section, summarized in verse, says:
One should inscribe the donor’s name on the Sangha’s robes; Private gifts should be marked as such;
Rugs are permitted for private use; And nuns should repair them during the rainy season retreat.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

There were two brothers who had both gone forth into the religious life. One of them was a supervising bhikṣu who wore the saṃghāṭī robe; he then entrusted his communal robe to his brother, the bhikṣu, and departed for another place.

The younger brother-monk took his own outer robe and went to his elder brother; he placed his robe next to the master’s robe, and later, when departing, he mistakenly took the communal robe, thinking it was his own, and put it on before leaving.
Later, when the overseer arrived and saw that there were extra robes, he said:
"Venerable one! The Saṃgha has now obtained a great abundance of material goods."
He replied, "I cannot. He asked:
"Whose robe is this? He replied,
"It is your monastic robe."
He replied, "My cloak is wide and large, while this garment is narrow and small; surely someone else must have come here and taken my clothes. If anyone comes, I shall go now to ask them."
Having arrived there, he saw a monastic robe and asked for its origin.
The man replied, "I did not bring this cloak intentionally; if it is a monastic robe, you may take it with you."
The bhikṣus had doubts and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One should mark the robes of the Saṃgha as a sign.
The bhikṣus did not know how to make the mark.
The World-Honored One said:

"If these are communal items, they should be inscribed with characters, stating: 'This is the robe of the donor so-and-so. If it is the robe of an individual, it should be marked as private property."
At that time, there were those who brought woven multicolored carpets and small leather cushions to offer to the Saṃgha. The Buddha said:
"I permit this for the Great Assembly, and I also allow it for individuals."
Furthermore, many people offered large beds with lathe-turned legs to the Saṃgha. The World-Honored One declared:
"The Saṃgha may accept and keep them, but individuals should not."
As the Blessed One has said:
"A bhikṣuṇī who is observing the summer retreat is permitted to travel among the people for a valid reason.
Yet, they do not perform repairs at their residence and all depart together, whereupon the dwelling subsequently falls into ruin.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The dwelling places of the bhikṣuṇīs must be repaired during the rainy season retreat; if they do not do so, they shall all incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
The sixth section is summarized in a verse:
If one returns clothing or goods, One should accept them when they are sent back;
When taking another's property for the sake of the community, One must repay the value with communal funds.

At that time, there was a layperson whose relatives had passed away; having escorted their remains to the charnel ground, he took back the banners and cotton cloths and offered them as a gift to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not accept it and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This shroud for carrying a corpse should indeed be accepted.
At that time, a poor man came again to borrow one; the Buddha said:
"If a poor person comes to borrow something, you should lend it to them for a short time.
When that person returned the item with a sense of hesitation, the bhikṣus were unwilling to accept it. The Buddha said:
"When it is brought back, you should accept it."
At that time, there was a supervising bhikṣu who, for the sake of the Saṃgha, had borrowed much wealth from laypeople; before long, he passed away.
When the laypeople heard that the bhikṣu had died, they came in haste to demand and inquire: "Where is the bhikṣu so-and-so now?"
He replied, "He has already died.
He borrowed a great deal of wealth from me."
The bhikṣu replied,
"You may go to the charnel ground and seek it there.
The layperson replied:
"He acted for the sake of the community and not for private reasons; you should therefore return the value of my debt.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it is known that a bhikṣu acted for the sake of the Saṃgha, one should use communal property to repay the prior price."
I shall now establish the rules of conduct for those bhikṣus who oversee construction work.

Any bhikṣu acting as a supervisor of construction must first inform all the senior monks within the monastery before lending out persons; he must either provide a written contract or ensure that clear guarantees are established.
If a monk engaged in construction does not follow the prescribed rules, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in every case.
The seventh sub-section is summarized in verse as follows:
"Sugar cane and other such items shall be divided equally; one should not divide them for personal consumption."
The four matters that do not admit of sharing: bedding and seats may not be used at night.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Saṃgha obtained a great quantity of sugarcane. As the Blessed One had said:
"Śrāmaṇeras and others should be given one-third.
At that time, the bhikṣus divided the sugarcane into three parts and gave one part [to him]. Then, the long-walker sat with his head bowed, until he reached the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was at the very end of the procession, eating sugarcane while gazing up at the Blessed One’s countenance.
Having seen him, the Blessed One said: “Rāhula!
“Did you eat sugarcane? He replied, “I have.”
The Buddha asked,
"Do you still have any further expectations? He replied:
"Yes," he replied. The Buddha asked,
