"How much have you obtained?"
He replied, "I have obtained the third portion.
The World-Honored One said:
"I spoke these words based on the benefit of robes, not out of a desire for food or drink; therefore, I now establish this rule for all bhikṣus:
if there is any benefit from food, even as small as a single leaf, it must be divided equally among all."
"If one does not divide it equally, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Therefore, having obtained much sugarcane, as the Blessed One said:
"Do not divide up the profit from food."
The bhikṣus became doubtful; even when they obtained fresh roots, fruits, and sugarcane, they did not dare to share them. The Buddha said:
"They should be shared," and so on, as explained at length.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a layperson who constructed a dwelling place; all the bhikṣus residing in this monastery were provided with food and drink by that donor.
At that time, the bhikṣus deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Venerable friends!
It is not food and drink that we find difficult."

"However, we currently lack *cīvara* robes; it would be appropriate to sell this sum of money for food together to procure clothing, while each of us goes separately to beg for alms to satisfy our hunger."
Having deliberated thus, not a single bhikṣu went to the house of the donor to receive food.
When the donors saw the bhikṣus during their alms-round, they asked:
"Noble ones!..."
"I provide food for you all every day; for what reason do you trouble yourselves by going out to beg?
He related the circumstances in full to the donor, and the elder replied, "How could it be right for you to divide the portion intended for your own mouths among the entire assembly?"
Consequently, they felt resentment and shame.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of things that should not be divided."

What are the four? First, the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions; second, the property of a stūpa; third, medicine provided by lay families for the sick; and fourth, food and drink for one's own body.
"If there are those who share in this [fault], they shall all incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six monks was traveling through the human world; only when the sun had set and the stars appeared did they enter the monastery.
Then, as the other bhikṣus relieved their fatigue according to their respective friends, the group of six addressed the people, saying:
"Venerable ones!
Have you truly accepted the Blessed One’s teaching with such complacency as to allow it to perish?
Those who possess a sense of shame and integrity should distribute the bedding and furniture according to seniority."
Then the bhikṣus distributed the bedding according to the order of seniority. Once they had received it, each lay down to sleep; before they had even reached the end of their journey, dawn broke.
The group of six replied, "Venerable ones!
Pack away your bedding; we wish to set out on our journey."
The people said, "For what reason do you, sirs,
seek only one night’s rest for your own comfort, causing our great multitude to undergo such extreme hardship?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Whenever any bhikṣus arrive at a monastery at dusk, they must not cause others to be assigned bedding for the night by force; one who so forces them commits an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
The eighth sub-section, summarized in verse, says:
“Fruit offered by yakṣas must be purified before one may eat it.”
The remainder was used for drinks; they did not burn lamps on the ground or on lamp-stands.
At that time, the Blessed One, while traveling among the people of the land of Caṇḍāla, arrived at the village of Rohitaka and stayed there in the temple of the yakṣa Mahābala.
At that time, the yakṣa came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my humble invitation to stay overnight in this temple."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his silent consent.

Having seen that the World-Honored One had consented, the yakṣa then manifested five hundred rooms, fully equipped with beds, mattresses, pillows, bolsters, and square rugs; there were also five hundred braziers, each filled with glowing coals and entirely devoid of smoke or flame.
At that time, after the yakṣa deity had first offered the superior chamber to the World-Honored One, he further divided the remaining chambers among each of the individual bhikṣus.
Then the yakṣa deity came to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"I further pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my humble offering in this temple tomorrow."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
This yakṣa deity had an old friend named Daṭṭhika, a great yakṣa in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to inform his friends and relatives, saying:
"I have now invited the Buddha and the Sangha; tomorrow I shall provide them with offerings at my home.
There are particularly many fruits and delicacies from the north; I hope you will graciously join me in rejoicing and assist in accomplishing this merit."

When that yakṣa had thus received the instruction with faith, he immediately filled baskets with grapes, pomegranates, sweet oranges, sugarcane, walnuts, *kapittha* fruits, and so forth, and commanded other yakṣas to deliver them to the courtyard for him to offer as an oblation.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to the Buddha,
"We do not know what this northern fruit is.
The Buddha said:
"One should consume it only after purifying it with fire.
At that time, the bhikṣus each purified their portions individually. The Buddha said:
"They should be gathered into a single heap; one need only purify three or four places with fire, and eating them will not constitute an offense."
When the distribution to the assembly was completed and there were still leftovers, the Buddha said:
"They should be crushed and made into non-time gruel (vikāla-pāna), which may be drunk as one pleases.
When there were yet more leftovers, the Buddha said:
“Having boiled [the liquid], store it in jars; you shall drink it on another day.
During the cold months, a bhikṣu lit fires here and there upon the brick floor, causing the bricks to be damaged. The Buddha said:
“One must not light fires indiscriminately upon a brick floor; one should instead use a tile to support the fire.”
There was still damage from smoke. The Buddha said, "One should construct a brazier.
Because it was made inside the room, it was again ruined by smoke. The Buddha said:
[The monks] prepared it outside the door;
as the smoke dispersed, it still stung their eyes. The Buddha said:
"Wait until the smoke has subsided, then sprinkle it lightly with water before bringing it into the room."
At that time, the Saṃgha obtained a single-tiered lamp-stand. The Buddha said:
"Its possession is permitted; it is also allowed for individuals.
Subsequently, they obtained two-tiered and multi-tiered lamp-stands. The Buddha said:
"All may listen and keep [the precepts]; even if an individual keeps them, there is no offense.
The ninth section, the summary verse, says:
"Guests and residents should examine matters thoroughly; when giving and receiving, let the handover be clear and distinct."
The five openings should all be closed; the short elbow-length [robe] may be worn according to one's body.
At that time, many visiting bhikṣus came into the monastery; after the resident bhikṣus had relieved them of their fatigue, the visitors then stole [the robes] and departed.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who have known each other for a long time should provide relief; however, do not attempt to dispel the fatigue of those with whom you have no prior acquaintance."
As the Blessed One said:
"Do not relieve the fatigue of one whom you do not know.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was already acquainted with another; having had him rest, a second bhikṣu who did not previously know him suddenly arrived behind him. While the first bhikṣu went out briefly on some business, the latter, who had come later, stole his robes and bowl.
At that time, the resident bhikṣu thought to himself,
"This must be his companion," and so he did not stop him;
the thief then took [the goods] and departed with them.
When the bhikṣu arrived and saw that his robes and bowl were missing, he said to the host,
"Who has taken my robes and bowl?
The host replied:
"Take your companion with you.
He replied, "I have no companion."
The host said to him,
"Is not he who drove you here your companion? He then replied:
"You have lost my robe; you must return it to me immediately.
Since he had already lost it, [the monk] was consequently deprived of his garment.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whenever a host sees a guest arrive, he should first ask him:
'Are you his companion? If he requests the robe and bowl, shall they be given to him?'"
If one says, "Do not give it," yet proceeds to give it, one should pay back its price.
If one says,
"I give it," then the obligation to repay it is forfeited.
Next, another guest bhikṣu arrived; after the host had relieved his fatigue, yet another bhikṣu who was an acquaintance also came to him.
At that time, the host briefly went outside to chew his tooth-stick, and a later-arriving person stole his robes and bowl. The newly arrived bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This must surely be the owner of this room."
Because he had not previously restrained them, they were eventually stolen away.
At that time, the former resident returned after a short while; seeing that the robes and bowl were missing, he asked the guest, "Who has taken my robes and bowl?"
He replied, “The former occupant of this room took his belongings with him when he left.
He reported this, saying:
"How could there be an old resident in this room?
You have lost my robe; you must urgently pay its price.
Since he had already lost it, the matter was consequently abandoned and settled.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whenever a visiting bhikṣu enters another's room, he should ask the host:
'If someone comes seeking a robe or a bowl, may I give them one?'"
If one says, "Do not give it," yet gives it anyway,
one must calculate its value and pay the price.
If one says,
"I shall give it," then there is no need for compensation for what was lost.
At that time, a visiting bhikṣu entrusted his robe to a resident bhikṣu; encountering circumstances that required him to depart, he said to his host:
"If a junior bhikṣu arrives, you should give this robe to him."
Not long thereafter, a junior bhikṣu arrived and, upon receiving the entrusted robe, immediately stole it.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"If a visiting bhikṣu entrusts [an item] to someone, even if it is subsequently stolen, he should not be made to reimburse it; however, one must clearly provide a written record or proof before giving it."
He then gave the instructions in a public manner; when bystanders heard this, they came under false pretenses to demand the goods, and because of this, he lost his wealth. The Buddha said:
"One should rather give the explanation and the signs in a secluded place, clearly distinguishing and demonstrating the nature of the deposited object, and only then give him the robe."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling along a road who, upon reaching a river crossing, boarded a boat intending to depart.
He said to his companion, "Hand me the robe-bag."
He then handed it over; however, as the handover was not firm, the robe fell into the water.
The bhikṣu said, "Give me back my robe-bag!"
He, however, would not submit.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not release [the animal] prematurely; if it is released before the price has been received, one must pay the price."

There was one who passed a bowl-carrying bag to another person; it fell from his hands and landed in the water. Having lost the bowl-bag, he demanded compensation from that person. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"As long as you have not yet received [the payment], you should not release the bag. If you intentionally release it, you must pay for its value."
The temple keeper had his property stolen by a thief, and the community deliberated together, ordering the keeper to compensate for the lost items.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said: "You should know this!
There are five distinct ways in which the person in charge of affairs closes the monastery gate:

namely, by turning the upper and lower bolts, the ringing lock, the secondary lock, the door-bolt, and the latch. If these are not closed and a thief steals property, compensation shall be paid according to the facts of the case. If one of these is missing, one portion must be repaid; if they are all absent, the full value must be reimbursed.
"If the temple manager maintains a mind of protection and none of these five deficiencies exist, even if a loss should occur, he should not be required to compensate.
Then Upāli said to the Buddha: "As the World-Honored One has said:"

"Regarding the rule that all bhikṣus should take the cubit as the measure for making robes: if there are those whose arms are short but whose bodies are tall, should they also make their robes according to the cubit measurement?"
The Buddha said: "One should rely on the measurement of the body; one should not rely on the cubit.
The summary verse for the tenth section says:
The lower robe and the *saṃkakṣikā*; washing clothes soiled with fragrant mud;
taking food and removing the excess; one must know these ten kinds of dust.
At that time, the monks' lower robes were stained with oil, which caused them to become foul-smelling.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should keep a spare lower garment.
This continued until [the case of] the saṃkakṣikā; when sweat stained it, the moisture also flowed through and soaked the great robe (saṃghāṭī). The Buddha said:
"One should keep a spare *saṃkakṣikā*.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were performing a great offering, their robes were stained and ruined by fragrant mud, powdered incense, and oils. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If powdered incense damages them, one must shake them out before putting them on; if they are soiled by fragrant mud, one should wash them before wearing them."
"If it becomes stained with oil, one should wash away the grease using soap powder, ash, or similar substances, and only then should one put it on.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were receiving food, before they had even received it, it fell to the ground; they should receive the food again. If there is no one to give it to them, they should take it up themselves, remove the majority [of the fallen portion], and only then eat it.
Soup broth fell into the separate liquid within [the bowl], and the Buddha said:
"One should pour most of it away; the remainder should be eaten.
Later, when the bhikṣus went out to beg for alms, wind and rain suddenly arrived and dust fell into their bowls; they became doubtful and did not eat.
Furthermore, while eating, dust entered the bowl. The Buddha said, "You bhikṣus, there are five kinds of dust.
What are the five? They are: dust from the feet, dust from the head, dust from the body, dust from food, and dust from water."
First, tangible objects; second, non-tangible objects; third, pure objects; fourth, impure objects; fifth, minute particles.
Among these, if a tangible object adheres to a garment, it may be washed away.
If food falls into the bowl, one must remove it before eating.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of dust:
first, the dust of food; second, the dust of drink; third, the dust of clothing; fourth, the dust of flowers; and fifth, the dust of fruit.
"Of these various foods, those visible to the eye may be eaten after being received; those not visible may be eaten at will.
— *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka*, Fascicle Ten.
